entry.title: Follow the Hops and Reassemble the Symbols | Hopscotch | GaianSpace CTF 2026
entry.content:
🌐 中文版：繁體中文

Seventh and final post in the series. Over the previous six posts the LoRa demodulator grew from single-frequency, fixed-parameter all the way to implicit header, different-SF-per-packet, and drift correction. Here the satellite does one last thing: it hops across multiple frequencies (FHSS), and the demodulator has to reassemble the symbols, scattered across different frequencies, back into time order before it can decode.

Rest of the series: Channel Hop、True Color Is a Lie、Isodata Seven、Subsidy Claim、Two Voices、No Name on the Door

What the challenge is about

The stranger has switched GAIAN-723’s downlink into a frequency-hopping mode, changing frequency every few symbols to shake off a recorder stuck on a single frequency. David opens the SDR’s bandwidth to the max and records the whole thing.

Goal: decode the contents of this hopping downlink and pull out the flag. The files given are a wideband .sigmf-data and the ground-station notes.

Flag format: GAIANSPACE{...}

First, spot that it’s hopping

Make a wideband waterfall of the whole segment and you can see at a glance that the signal doesn’t stay on one frequency. It hops regularly between a few frequency slots. That’s FHSS (frequency-hopping spread spectrum):

Measure it: the carrier switches among a fixed set of channels, each dwell is roughly a fixed number of symbols, then it jumps to the next channel.

The LoRa modulation parameters (SF, BW) are the same in every dwell; only the centre frequency changes.

Reassemble the hop sequence

The solution has two layers:

  1. Estimate the hopping plan. Run an FFT over each time window to find the dominant frequency, giving you a time → frequency sequence. The channel set is a fixed handful of values, the dwell time is fixed, and the hop order is periodic (pseudo-random but repeating). Organize it into a hop table:

  2. Follow the hops and stitch the symbols together. For each dwell, bring the signal back to baseband (multiply by exp(-j2πf·t) to move that channel to 0), decode that segment’s symbols with the same demodulator from the earlier posts, then join all the dwells’ symbols end to end in time order to recover the full symbol stream.

The trap here is the dwell boundary: there’s a short transition at the instant of a hop, so drop half a symbol at each end of a dwell and align each dwell’s symbol phase, so they don’t misalign when joined. After alignment, the whole symbol stream decodes through the standard pipeline (Gray → de-interleave → de-whiten XOR), and the packet ends with a CRC that checks out.

Flag

The decoded downlink carries the flag directly:

Takeaways

  1. The first step of FHSS is always “estimate the hopping plan.” A wideband waterfall plus a per-window FFT for the dominant frequency lets you plot “time → channel”; hopping is usually a periodic pseudo-random sequence, and once you spot the period the whole table is fixed.
  2. Hopping just scatters the symbols across frequencies; the decoding core is unchanged. After bringing each dwell back to baseband, it’s still the same LoRa demodulator, which is exactly why the earlier posts spent the effort getting the skeleton solid.
  3. Watch the dwell boundaries. There’s a transition at the moment of a hop, so leave a little margin at each end and align the phase before joining, or the symbols misalign at the seams.
  4. By this point, the LoRa demodulator hand-built since True Color Is a Lie can handle everything thrown at it: two transmitters, implicit headers, a different SF per packet, Doppler drift, and frequency hopping. One demodulator, seven challenges. That’s the most satisfying part of this whole series.

entry.title: High SF, Dragged Down by Drift | No Name on the Door | GaianSpace CTF 2026
entry.content:
🌐 中文版：繁體中文

Sixth post in the series. In the previous post, Two Voices, the satellite was still using a standard SF9. Here the stranger has changed its downlink config into implicit header + a different SF per packet, and because high-SF symbols are long, Doppler/clock drift makes the decode start going wrong partway through. This is the post where the demodulator is finally forced to add drift correction.

Rest of the series: Channel Hop、True Color Is a Lie、Isodata Seven、Subsidy Claim、Hopscotch

What the challenge is about

01:40. The stranger is still talking to GAIAN-723, and the satellite responds every few minutes, but every response uses a voice the ground-station modem “refuses to listen to.” GAIAN-723 has changed how it speaks: packets no longer mark their length, and every packet sounds slightly different from the last. The ground-station log has a line at 01:31: DL CFG CHANGED BY TC — NOT FROM MOC.

Goal: find the CO₂ reading GAIAN-723 reported when it acknowledged the stranger’s command at 01:37, and how long it says it’s been awake.

Flag format: GAIANSPACE{[CO2 in ppm]_[uptime in seconds]}.

Every packet has a different SF

The log shows the downlink config was changed by a telecommand at 01:31, after which “the header is gone and the length is unknown”, i.e. an implicit header.

This recording is a fresh segment after the 01:36 roll-over, starting at 01:36:45, so 01:37 is after the 15-second mark in the recording.

Measuring per-band energy, I find 8 satellite packets, then search the preamble peaks over SF 7–12, and it turns out every packet has a different SF (SF7, 8, 9, 10 in rotation), which should be what the challenge means by “each one sounds slightly different”:

Start (s)LengthSF
7.500.84 s10
13.070.57 s8
34.880.84 s10
………

The stranger’s commands are short, strong pulses (SF7, BW250k). Recording start 01:36:45 + 34.65 s ≈ 01:37:19, so the satellite packet closest after that command (34.88 s, SF10) is the ACK the challenge wants.

Drift correction for high SF

The hardest packet here is SF10. The bigger the SF (Spreading Factor), the longer each symbol. An SF10 symbol takes 4096 samples (SF7 is only 512), so the longer a symbol drags on, the more deadly the following problem becomes.

What is drift? The satellite flies overhead at several kilometres per second, so the frequencies on each end keep shifting due to the Doppler effect (like an ambulance’s pitch changing as it passes). Add the clock error of each side’s quartz oscillator, and the signal’s frequency isn’t off by a fixed amount. It slides slowly the whole time. The longer a symbol, the more it slides within a single packet.

How does that hurt decoding? Recall the demodulation skeleton: after dechirping each symbol you get an FFT peak, and whichever integer bin the peak lands in is the symbol’s value.

But drift makes the peak not land exactly on an integer bin. It carries a fraction (e.g. bin 100.2, 100.35, 100.5…), and that fractional part grows steadily over time.

I measured it drifting from −0.2 slowly to −0.5, then flipping to +0.5.

At first, off by 0.2, rounding still lands in the right bin; but as it approaches 0.5, rounding jumps to the wrong bin, so the first half of the packet decodes correctly and the second half turns to garbage right around CO2=. That’s why “a single fixed offset collapses partway through.”

So first confirm the problem is purely drift: this ACK packet’s spectrogram is a clean chirp, with no frequency hop or interference midway:

The fix is three steps:

  1. Extract each symbol peak’s fractional part and line them up over time into a curve;
  2. Because the fraction “wraps around” when it crosses ±0.5, use np.unwrap to stitch those jumps into a continuous curve;
  3. Fit it with a quadratic polynomial (drift is smooth, so quadratic is enough), then subtract that fitted curve from each symbol’s bin, and the peaks settle back onto integer bins.

The left panel shows the symbol peaks’ drift (blue dots) and the quadratic fit (red line); the right panel shows the timeline of packets and commands:

With the drift subtracted, the whole packet decodes cleanly. This packet also ends with a CRC-16 (*18FC), which I recomputed with CCITT parameters and matched exactly, a stamp of approval on “decoded correctly.”

Result

The challenge wants CO₂ and UP (uptime in seconds): CO2=432, UP=132. There’s a trap here: the ACK at 01:36:52 is almost identical (CO2=424,UP=105), and the only way to tell them apart is by time, so you have to convert the recording’s start into real time to land on the 01:37 one. The two UP values differ by 27 seconds, matching the gap between the two responses, which cross-checks nicely.

Flag

Takeaways

  1. “Every packet is different” usually means SF or BW is hopping. Do an independent parameter search per packet; don’t assume the previous packet’s parameters carry over.
  2. An implicit header has no length and no CR: infer the length from the symbol count on the air, and pick the CR by “which one decodes clean text or passes CRC.” First few bytes matching but the rest garbled is often a CR or drift issue, not a wrong overall direction.
  3. High-SF symbols are long and very sensitive to drift. Plot the trend of the symbol peaks’ fractional part and the drift is obvious; correct it with unwrap + polynomial fit.
  4. Two identical-looking ACKs can only be told apart by time. Convert the recording’s start to real UTC first, then match the moment the challenge states, so you don’t grab the wrong one. In the next post, Hopscotch, the satellite goes one step further: it hops across multiple frequencies (FHSS), and the demodulator has to reassemble the hop sequence before it can decode.

entry.title: A Downlink Hijacked in the Dead of Night | Two Voices | GaianSpace CTF 2026
entry.content:
🌐 中文版：繁體中文

Fifth post in the series, and the storyline shifts to “the night shift”: GaianSpace Mission Control’s GAIAN-723 satellite has been hijacked. The first four posts (the farm arc) got the LoRa demodulator well-practiced; these three (this one, No Name on the Door, Hopscotch) throw increasingly nasty situations at that same demodulator.

This post’s theme: within one recording, two LoRa transmitters with completely different parameters are talking to each other.

Rest of the series: Channel Hop、True Color Is a Lie、Isodata Seven、Subsidy Claim

What the challenge is about

On the night shift, GAIAN-723 dropped off the telemetry terminal at 01:12, yet the schedule says it’s overhead right now. David Aroz is alone in the SOC; the ground-station modem reports nothing, but the station’s raw recorder has been running the whole time, and he pulls out the last 40 seconds of the band.

The waterfall isn’t empty. There are two voices in it: one is GAIAN-723, and the other isn’t on any GaianSpace frequency plan, and it’s talking to the satellite. The old frequency sheet on the desk still says 433.000 MHz.

Goal: find what GAIAN-723 answered when the stranger made its first call.

The file given is a ~180 MB .sigmf-data (2 MS/s, 433.55 MHz) plus the desk notes.

Flag format: GAIANSPACE{...}

Two voices with different “accents”

The 433.000 MHz on the old sheet isn’t where any signal actually is (the note itself says “might be wrong”). Looking at the waterfall and the per-band energy, there are two transmitters, repeating a cycle about every 12 seconds:

A (satellite)B (stranger)
Frequency~433.170 MHz~433.920 MHz
ModulationLoRa SF9, BW125kLoRa SF7, BW250k
Sync word0x12 (public)0x34 (LoRaWAN)
Preamble12 symbols8 symbols

This is the “different accents” the challenge mentions: the sync word, SF, and bandwidth are all different. So you can’t decode both sides with the same parameters; the demodulator has to run against each parameter set separately. Zoom into one cycle and the order is: A long packet → B strong pulse → A short packet:

Decoding the conversation

Running the demodulator with each parameter set, all packets decode cleanly with parity check 0.

The conversation (TC = telecommand, TM = telemetry response):

TimeWhoContent
4.017 sBTC HELLO (seq 0)
4.224 sATM,ACK,0,HELLO,GAIANSPACE{...}
15.89 sBTC GET HK; A replies with housekeeping
28.25 sBTC GET CFG; A replies NAK
39.08 sBTC SET DLCFG B; A replies OK,DLCFG=B

B is the stranger: it says hello, queries status and config, and finally switches the satellite’s downlink config to B, which explains why the ground-station modem, stuck on the old config, stopped receiving anything.

The challenge asks what the satellite answered on the stranger’s “first call,” which is the ACK at 4.224 s, and it coughs up the flag directly.

Flag

Takeaways

  1. “Two voices” means compare modulation parameters. Here the two sides differ in SF, BW, sync word, and preamble length; building out all the transmitters and a timeline first, then decoding each, is more efficient than trying parameters one at a time.
  2. The old frequency sheet is wrong, so trust the recorded data, not the documents. Very common in SDR challenges.
  3. Pair commands with responses using the sequence number. TC/TM looks like a protocol, and the seq in TM,ACK,<seq>,... lets you pin down the “first call” answer exactly.
  4. Here the satellite side used SF9 and the stranger SF7, both fairly standard. In the next post, No Name on the Door, the satellite switches to no header, with every packet looking different, and the demodulator has to evolve again.

entry.title: Rebuilding the Agriculture Office's Satellite Check | Subsidy Claim | GaianSpace CTF 2026
entry.content:
🌐 中文版：繁體中文

Fourth post in the series, and the finale of the “farm arc” (Babb’s AgriLink world). The first three posts got the LoRa demodulator in shape; this one adds a layer of GIS and classifier reconstruction on top of the demodulation.

In a way, it’s everything from the earlier posts applied together.

Rest of the series: Channel Hop、True Color Is a Lie、Isodata Seven、Two Voices、No Name on the Door、Hopscotch

What the challenge is about

At the county agriculture office, the area-payment claim for Babb’s north parcel was rejected: “parcel already declared as pasture, satellite check passed.” Someone filed a claim using Babb’s corn field, and the office’s satellite check actually sided with them.

A clerk lets something slip: this year the office’s classification stats left out one class, because “nobody around here declares that crop, and field surveys are expensive.” Separately, at 12:05 the shared SDR recorded a stranger transmitting this batch of claims on “yet another channel.”

Goal: find all the false claims in the stranger’s batch, and join their claim codes with hyphens in the order they were sent.

The files given are the SDR recording, the office’s check imagery (5-channel GeoTIFF), the class statistics, the training-field and parcel registry, and the rejection letter.

First, demodulate the claim batch from the SDR

The radio this time is 434.65 MHz, SF9, BW125k, preamble 8, explicit header, CR4/5.

Reusing the demodulator, 64 bursts decode to: one batch header + 30 claims + one short packet, and then the whole batch is sent again (so every record has two copies to cross-check).

Each claim has the format <seq>;<parcel>;<declared crop>;<area>;<claim code>, e.g. 01;MZH-8140;legelo;44.67;CUVE (legelo = pasture).

The key: the class that got deleted

The office’s .sta file uses Gaussian maximum-likelihood classification with equal priors, but it has only four classes: pasture, stubble, cropland, settlement. You can see that corn (kukorica) was removed, and only its training field is still there.

A supervised classifier can only output classes it was trained on, so with no corn statistics, a corn field gets forced into the most similar class (pasture), and the check “passes.” That’s the core vulnerability of the whole challenge.

I first rasterized the training-field polygons onto the image grid and recomputed each class’s mean and covariance. They matched the .sta file byte for byte, confirming my coordinate and sampling conventions were correct.

Then I used training field T-01 to restore corn’s statistics, ran a 5-class classification, and compared record by record:

Under the office’s 4-class classification, all 30 records “pass.”

After restoring corn, only 3 records don’t match, and all three are “declared pasture, actually corn”:

#ParcelDeclaredAfter restoring cornCode
1MZH-8140 (Babb’s parcel)pasturecorn 93%CUVE
10MZH-9183pasturecorn 84%UKEJ
28MZH-1402pasturecorn 80%TRP6

Flag

Takeaways

  1. “One class is missing” is the whole key. A supervised classifier can only output classes it was trained on; with no corn statistics it crams corn into the most similar class, pasture, so “check passed” doesn’t mean the claim is honest. It’s a very realistic remote-sensing fraud scenario.
  2. Validate your own pipeline against known data first. Only after the training-field pixel counts and the .sta means and covariances matched byte for byte did I go restore the missing class, which is what makes the conclusion hold up.
  3. Make use of the re-send when decoding SDR batches. The two transmissions are identical, so you can cross-confirm every character instead of guessing.
  4. By this point the farm arc’s LoRa demodulator is quite mature. Next the series jumps to a different storyline, a night shift, a hijacked satellite, where the same demodulator meets trickier situations.

entry.title: The Word Hidden Across Five Channels | Isodata Seven | GaianSpace CTF 2026
entry.content:
🌐 中文版：繁體中文

Third post in the series. After the demodulator got its skeleton in True Color Is a Lie, this one swaps in new parameters (implicit header) and upgrades the stego trick from subtracting two copies to clustering across multiple channels.

Rest of the series: Channel Hop、Subsidy Claim、Two Voices、No Name on the Door、Hopscotch

What the challenge is about

Since dawn the tractor has stopped listening to the mast and started listening to a different, unknown transmitter. The Johnripper terminal receives tiles under the dealer’s proprietary settings, and the dealer won’t publish those settings. Babb only has photocopies of pages 14 and 16 of the service manual. Page 15, in between, is missing.

The shared SDR was moved into the tractor shed and recorded that channel. What the stranger sends to the tractor is a whole tile (all channels), and it looks real, except for one patch in the north field that Babb can’t explain.

In the margin of the course notes, double-underlined: “count what actually grows here.”

Goal: find what the stranger planted in the tile. The files given are a ~213 MB .sigmf-data, manual pages 14/16, and the remote-sensing course notes.

Flag format: GAIANSPACE{...}.

This time it’s an implicit header

The radio parameters (manual page 14) are 433.4 MHz, SF7, BW500k, CR4/5, sync word 0x2C, 10-symbol preamble, and no RF header (fixed-length frames).

The missing page 15 holds the frame-length table, so we’ll have to infer it from the data.

Reusing the demodulator skeleton from the last post, the difference here is the implicit header: the first 8 symbols are a low-rate block (CR4/8), after which every 5 symbols form a block; the length is inferred from how many symbols the packet spans in the air.

Once all 779 frames pass the CRC-16 check from manual page 16, they reconstruct into five 128×128 grayscale images:

Looked at one channel at a time, that patch looks like random noise in every one, unlike the previous challenge. That’s probably exactly what the challenge means by “no band leaks anything.”

First, understand what this “image” is

A satellite doesn’t take an ordinary RGB camera photo. It records different wavelengths of light separately, storing each wavelength as its own channel (band).

This challenge uses three kinds:

  • Visible light: the red/green/blue your eyes can see. A healthy plant’s chlorophyll absorbs red light, so vegetation looks dark in visible light while bare soil looks bright.
  • Near-infrared (NIR): a bit longer in wavelength than red, invisible to the eye. Healthy leaf tissue reflects NIR strongly, so “high NIR” is almost the same as “this is a living plant.”
  • Short-wave infrared (SWIR): longer still, and especially sensitive to water. More water (wet soil, after irrigation, moist leaves) absorbs SWIR and looks dark; dry ground looks bright in SWIR.

So every pixel carries a little fingerprint: bright or not in visible light, high or low in NIR, high or low in SWIR. Feed those fingerprints to a clustering algorithm and pixels with similar fingerprints get grouped together.

ISODATA / k-means: count what grows here

The course notes hint at using ISODATA with 7 classes (ISODATA is a common unsupervised clustering method in remote sensing, conceptually just k-means).

Running k-means on the 5-dimensional pixels of the noisy patch, the error drops sharply at k=4 (adding more classes beyond that only lowers it slowly), which says the patch really has only 4 true classes. And those 4 aren’t random. They’re exactly the combinations of two switches, each with only two values:

ClassVisibleNIRSWIR
vegetation-like + SWIR lowdarkhighlow
vegetation-like + SWIR highdarkhighhigh
soil-like + SWIR highbrightlowhigh
soil-like + SWIR lowbrightlowlow

Read the table as two switches and it’s clear:

  • Switch A: does this patch “look like vegetation” or “look like soil” (decided by visible dark/bright and NIR high/low).
  • Switch B: is SWIR “high” or “low.”

A × B = 2 × 2 = 4, which lines up perfectly with k=4.

Here’s the key. Normally these two switches pair up naturally (real vegetation shows the combination you’d expect for A and B). But the stranger’s trick is to secretly flip switch B only on the pixels that “draw the text.” The result:

  • Looking at NIR alone: the text pixels and the background are both “vegetation” (same A), so there’s no visible difference → nothing leaks.
  • Looking at SWIR alone: the text pixels just happen to have SWIR flipped, but SWIR is high and low all over the place anyway, so it looks like noise → nothing visible there either.
  • Only by comparing “whether A and B agree“ does the text appear. In digital terms, you XOR the two switches: agree = 0, disagree = 1, and the text is painted exactly on the pixels where XOR = 1.

That’s why you must cluster rather than look at a single channel: clustering considers all channels’ fingerprints at once, so it naturally groups the self-contradictory pixels (“A says vegetation but B is flipped”) into their own small classes, and those small classes are the text. Running k=7 clustering over the whole image, those two “contradictory” small classes each show part of the text:

Merge those two classes and draw them, and three lines of text clearly emerge:

Reading the last line

The font is a “bold” variant: each character is a 5×6 base glyph plus a copy shifted 1 pixel to the right.

I used the already-known letters in the first two lines (GAIANSPACE{, 7TH-CLASS-) as a reference and confirmed the last line cell by cell. I hesitated between W/V here; W turned out to be correct.

Flag

Takeaways

  1. The “implant” here isn’t painted into one channel. It’s the text split into two noisy halves (XOR) spread across different bands. Any single channel is just noise; it only appears when you look at all channels at once (clustering), echoing the note’s line, “the computer only knows which pixels look alike in all channels at once.”
  2. The k-means error curve tells you how many classes really exist. The error plunges at k=4 and only crawls down afterwards, which is the implementation of the note’s “count what actually grows here.”
  3. You don’t need the missing manual page. Frame length, channel, and row number can all be inferred directly from the field layout in the data.
  4. For a tiny font, figure out the drawing rule before reconstructing the glyphs. This one is “bold, shifted 1 pixel right”. Once you know the rule, cell-by-cell comparison is more reliable than just eyeballing a zoomed image.

entry.title: Hand-Building My First LoRa Demodulator | True Color Is a Lie | GaianSpace CTF 2026
entry.content:
🌐 中文版：繁體中文

Second post in the series, and the one where we actually start hand-building a LoRa demodulator. The previous challenge, Channel Hop, just read an already-decoded packet log. From here on we get raw IQ and have to do everything ourselves.

This demodulator sticks with me all the way to the end of the series, so this post goes into more detail to lay out the skeleton of LoRa demodulation. The later posts only cover what’s different about each one.

Rest of the series: Isodata Seven、Subsidy Claim、Two Voices、No Name on the Door、Hopscotch

What the challenge is about

On the second satellite pass the tractor accepts the map and the sprayer rolls out. But the lead unit, Johnripper, marks every green thing on the map as “dead” and fertilizes at maximum dose. Babb walked the field an hour ago, and the corn was perfectly fine.

The shared SDR recorded the raw signal on the AgriLink frequency this time. AgriLink says there was only one transmission on this pass; the SDR disagrees. And since last night, AgriLink has been sending channels without names (to save airtime), ordered by the mast according to band_order.conf, a file that was rewritten at 02:13 by a remote session nobody remembers opening.

Goal: figure out what AgriLink actually transmitted. The files given are a ~200 MB .sigmf-data (ci8, 2 MS/s, 434.3 MHz), the band-order config, and the true-colour image shown on the tablet.

Flag format: GAIANSPACE{...}.

The skeleton of a LoRa demodulator

The signal is LoRa, but the parameters in the notes (BW250k) are a decoy. Measured for real, it’s SF7, BW500k. There’s no off-the-shelf decoder here, so we write our own.

First, what LoRa looks like. Each LoRa symbol is a tone that sweeps from low frequency up to high, called an up-chirp; on a spectrogram it’s a diagonal line. One burst looks like this (frequency on the vertical axis, time on the horizontal):

So how is data encoded? Each symbol “launches” from a different starting frequency, and that starting point is the number the symbol represents (0–127, so 128 possibilities for SF7). The core of demodulation is therefore measuring where each symbol launches from.

The technique is called dechirping: multiply the received up-chirp by a down-chirp going the opposite way. One sweeps up, one sweeps down, their slopes cancel exactly, and the product becomes a steady, single-frequency tone. Whichever FFT bin that tone lands in maps directly to the symbol’s launch point.

The figure below shows this (blue = received up-chirp, grey = down-chirp reference, red = the steady tone after multiplying):

The full pipeline (used in every post from here on):

  1. Synchronize first. Run one FFT over the preamble’s up-chirps and one over the following down-chirps; the two peaks together give you both the timing (which sample the packet starts on) and the carrier frequency offset (CFO, the frequency difference from imperfect crystals on each end). See “the half-symbol trap” below.
  2. Dechirp each symbol and take the peak bin. One implementation detail matters: do it at the native 2 MS/s rate (512 samples per symbol), add up the two energy chunks that fold into v and v−128, then take the peak with parabolic interpolation. Downsampling to 500 kS/s first loses edge energy and raises the error rate.
  3. Symbol value = peak bin − preamble bin − 1 (subtract the preamble’s reference start point).
  4. Turn symbol values into bytes: Gray decode → de-interleave → take the data bits → assemble bytes → XOR with the whitening sequence. How do you know each step’s direction (bit order, endianness) is right? Validate with known plaintext: these packets all start with AL (0x41 0x4c), and when decoded correctly every code word’s parity check comes out 0. If it doesn’t, some step’s convention is flipped.

The half-symbol trap (detail of step 1)

There’s an easy trap during step 1’s synchronization: the packet start resolves to two equally valid answers, and the formula alone can’t tell which is right.

Why? After dechirping you take the FFT peak bin, and FFT bins are circular (the bin after 127 wraps back to 0).

That “wrap-around” means the computed packet start lands on two candidate offsets that differ by exactly half a symbol (64 bins for SF7), and both line up with the preamble when plugged into the formula, so you can’t pick one by formula alone.

The fix is crude but effective:

Decode with both candidates and keep the one whose FFT peaks are tall and clean. When the alignment is right, each symbol’s energy concentrates into a single bin and the peak is tall and sharp. Off by half a symbol, the energy spills into the neighbouring symbol and splits into two short peaks, which is easy to tell apart at a glance:

Two transmitters, one strong and one weak

After decoding all 781 bursts, the truth comes out: there are actually two transmitters on this frequency.

  • Weak signal (641 bursts): 5 channels × 128 rows, a complete tile. This is the real satellite data.
  • Strong signal (139 bursts): far stronger, but it only re-sends some rows of ch0 and ch3, and its contents are a tampered version of the weak signal.

That’s the lie underneath a “single transmission”: one real satellite, and a forged transmitter talking over it.

The mast received the stronger one, so it used the altered data. Subtract the weak version from the strong version for the same (channel, row), and the ch3 difference spells out three lines of text:

Reading the last line

The strong signal was initially missing a few rows that failed to demodulate, so the text had horizontal gaps. After fixing the half-symbol ambiguity and filling in all the rows, the glyphs came together. The last line’s characters are only 5 pixels wide and a bit blurry, so I upscaled with cubic interpolation and checked them cell by cell:

Reads HR6TNM.

Flag

The flag name TRUE-NDVI echoes the challenge too: the channels the forger tampered with, ch0 and ch3, are exactly the ones the mast treats as red and short-wave infrared, and red is the key band for computing NDVI (the vegetation index).

That’s why the tractor judged healthy corn to be dead.

Takeaways

  1. A “single transmission” can have two transmitters. The strong one drowns out the weak one (capture effect), and only the raw SDR IQ can tell them apart. The log only shows the one that got received.
  2. The hardest part of LoRa demodulation is synchronization. CFO and timing are coupled together across the up/down chirps; you separate them using their difference and sum, and there’s the half-symbol ambiguity. Once this skeleton is correct, the rest of the series is just bolting features onto it.
  3. When rolling your own, validate every convention with known plaintext. Here, the AL prefix and the header nibble confirm the direction of Gray/de-interleave/byte-order, far faster than cross-referencing the LoRa spec from memory.
  4. The message hides in the difference between two “noisy” copies. Neither version alone reveals the tampering; only the subtraction does, a trick that returns in a different form in Isodata Seven.

entry.title: The One Line That Got Rewritten | Channel Hop | GaianSpace CTF 2026
entry.content:
🌐 中文版：繁體中文

This is the opening post of my favourite storyline in GaianSpace CTF 2026. The whole series is built around one idea: you hand-build a LoRa demodulator yourself, and then keep growing it: from a single fixed parameter set, to implicit headers, to Doppler drift, and finally to frequency hopping.

This first post doesn’t touch IQ yet; it’s a warm-up at the packet layer. The real IQ work starts in the next post, True Color Is a Lie.

Rest of the series: Isodata Seven、Subsidy Claim、Two Voices、No Name on the Door、Hopscotch

What the challenge is about

Every morning, Babb’s corn farm receives a GaianSpace AgriLink satellite tile through a LoRa mast. This particular morning the tractor shows map integrity: unverified and refuses to use the tile. Support won’t open a ticket without the tile’s delivery stamp, but the farmer can’t find it anywhere on the tablet. Luckily, the mast kept a log of what it received.

Goal: find the delivery stamp.

The files given are mast_rx_0540.log (the receive log, 641 lines of hex packets) and agrilink_welcome.txt (the sign-up welcome letter, “some of it may be out of date”).

Flag format: GAIANSPACE{...}

Read the log, rebuild the tile

The first packet in the log decodes to a chunk of text metadata:

That one line tells us everything:

  • The data comes from Sentinel-2, 128×128 pixels, 10 m resolution.
  • And there are 5 channels:
    • B02 (blue)
    • B03 (green)
    • B04 (red)
    • B08 (near-infrared)
    • B11 (short-wave infrared)
  • But the welcome letter only mentions 4 channels (blue/green/red + NIR). It quietly left one out.

The remaining packets follow the format AL 02 04 07 'D' <channel 0–4> <row 0–127> <128 pixel bytes>.

5 channels × 128 rows = 640 data packets, plus one trailing packet. Drop them back into five 128×128 grayscale images and the whole tile comes back.

Compose blue/green/red (B04/B03/B02) into a true-colour image and you get exactly what the farmer sees on the tablet: circular pivot-irrigation fields, roads, solar panels. Everything looks normal, and there’s no stamp in sight:

The stamp is hiding in a channel the tablet never shows

The tablet only builds true colour from blue/green/red, so if the stamp lives in another channel, the farmer will never see it. I ran a high-pass filter on each channel (subtract a Gaussian blur, then boost the contrast) to amplify the tiny brightness variations:

Line the five high-pass images up side by side and the answer jumps right out.

Only B08 (near-infrared) has three lines of text written across the fields:

The brightness difference in the raw image is tiny and completely invisible to the eye, and the true-colour composite doesn’t use B08 at all. That’s the whole trick: the stamp was written into a channel the tablet simply never renders.

Flag

Takeaways

  1. When something is “invisible,” first list what data isn’t being displayed. The way in here: the metadata lists 5 channels, the welcome letter claims 4, and the tablet only uses 3. The stamp is hiding in the channel everyone ignores.
  2. For image stego, a per-channel high-pass or contrast stretch makes hidden watermarks pop. Especially with multispectral satellite imagery, where different bands carry wildly different amounts of information, so don’t just stare at the visible light.
  3. Don’t rush to chase the noise in the log (dropped packets, RSSI, SNR). I spent a while hunting missing packets and looking for patterns in RSSI, and they were all red herrings. Reconstruct the actual data and look at it first; that beats drilling into details.
  4. The challenge name channel-hop means “search across different channels (bands),” not LoRa frequency hopping. Real hopping doesn’t show up until the final post in the series, Hopscotch.

entry.title: A Sentence Hidden in Sensor Drift | Degradift | GaianSpace CTF 2026
entry.content:
The final post of the GaianSpace CTF 2026 “05-rad-hard-rampage” series.

🌐 中文版：繁體中文

This chapter has four radiation faults; the first three posts covered Single Event Upset (SEU), Single Event Latch-up (SEL), and Total Ionizing Dose (TID).

This one wraps up with the fourth: Displacement Damage (DDD): not a single high-energy particle strike, nor burning out the circuit, but the lattice being knocked askew hit after hit, so the readings slowly creep and slowly drift.

And this challenge has a little twist: the recovered numbers look like perfectly reasonable CO₂ readings, but they aren’t actually CO₂ at all.

What the challenge is about

Displacement damage builds up: the lattice takes hit after hit, the readings creep, and by the end of the run the numbers have wandered far from the truth. We logged the whole decline. The characterization team worked out exactly how fast it drifts.

In plain terms: Foundation One’s CO₂ sensor didn’t break in a day. Displacement damage is cumulative: the lattice takes hit after hit and the readings slowly climb, until by the end of the run the numbers are far from the truth. We logged the whole decline, and the characterization team worked out the exact drift rate.

Subtract the drift from each reading and what’s left is what the sensor really saw at the time. The on-call operator will tell you the recovered values are just cleaner CO₂ readings, but look again, they’re not CO₂.

Files given:

  • sensor_log.csv: sample index and the degraded readings (30 records).
  • ddd_characterization.md: the measured drift model.

The model is written right in the file:

logged reading = actual in-flight value + this drift

The recorder also has a fixed CO₂ baseline, and the gas team will only say “somewhere around three hundred thirty ppm,” refusing to be more precise.

First, subtract the drift

Matching the hint “Creep, not jump.”

Displacement Damage Dose (DDD) is yet another distinct radiation effect: high-energy particles knock atoms in the semiconductor lattice out of position, creating permanent lattice defects. These defects slowly change the sensor’s response, showing up as readings that creep upward over time, a cumulative drift rather than a one-off jump, which is why the challenge stresses “creep, not jump.”

And this drift is quadratic (0.013 * n^2), so it drifts faster the later it gets.

The subtraction is simple:

The resulting in-flight values fall between 385 and 458, which still looks like reasonable CO₂ ppm numbers.

But that’s exactly the trap the challenge means by “the operator will tell you these are just cleaner readings.”

Look again: they’re not CO₂

Matching the second hint, “Not parts per million.”

The challenge says the baseline is “around three hundred thirty” and deliberately won’t give an exact number. So what if these numbers are actually character codes (in-flight value = baseline + ASCII code)?

Then the baseline is the unknown to solve for. For each candidate baseline between 300 and 360, decode “in-flight value − baseline” as ASCII and see which baseline makes all 30 bytes land in the printable range and spell out GAIANSPACE{...}:

The left panel shows the curves before and after subtracting the drift (the blue line clearly climbs, the orange line is flattened but the numbers still look mundane); the right panel is the baseline scan, where 333 ppm is the only baseline that spells out the flag:

One detail here: nearby baselines (332, 334…) also decode to “all printable” characters, so “is it printable” alone can’t be your filter. 332 decodes to HBJBOTQBDF|ejtqm5..., jumbled symbols that aren’t text at all. You have to tighten the criterion to “does it actually spell a meaningful flag” to uniquely pin down 333.

The final result:

Flag

Takeaways

  1. When a key constant is described vaguely, enumerate it. For a deliberately imprecise “around three hundred thirty,” rather than overanalyzing the wording, just enumerate nearby integers and filter by “does it decode to a valid result”. A baseline is exactly the kind of thing you sweep.
  2. Numbers that look normal don’t mean they’re the data’s actual intent. The post-drift values look like mundane CO₂ ppm, which is precisely the trap. “Look again” usually means reinterpret from a different angle (here, “as character codes minus a baseline”).
  3. Your filter criterion has to be precise enough. “Is it printable” isn’t strong enough here (several baselines are all-printable); you must tighten to “does it spell meaningful text” to anchor uniquely.
  4. (Series wrap-up) One “radiation” theme can produce four challenges with completely different solutions. SEU is brute-forcing a key, SEL is using CRC to find the stuck bit, TID is reconstructing logic, DDD is subtracting drift then shifting perspective. Those are four real space-radiation failure mechanisms (upset, latch-up, ionizing dose, displacement damage), each mapping to its own solving mindset. This chapter was genuinely thoughtfully designed.

entry.title: A Logic Gate Shorted by Radiation | Ionized Transistangle | GaianSpace CTF 2026
entry.content:
Third post of the GaianSpace CTF 2026 “05-rad-hard-rampage” series.

🌐 中文版：繁體中文

The first two posts (SEU, SEL) were both single-event effects: one particle, one bit, one instant. This one is a cumulative effect: not a single hit, but months of radiation dose slowly wrecking the transistors. The failure model shifts from “data got changed” to “the logic itself is broken,” so the approach is completely different.

Other post in the series: Sensor Drift / Degradift

What the challenge is about

Total ionizing dose does not flip a bit and move on — it leaves transistors shorted, stuck, permanently. The encoder now spits nonsense. We still have the original design, gate for gate, with the damaged nodes marked.

In plain terms: months of accumulated radiation dose have finally taken out Foundation One’s status encoder. Total Ionizing Dose (TID) doesn’t flip one bit and move on. It shorts transistors permanently and jams them. The encoder now spits out garbage. We still have the original design, gate for gate, with the damaged nodes marked.

The encoder turns a string of probe words into a line of status words, but what’s measured on the board is garbage, because a few gates have shorted: no matter the input, their outputs are jammed.

In other words, we need to reconstruct what the encoder was supposed to do: run the probe words through the “as-designed” logic, and the status line comes back.

The file given is a gate-level netlist status_encoder.netlist, with the shorted gates marked and the probe words listed at the end.

Flag format: GAIANSPACE{...}.

Reading the netlist

8 inputs, 8 outputs, all XOR chains plus some NOTs. Two nodes, n6 and n15, are marked [SHORTED=0] and [SHORTED=1].

This is the challenge’s “transistors shorted, outputs permanently jammed at some value no matter the input.”

The short value is a lie, so use the design value

This is the twist of the whole challenge, matching the hint “A short is a lie.”

Total Ionizing Dose (TID) is a completely different radiation effect: not the instant event of one particle, but long-term accumulated charge trapped in the oxide layer, slowly drifting the transistors’ threshold voltage and leaking, until some gates “stick” at a fixed output and never respond to input again.

So what’s measured on the board now is the two post-damage jammed values, which are the result of the fault, not the design intent. [SHORTED=0]/[SHORTED=1] are just recording what it’s broken into now, so when reconstructing you must completely ignore those markers and compute n6, n15 by their original logic (n6 = i0 XOR i1, n15 = i1 XOR i3), no different from any other healthy gate.

Feed the probe words through the “as-designed” logic

The netlist comments spell out that each probe byte’s bits map to i7..i0 (bit 0 → i0, bit 7 → i7).

Feed the 32 probes in order through the as-designed logic (ignoring the short markers), compute each group’s o0..o7, and reassemble into a byte.

To see the damage’s effect clearly at the same time, I simulated both “run as damaged” and “run as designed”:

Put the two outputs side by side and the conclusion is obvious:

Interestingly, the damaged output’s first few characters still coincidentally show hints of GE and ENSPE (probably because some output bits happened not to be affected by those two jammed gates), but overall it’s not text at all. Only running fully as-designed (both gates treated as normal XOR) makes the 32 probes map to the complete, clean flag.

Flag

Takeaways

  1. “Stuck” and “flipped” are two completely different failure models. A flip (SEU) changes just one value, so you enumerate to recover it (see the first post); a stuck gate (TID) returns the same value for all inputs and propagates downstream. The solution isn’t to guess “what the correct value is,” but to directly reconstruct the as-designed logic.
  2. When the challenge explicitly says a marker is “the broken state,” don’t let it lead you around. The [SHORTED=...] value describes the fault; it’s not meant to be used, so treat it as noise to ignore. The real work here is “correctly turning the netlist into a simulator”; the logic itself is simple.
  3. Building both “run as damaged” and “run as designed” for comparison does more than verify understanding; it’s also vivid. You see at a glance how far the short corrupts the downstream signal, and it confirms your simulator isn’t buggy.

entry.title: The One Bit Stuck High | Lunar Latch-Up | GaianSpace CTF 2026
entry.content:
Second post of the GaianSpace CTF 2026 “05-rad-hard-rampage” series.

🌐 中文版：繁體中文

The previous post, Cosmic Bit Blunder, was about a Single Event Upset (SEU): one bit knocked over, either 0↔1. This one is similar, but the failure mechanism is a bit different: a Single Event Latch-up (SEL), where a bit gets forced high and stuck there. The distinction is subtle, yet it’s enough to cut the search space in half again.

Other posts in the series: A Logic Gate Shorted by Radiation / Ionized Transistangle、Sensor Drift / Degradift

What the challenge is about

A single heavy ion hit the Foundation One power-management block and triggered a latch-up — a parasitic path that slams one bit high and holds it there, drawing current until someone cuts the rail. One bit in there is stuck high that should not be.

In plain terms: a heavy ion hit Foundation One’s power-management block and triggered a latch-up, a parasitic current path that forces a bit high and holds it there, drawing current until someone cuts the rail.

In the dumped registers, one bit is stuck high that shouldn’t be, and everything downstream uses these registers as a key, so until that stuck bit is reset, the sealed mission payload can’t be opened.

The only files given are reg_dump.bin (84 bytes) and a recovery_spec.md describing its format:

OffsetSizeField
0x0032R0..R7, eight 32-bit registers (little-endian)
0x204Integrity word: CRC-32 of these 32 bytes’ healthy state (zlib/ISO, little-endian)
0x24restSealed payload: AES-128-ECB ciphertext of the flag (PKCS#7)

Key scheme: key = SHA-256(R0..R7 bytes)[:16].

The challenge spells out how to find the answer very plainly: use the only honest method: the single bit that makes the integrity word match again.

Flag format: GAIANSPACE{...}

Latch-up only “pushes a bit high,” never “pulls it low”

This is the key to the whole challenge, matching the hint “One bit too high.”

A quick intro to the physics of Single Event Latch-up (SEL): a particle triggers a parasitic PNPN (thyristor/SCR-like) conduction path in the CMOS structure, pulling a node high and self-sustaining it. The difference from the previous post’s SEU is that SEU can go 0→1 or 1→0, but latch-up slams one bit high. It can only stick a bit that was 0 at 1, and can never turn a bit that was 1 into 0.

So that directionality cuts the search space in half again: the faulty bit must have been 0 before the damage and 1 after. I only need to check the bits currently equal to 1 (clearing them to 0 one at a time), and never touch the bits that are 0.

Use the integrity word as a “search tool,” not just a verifier

For each bit currently set to 1 in the registers, try clearing it to 0, recompute the CRC-32 of those 32 bytes, and check whether it matches the integrity word stored in the file, 0xa70b003b:

This feels like the “only honest method” the challenge mentions: not guessing which bit is suspect, but letting the integrity check itself tell you the answer.

Of all the bits currently set to 1, only one makes the CRC match after clearing, bit 37 (byte 4, i.e. the lowest byte of R1, 0x20 → 0x00):

recovery_spec.md actually plants a distractor: “R7’s reserved high nibble is where the clear routine often operates, but this event didn’t hit there”, which is the challenge kindly reminding you not to fixate on R7 out of preconception. The real fault is in R1.

The registers are the key

Matching the second hint, “The registers are the key.”

Compute SHA-256 of the repaired 32 bytes and take the first 16 as the AES-128 key:

AES-128-ECB decrypt the ciphertext (48 bytes = 3 blocks), strip the PKCS#7 padding, and out comes a clean, correctly-formatted flag, confirming once more that bit 37 was the right one.

Flag

Takeaways

  1. The fault’s directionality cuts the search space in half again. SEU requires checking 256 bits (either 0↔1); SEL only “pushes high,” so only bits currently set to 1 are candidates. Understanding the fault’s physics isn’t just flavour; it genuinely reduces the work.
  2. CRC isn’t only for “verifying” an answer; it can also “find” one. This challenge stores a CRC of the healthy state, so “try each candidate + filter by CRC” becomes a deterministic search algorithm, far more reliable than guessing which field is broken, exactly the challenge’s “only honest method.”
  3. A spec line like “this field is a common target, but not this time” is usually there to rule out a decoy. This challenge deliberately calls R7’s reserved nibble “the clear routine’s favourite spot” precisely so you don’t dive in.
  4. Binding the key to the repaired data itself gives built-in verification. The key is SHA-256(registers), so a correct repair decrypts correctly with valid padding, and a wrong one gives garbage. You know whether the answer is right without submitting it.

entry.title: Single Event Upset and 128 Candidate Keys | Cosmic Bit Blunder | GaianSpace CTF 2026
entry.content:
🌐 中文版：繁體中文

This is the first post of the GaianSpace CTF 2026 chapter “05-rad-hard-rampage.”

The whole series is beautifully designed: four challenges, each mapping exactly to one of the four real failure mechanisms that space radiation causes in electronics: Single Event Upset (SEU), Single Event Latch-up (SEL), Total Ionizing Dose (TID), and Displacement Damage (DDD). I’m writing one post per challenge.

The other three posts: Single Event Latch-up / Lunar Latch-up、A Logic Gate Shorted by Radiation / Ionized Transistangle、Sensor Drift / Degradift

The backdrop here: a high-energy proton passed through the flight computer and flipped exactly one bit in the key. This is very common in space, where high-energy particles and radiation easily cause bit flips or errors in electronics and signals.

What the challenge is about

High in the Foundation One orbit, a single cosmic-ray proton punched through the flight computer and flipped exactly one bit in the key that protects the mission log. The log still decrypts to garbage. The reliability team wants the log back, and they are sure the rest of the key survived intact.

In plain terms: high in orbit, a cosmic-ray proton punched through Foundation One’s flight computer and flipped exactly one bit in the key that protects the mission log. The log now decrypts to garbage. The reliability team wants it back, and they’re sure the rest of the key is intact.

The on-call engineer’s instinct is: “the whole key is toast, just rewrite a fresh one”, but the challenge warns that doing so would lose the log along with it (change the key and the already-encrypted ciphertext can never be decrypted again).

Only two files are given:

  • cipher.bin: 32 bytes, the encrypted mission log (AES, single-block scheme).
  • corrupted.key: 16 bytes, the damaged 128-bit key.

Flag format: GAIANSPACE{...}

First, figure out what a “Single Event Upset” actually changed

Single Event Upset (SEU) is the most classic radiation effect in space electronics: a high-energy particle passes through a memory cell and, in that instant, knocks over the stored charge, flipping one bit from 0 to 1 or 1 to 0. The data is changed, but the circuit itself isn’t damaged, so rewrite it and it recovers.

For this challenge, the key inference is: since only one bit is wrong, there are only 128 possible correct keys.

A 128-bit key has only 128 bit positions. The correct key must be corrupted.key with one of its bits flipped back, and that search space is small enough to brute-force directly, which matches the challenge’s blunt hint, “try them all.”

Flip each bit back and see which one decodes to readable text

The challenge says “AES, single-block scheme,” i.e. ECB mode with no IV needed. The approach is direct: for each of the 128 candidate keys, flip one bit back, AES-128-ECB decrypt cipher.bin, then count how many of the resulting bytes are printable ASCII.

Of the 128 candidates, 127 decode to random noise (printable count drifting between 5 and 19), and only flipping bit 50 (byte 6, bit 2, d2 → d6) decodes a full 30 consecutive printable characters, standing out from the noise on its own:

Why is this signal so clean and easy to spot? Because AES has an avalanche effect: if the key is right, the whole block reverts to correct plaintext, and if even one key bit is wrong, the whole block is unrecognizable.

So you don’t even need to know what the flag looks like. The printable-character count alone is enough to pick out the right answer.

The decoded content

Decrypting with the repaired key gives:

That trailing \x02\x02 is PKCS#7 padding (padding length 2). Strip it and you get exactly a 30-character flag; add the 2 padding bytes and it’s exactly 32 bytes, matching the ciphertext length perfectly. That’s effectively a second layer of validation, since only the correct key yields valid PKCS#7 padding, confirming once more that bit 50 was the one that got flipped.

Flag

Takeaways

  1. The challenge’s physical constraint directly determines the solution. “Only one bit is wrong” compresses “guess the whole key” ($2^{128}$, impossible) down to “128 possibilities” (runs in a second). When reading a challenge, first convert the conditions into a search-space size, then decide whether to write a brute-forcer. Many crypto challenges that look brutal are really just a tiny enumeration.
  2. AES’s avalanche effect makes filtering extremely reliable. Right key → whole block correct, wrong key → whole block garbage, with no grey zone in between. So a crude metric like “printable-character count” is enough to uniquely pick the answer, without knowing anything about the plaintext first.
  3. PKCS#7 padding is free secondary validation. The end of the decryption is exactly a valid padding pattern, giving near-certainty you picked the right key. With block-cipher challenges, glance at the padding after decrypting.

entry.title: Klingon on the Wall, Tripped Up by Romanization | Strange Holos 2 | STARPWN 2026
entry.content:
🌐 中文版：繁體中文

This is the follow-up to Strange Holos 1, with the same setting and structure. Recognizing the script as Klingon wasn’t actually hard. What tripped me up was the last step: Klingon’s romanization and the letter it stands for as an English substitution cipher are two different things.

What the challenge is about

Again just one image, space2-glitter.png (1536×1024, 2.4 MB), with no other leads:

Same setup as the first one: a cyberpunk alley, a wall covered in strange neon graffiti, and background signs reading “GLITTERCITY”, “FORTUNE”, and one in Japanese saying「ホテル」(hotel).
But the writing system is completely different this time: flowing, blade-like curves with hooks and sharp points.

File-level checks

binwalk found no embedded data, pcrt reported all CRCs correct, and zsteg only turned up the bit-plane noise any ordinary photographic image has. The only non-standard chunk is again C2PA provenance info (gpt-image / OpenAI generation certificate plus SSL.com’s signature chain), the same conclusion already established in part 1: not a payload.

Same conclusion: the flag is in the picture, so look at the graffiti.

The characters this time are flowing curves, 8 of them:

Identifying the writing system

These flowing, hooked, blade-like strokes, plus one character that’s a very clean “工” shape, point to Klingon (pIqaD).

It fits thematically too. Part 1 was Star Wars Aurebesh, and the title “Strange Holos” is itself a nod to Star Trek: Strange New Worlds.

As in part 1, I pulled the official chart to compare:

Klingon’s gh is an 工 shape, y is a bowl with an enclosed inner loop, and o is a bar plus an S-curve. All three shapes are clearly present on the wall, which confirms the writing system.

Comparing by eye gives the phrase boldly go.

This fits the Star Trek theme, from the most famous line in the series’ opening monologue: “to boldly go where no one has gone before.”

  • B O L D L Y: letters 3 and 5 are both L
  • G O: the second letter is O, matching the second letter of BOLDLY
  • Character 7 = G (Klingon gh, the 工 shape)
  • Characters 2 and 8 = O (Klingon o)

With the answer settled, the full mapping is clear:

#Klingon letterEnglish letter
1bB
2oO
3lL
4DD
5lL
6yY
7ghG
8oO

The transliteration trap

My first submission was STARPWN{boldlh gho}, and it was rejected.

The mistake was that I read the characters correctly but wrote down Klingon’s romanization rather than the English letters they represent. In Klingon romanization, gh, ch, ng, and tlh are single letters spelled with two or more characters. So that 工-shaped symbol is written gh under Klingon spelling rules, but when used as an English substitution cipher it stands for the single English letter G, making the word GO.

Flag

Lowercase with a single space, consistent with the previous challenge’s STARPWN{nerf herder} format.

Appendix: dead ends I walked down

IdeaResult
Extra data / extra chunksbinwalk clean, pngcheck clean, only caBX (C2PA)
zsteg bit planesNoise fragments only, no structure
Reading it as an actual Klingon phrase (Qapla', nuqneH, toDSaH, etc.)None fit a 6+2 split with letters 3=5 identical and characters 2=8 identical
Using Klingon romanization directly as the flag content (boldlh gho)Rejected, since multi-character romanizations must collapse to single English letters

entry.title: The Graffiti on the Wall Is an Alien Script | Strange Holos 1 | STARPWN 2026
entry.content:
🌐 中文版：繁體中文

This challenge gives you a single image and no hints at all. The whole solve needs no complicated code, just looking at the picture carefully.

What the challenge is about

You get exactly one file: space1-glitter.png (1536×1024, 2.3 MB).

Opening it looks like this:

The image shows a cyberpunk-style alley at night, with a wall covered in neon graffiti written in some unreadable script, plus a few projected billboards in the background. The style fits this CTF’s GLITTERCITY theme nicely, and if you look closely there’s a “GL177” neon sign further back next to a spire. There’s no text explanation anywhere, so the flag is obviously hidden somewhere in this picture.

Step 1: check the file

With one image and no other leads, the instinctive first move is to inspect the file itself. All of these checks came back clean:

Walking the PNG chunk structure manually to confirm there’s no custom data block:

Output:

The only non-standard chunk is caBX, a C2PA (Content Provenance and Authenticity) manifest. Decoding it with exiftool shows it means exactly what it says: this is certification info for an AI-generated image, not a puzzle:

So the image was produced by an image-generation model, and caBX is just that generation process’s signature chain (SSL.com certificate, OCSP response, timestamp). Nothing is hidden inside it. Knowing this saves the time you’d otherwise waste base64-decoding a pile of certificate data on a hunch.

Next, testing for LSB (least significant bit) steganography, also nothing. The LSB plane looks like pure sensor noise, and the proportion of 1s is nowhere near a suspicious 0.5:

Because the image has a heavy chromatic-aberration glitch look, I also split the R/G/B channels apart, guessing one of them might hide clean text. That came up empty too. All three channels show identical glyph shapes, just offset from each other by a few pixels. The colour fringing is purely a cyberpunk art effect, not a three-layer cipher.

So the conclusion so far: the flag is in the picture itself, to be read with your eyes. That patch of strange graffiti in the middle is the puzzle.

Looking closely, you can see:

  • Characters 2, 6, and 9 are identical in shape (a V with a vertical bar and a serif flourish on top).
  • Characters 3, 7, and 10 are identical in shape (a thickened 7).

So the overall structure is ? A B C | D A B ? A B: a 4-letter word and a 6-letter word sharing repeated letters at fixed positions.

Step 2: the wrong turn, Standard Galactic Alphabet

When alien-looking angular symbols show up in a CTF, the instinctive first guess is the Standard Galactic Alphabet (SGA, the symbol system from Commander Keen and Minecraft’s enchanting table). It is far and away the most commonly used substitution alphabet in CTFs.

So I pulled down the official chart to compare:

SGA turned out to be completely wrong, and not even close. Real SGA glyphs are built from dots, short hooks, and right angles (a is a hook, f is a bar with three dots above, i is a line split into two segments, w is three dots). Not one of its 26 letters looks like a three-bar Ξ, a 7, or a V with a bar. Wrong direction.

Step 3: the real answer, Aurebesh

The same Omniglot index of fictional scripts also lists Aurebesh, the galactic standard script from Star Wars. Aurebesh glyphs are hard-edged and blocky, built from bars and diagonals, matching the wall text’s visual style exactly.

Every one of the 10 characters on the wall maps to an Aurebesh letter. Here’s a side-by-side comparison, with the wall characters on top and the matching glyphs cropped from the Omniglot chart below:

#Wall characterAurebesh nameLetter
1hook + peaknernN
2V + bareskE
3thickened 7reshR
4cross + curvefornF
5three bars ΞherfH
6V + bareskE
7thickened 7reshR
8notched ƎdornD
9V + bareskE
10thickened 7reshR

The repeated-character structure I noticed earlier independently confirms this: characters 2/6/9 are esk (E) and characters 3/7/10 are resh (R), which matches the letter repetition in NERF / HERDER exactly. That’s the answer.

“nerf herder” is more than just a plausible answer

Three independent clues corroborate each other:

  • “Strange Holos”: holos means holograms, and the image contains a holographic billboard. Holograms are an iconic communication medium in Star Wars (Princess Leia’s distress message). The challenge name itself is a categorical hint pointing at Star Wars script.
  • Aurebesh is the official Star Wars script, so the writing system matches the theme perfectly.
  • “nerf herder” is one of the most famous lines in the saga. Princess Leia insults Han Solo in The Empire Strikes Back: “…you stuck-up, half-witted, scruffy-looking nerf herder!” (a nerf is a livestock animal in the Star Wars universe). That’s exactly the kind of iconic line a challenge author picks as the payoff for decoding an alien script.

Flag

Transcribe the decoded text directly, keeping the space separator rather than an underscore:

I first submitted STARPWN{nerf_herder} and it was rejected. This CTF’s flag format isn’t actually consistent, so when the decoded content is a natural-language phrase, try the original space separator first instead of assuming it must become snake_case.
