entry.title: A Tumbling Satellite and an Answer Blocked by Floating-Point Error | Tumbling Through Space | STARPWN 2026
entry.content:
🌐 中文版：繁體中文

Like Time to Intercept, this is an interactive orbital-mechanics challenge where you talk to a server over nc. The difference is that here the server practically writes the formula out for you in the hints. What actually blocked me was something boring that every engineer has run into: floating-point precision.

What the challenge is about

Our friends are having difficulties with one of their satellites. It appears it has been struck by space debris and is now tumbling out of control. This is where you come in. The Attitude Determination and Control System (ADCS) is still online, but the automated detumbling sequence has failed. You will have to compute the correct control torques manually.

In plain terms: a satellite has been hit by space debris and is tumbling out of control. Its ADCS (Attitude Determination and Control System, the subsystem that senses and controls which way the satellite points) is still alive, but the automated detumbling routine (stopping a tumbling object’s rotation) is broken, so you need to compute the correct control torques by hand to stabilize it.

After connecting, the server tells you the satellite’s moments of inertia (Ixx, Iyy, Izz, roughly “how much the object resists rotation,” determined by how mass is distributed across the three axes) and its current angular velocity (ωx, ωy, ωz, how fast it’s spinning about each axis). You send back four numbers:

Tx/Ty/Tz are the three-axis control torques (N·m), and duration is the burn time (between 0 and 100 seconds). The torque vector’s magnitude (not the individual axis values) is capped at 1.0 N·m. Success means driving the angular velocity magnitude |ω| below 0.01 rad/s, with 5 attempts per connection.

The server practically writes the answer in the hints

What you see on connecting:

The server has already computed and printed the angular momentum (L = I * ω, essentially “momentum for rotation,” inertia times angular velocity), and hint 3 spells the control law out directly as T = -L / t. There’s no need to derive any dynamics here. The only real work is choosing the burn time t under the constraint that torque magnitude cannot exceed 1.0 N·m.

The physics: cancel all the angular momentum in one burn

For a body whose inertia tensor is diagonal (Ixx, Iyy, Izz independent, with no cross-coupling), the angular momentum is:

Applying a constant torque T for a time t subtracts an impulse T·t from the angular momentum.

So to zero out the angular momentum in a single burn:

The only constraint is the torque vector’s magnitude (not each axis’s absolute value), so |T| ≤ 1.0 N·m. To solve it in one burn with as short a burn as possible (a shorter burn means a smaller window for error between the real dynamics and this simplified linear model), the ideal move is to burn at the full torque limit and back out how long that takes to cancel L:

Computing the numbers

First attempt: blocked by floating-point error

In theory this torque vector’s magnitude is exactly 1.0, but what actually gets sent are values rounded to six decimal places. Recomputing sqrt(Tx²+Ty²+Tz²) from those rounded numbers lands just barely above 1.0 (something like 1.000000008), and the server’s check is ≤ 1.0, so it gets rejected.

The server checks the literal numbers you actually sent, so when designing a numerical solution, don’t sit exactly on a limit boundary. Leave yourself some margin.

Second attempt: leave a safety margin

Scale the whole solution down by a small factor (0.999) so the torque magnitude is clearly under the cap, and scale the burn time up by the same factor to keep the impulse (and therefore the cancellation) unchanged:

|ω| dropped from the original 0.527145 to 0.003808, far below the 0.01 threshold, which also proves this linear model (ignoring gyroscopic coupling terms) is plenty accurate over a burn of this length.

Flag

Takeaways

  1. Hints aren’t decoration; they can be formulas to copy directly. The server prints the control law T = -L/t outright, so this challenge needs no control theory derivation, only correct arithmetic and unit handling.
  2. A “magnitude cap of 1.0” means the vector magnitude, not individual axes. Normalizing -L to a unit vector, multiplying by the maximum allowed torque, and cancelling in one burn with duration = |L| is the most natural solution.
  3. When floating point is involved, never sit exactly on a hard limit. A vector whose magnitude is theoretically exactly 1.0 can easily come back as 1.000000008 once formatted to six decimals and parsed again. Multiplying by a small safety factor (say 0.999) before submitting avoids wasting an attempt, which matters when a connection only gives you 5.
  4. Five attempts is generous for a converging linear model. Even without perfect precision, the first burn usually brings |ω| close to the threshold, and a second corrective burn (here, literally the same solution retried with a safety margin) is enough to cross the 0.01 rad/s line.

entry.title: Supply-Chain Poisoning a Satellite's Ground-Control Software | Starry Hacks | STARPWN 2026
entry.content:
🌐 中文版：繁體中文

Unlike the earlier drone / orbital-mechanics posts, this is a genuine Web / Supply Chain challenge, with the scenario swapped to ground-control software. The gameplay is the classic dependency confusion supply-chain attack, and in the end it came down to using the server’s error message as a data-exfiltration channel to pull the flag out of an environment variable.

What the challenge is about

One of your daemons found a low-rent orbital control stack talking to its bird in the clear. That’s kind of mistake gets people burned, and you just happen to have a lighter and too much time on your hands tonight.

You’ve already found an archive of the flight software repo, a live target, and a supply chain that looks just soft enough to ruin somebody’s night.

In plain terms: you have a leaked flight-software repo, a live online target, and a supply chain soft enough to crush. The task is to get a malicious package update to slip into the normal deployment flow and ultimately extract the satellite’s secret.

Two things are given:

  • A 566-byte fligh_repo.tar.gz (a fragment of the leaked flight-software repo)
  • An online Mission Control web backend

First, the leaked repo: a textbook dependency-confusion flaw

The repo has only three files:

requirements.txt has a single line:

The key snippet in main.py:

This is a classic dependency confusion setup: the flight software imports a third-party package whose name sounds like an internal one (cubesat_upstream_driver), and requirements.txt only pins a lower-bound version (>=1.0.0), with no source index specified and no hash verification.

The risk of writing it this way: if an attacker can make the build process resolve a same-named package with a higher version number from a source the attacker controls, that attacker’s code gets installed and runs along with the normal flow. Worse, handle_command()‘s return value gets dropped straight into the telemetry response, which is effectively a built-in data channel back out.

A look at the online target

The online Mission Control backend has: a command console (buttons for PING, STATUS, ORBIT, HELP, RESET, TRIGGER_BUILD, DEPLOY_SOLAR_PANEL, plus a free-text input), a file-upload widget (accepting .whl / .tar.gz), and a WebSocket pushing live telemetry.

But the UI alone isn’t informative; what matters is the protocol underneath. Instead of clicking buttons, I pulled down the front end’s bundled JS (/assets/index-*.js) to read what the buttons actually say to the backend. That confirmed a few things:

1. Commands are sent over WebSocket with no authentication at all. Free-text commands are wrapped as JSON like this and sent over wss://<host>/ws?sid=<uuid>:

That sid is just a UUID the browser makes with crypto.randomUUID() and stores in localStorage; a fresh one connects just as well, meaning the WebSocket has no session verification and anyone can connect and talk.

2. /openapi.json was left open. FastAPI mounts this API schema by default, laying the whole REST interface bare:

The upload widget uses POST /api/upload (multipart, field name file), and that submit_to_gateway=true parameter is exactly what makes the dependency confusion possible later.

3. The command box has a whitelist. Typing arbitrary text into the command box to test for command injection always returns:

Comparing against the HELP command’s output, the server-side whitelist is exactly the buttons on screen: PING,STATUS,ORBIT,HELP,RESET,DEPLOY_SOLAR_PANEL,TRIGGER_BUILD.

So command injection through the command box is a dead end, and the real path is the dependency-confusion angle spotted in the leaked repo.

The attack chain

The whole chain looks like this:

I built a pure-Python wheel named cubesat-upstream-driver, bumped the version far above 1.0.0 (9.9.x), and uploaded it:

The response has two independent fields:

The score field is actually a decoy. You’d naturally assume score.ok == true means success, but its reason reads marker matched / marker not matched, and that word “marker” is suspicious: it sounds less like checking whether the package runs and more like comparing a string.

So I tested it: I uploaded two packages that behave identically on the gateway side, differing only in whether the __init__.py source literally contained the line if cmd == "DEPLOY_SOLAR_PANEL":. The score.ok flipped between true / false with the presence of that text, while gateway_upload.ok never changed.

That proves score is just a static string comparison on the uploaded source, entirely unrelated to whether the package was installed or imported. It’s only there to lure you into chasing the DEPLOY_SOLAR_PANEL dead end.

What actually matters is gateway_upload.ok, which confirms your package really landed in the index (gateway) the build uses. That field sits quietly next to the eye-catching score, easy to overlook.

A few dead ends along the way

Dead end 1: DEPLOY_SOLAR_PANEL kept failing. TRIGGER_BUILD always returned BUILD|HTTP_200|{"status":"ok"}, but DEPLOY_SOLAR_PANEL always returned TM|ERR|FLIGHT_UNREACHABLE, regardless of the simulated link status shown in the UI.

I eventually realized DEPLOY_SOLAR_PANEL is a deliberate misdirection: it’s bound to a code path that only succeeds with real hardware, which the challenge environment doesn’t have. So no matter how successful the package implant is, that command always returns FLIGHT_UNREACHABLE; it was never the path to the flag. The score marker that checked for if cmd == "DEPLOY_SOLAR_PANEL": is the other half of the same trap: one lures your attention onto this command, the other makes you think you bet right. The command that actually calls the implanted package and succeeds is the unassuming STATUS (the next dead end reveals this).

Dead end 2: PING/STATUS looked completely unaffected. Repeating “upload → build → send PING” always returned the standard TM|HEALTH|OK, and I briefly thought the package wasn’t being picked up at all.

Using Python’s websockets library to bypass the front end and hit the raw WebSocket revealed the truth: PING and ORBIT never call handle_command() and are answered locally by the server, contrary to what the leaked main.py implied. Only STATUS and DEPLOY_SOLAR_PANEL actually call into the implanted package.

Key finding: the exception message itself is the exfiltration channel. Sending malformed messages to the WebSocket (e.g. a number or array in the command field) makes the server leak the raw Python exception message back, such as "'list' object has no attribute 'strip'".

Applying the same idea inside the implanted package, having handle_command() raise an exception instead of returning normally confirmed the server wraps the exception content verbatim into the response:

That’s the real channel for exfiltration: whatever string you put in the exception comes straight back to the browser.

Dead end 3: the first recon attempt failed silently. My first attempt had handle_command() run a scan that, among other things, recursively searched the whole filesystem via a subprocess call. It only returned a bare FLIGHT_UNREACHABLE, with no message at all.

I couldn’t see the server’s internal logs, but I could reason backward from behavior. The key evidence: the same exfiltration mechanism gave completely different results depending only on how fast the payload ran.

  • I’d just confirmed that raising an exception makes the server return the exception message (TM|ERR|EXCEPTION|...). The channel itself works.
  • But this version, with the recursive full-filesystem search, returned a bare FLIGHT_UNREACHABLE, with no exception message, as if the server were waiting on something that never came back.
  • Replacing the payload with a near-instant version (only scanning os.environ and reading a few fixed paths, dropping the subprocess and the filesystem-wide search) made the channel work again immediately, returning the exception with the flag.

In other words, the channel works, the fast payload works, and only the slow payload returns FLIGHT_UNREACHABLE. The one explanation that fits all three: the recursive search was too slow and blew past the server’s timeout for simulating the flight-control round trip. The server reported the link down first, so the exception never got a chance to be caught, formatted, and sent.

When debugging a blind injection like this, always separate “is my code even running” (a fast, simple probe) from “what can my code reach” (the real payload), or an unrelated timeout will make an injection that already succeeded look like a total failure.

The result

With a fast, environment-only scan (reading os.environ and checking a short list of likely flag file paths, no subprocess, no filesystem-wide search), packaged as cubesat-upstream-driver v9.9.20, uploaded, triggered with TRIGGER_BUILD, and queried once more with STATUS:

The flag was sitting right in the flight software’s FLAG environment variable.

Flag

In leetspeak this reads “Through victory my chains ~ break token,” echoing how the secret only leaked once this chain was broken by turning the exception message into an exfiltration channel.

Takeaways

  1. Dependency confusion is a real and quickly-exploitable flaw. As long as a same-named, higher-versioned package can be slipped into a source the build process trusts, the attacker’s code gets installed and runs. The root cause is pinning only a lower-bound version (>=1.0.0) without specifying a source index or hash verification.
  2. Don’t trust the field that merely looks like “success” on screen. score looks like a validation result but is just a static string comparison unrelated to whether the package works, there to steer you toward a dead-end command (DEPLOY_SOLAR_PANEL). The field that actually matters, gateway_upload.ok, is easily overshadowed by the flashier one beside it.
  3. Talk to the underlying protocol directly instead of only through the front end. The React page only sends fixed-format {"type":"command",...}; writing a Python WebSocket client to hit the raw protocol lets you feed malformed messages and catch the interleaving of requests and responses.
  4. Error messages are an exfiltration channel. Once you confirm the server returns exception content verbatim to the client, a deliberate raise is more useful than a normal return for probing unknown calling conventions, since you don’t need to know the correct response format in advance.
  5. The implanted payload has to be fast enough. Recon code that’s too slow can hit an unrelated timeout / protection first, making the whole attack look like a failure and masking the fact that the injection already succeeded. When debugging, separate “is my code running at all” (a fast, simple probe) from “what can my code reach” (the real payload).

entry.title: Right Formula, Wrong Clipboard, Four Failures in a Row | Time to Intercept | STARPWN 2026
entry.content:
🌐 中文版：繁體中文

Unlike the earlier drone-swarm posts, this is a pure orbital-mechanics calculation. You connect to an interactive shell with nc, the server prints numbers at you in real time, and you have to send two answers back within a limited number of attempts. The content itself is a solid physics problem, but what really stuck with me was reconnecting to a fresh instance later and being dumb enough to paste in the previous round’s answer, failing four times in a row.

What the challenge is about

An unknown aggressor satellite has been detected in a higher orbit and is threatening critical space infrastructure. Your mission: calculate a Hohmann transfer to intercept it.

In plain terms: an enemy satellite has been detected in a higher orbit than ours and is threatening critical space infrastructure. The mission is to compute a Hohmann transfer to intercept it. After connecting to the given shell, the screen tells you three things: your own circular orbit’s radius and velocity, the target satellite’s circular orbit radius and velocity, and your current phase angle (the angular difference between the two satellites around Earth). You must return two numbers:

delta_v_burn is how much velocity change (Δv, in m/s) to spend on the burn into the transfer orbit; wait_time is how many seconds to wait before burning so you and the target arrive at the rendezvous point at the same moment. Tolerances are Δv ±10 m/s and wait time ±60 seconds, with only 5 submission attempts per connection. Get it wrong or drop the connection and you reconnect to a completely fresh random problem.

Background: what is a Hohmann transfer

A Hohmann transfer is the most basic and most fuel-efficient orbital transfer in aerospace engineering. If you’re in a low orbit and want to move to a concentric higher orbit, you don’t accelerate the whole way up; you just make two burns at the right moments.

The first burn puts you on an elliptical “transfer orbit” whose one end touches your original low orbit and whose other end touches the target’s high orbit. The second burn, made when you reach that high end, straightens you out into the new circular orbit.

If you’re interested, this video explains it well: https://youtu.be/KdHI5Fn9Fu8

This challenge only scores the first burn (entering the transfer orbit), so the problem simplifies to: compute how much Δv the first burn costs, and pick the moment to burn so that you and the target meet on time at the far end of the transfer orbit.

It’s a fairly standard orbital-mechanics problem with two key parts: how much velocity change the burn costs, and how long to wait before burning.

Computing Δv: the standard vis-viva equation

The transfer ellipse’s semi-major axis is just the average of your orbital radius and the target’s:

Use the vis-viva equation (which relates velocity to radius at any point on an elliptical orbit) to get the transfer orbit’s velocity at the starting point, your current radius r1:

There’s a small trick here: don’t plug in the textbook Earth value for mu (the gravitational parameter, Earth’s mass times the gravitational constant) of 398600.4418 km³/s². Instead, derive it directly from the circular orbit velocity the challenge itself prints:

On a circular orbit, gravity supplies exactly the centripetal force, so v² / r = mu / r², and cancelling gives mu = v² * r. The Δv computed this way matches the server’s correct answer almost exactly (error on the order of 0.001 m/s), with no need to worry about whether the challenge’s Earth radius or GM constant matches the textbook definition.

Computing the wait time: where I actually got stuck

The time to fly half the transfer ellipse (from the start to the rendezvous point) is:

Classical Hohmann rendezvous phasing theory goes like this: suppose you’re on the inner, faster orbit (angular rate n1 = v1/r1) and the target is on the outer, slower orbit (angular rate n2 = v2/r2). For the two to meet at the far end of the transfer ellipse (180 degrees away), the target must lead you by a specific angle at the moment of the burn:

(Intuitively: during the transfer you sweep a full 180 degrees, while the target only advances n2 · t_transfer, so the target has to lead by that much for you both to arrive together.)

Now the problem: given the current phase angle φ0 the challenge prints, how do you derive the wait time from the difference between φ0 and φ_required? The textbook-intuition formula would be:

But this formula is wrong. My first submission of Δv=160.73, wait_time=16997.80 had the Δv accepted while the wait time was rejected (Wait time error too large).

That partial rejection is actually a very precise diagnostic: it means the transfer orbit’s own physics (a_t, v_p, t_transfer) is completely fine, and the only problem is the phase angle’s direction convention.

Since only the wait time was rejected, the issue has to be in how the challenge’s phase angle maps onto φ0 in the formula, not in the transfer orbital mechanics. Reversing the subtraction order, asking instead “how much further must φ0 rotate in the other direction to reach φ_required”, gives the formula that actually matches the server:

Full verification:

Submitting 121.935 26900.962:

That’s the complete solution for the original Time to Intercept.
The challenge later reopened as a V2: same service, same scoring, just a different port. In theory the formula carries over directly, and it did. What’s interesting is what happened next.

V2: same formula, four failures from a slip of the hand

V2’s description, format, and tolerances are identical to V1; the only difference is a fresh set of random parameters. Connecting to the new instance printed:

The trouble was that just before connecting to this fresh instance, I’d finished another connection (whose parameters were r1=6850.870 km, r2=7534.987 km, phase=199.425°, giving Δv 179.259). On the new connection, my first four submissions only adjusted the wait time while the Δv stayed at the 179.26 computed on the previous connection:

Every response was Delta-v error too large, which was the server spelling out that the Δv itself needed recomputing, not that the wait time was insufficiently precise. Each connection’s parameters are fixed (all 5 attempts on one connection share the same r1/r2/v1/v2/phase), but parameters are never shared between connections. Pasting the correctly-computed Δv from the previous connection into a new one gives a familiar-looking number that is already stale.

Recomputing with the new connection’s printed parameters:

The fifth and final attempt:

So this one cost me four attempts purely from lazily reusing the previous round’s answer.

Flag

Takeaways

  1. Don’t trust textbook constants for the gravitational parameter; derive it from the numbers the challenge gives you. The relation mu = v² · r always holds on a circular orbit, and the mu derived from it automatically matches the challenge’s internal Earth model, so you never have to guess which Earth radius or GM constant the author used.
  2. A “partially correct” server response is very precise debugging information. Having only the wait time rejected while the Δv quietly passed confirmed the transfer orbit’s physics (semi-major axis, vis-viva, transfer time) was already correct, narrowing the problem precisely to the phase angle’s direction convention without re-suspecting the whole algorithm.
  3. Phase-angle sign conventions are the classic trap in rendezvous problems. Textbook formulas assume a particular measurement direction and reference, so when a challenge hands you a “bare” phase angle without defining it, be ready to try the opposite direction. The two differ by exactly one synodic period, and when one is wrong the natural next step is simply to flip the direction.
  4. A “V2” of the same challenge does not mean the same numbers. Even with identical code and identical formulas, any service that randomizes per connection makes the previous connection’s correct answer stale data in the new one. The server will usually tell you honestly which field is wrong, which is far more reliable than blind guessing, and the right move is to recompute the whole set from the numbers currently on screen rather than tweaking only the number you happen to be staring at.

entry.title: Three Drones Lose GPS at Once | Deadly Parade | STARPWN 2026
entry.content:
🌐 中文版：繁體中文

This challenge is a sequel to the previous one, One to Rule Them All, in the same Prismantir drone-swarm world.

But the gameplay is completely different: the last one was protocol security, while this one is a pure signal-localization problem. And honestly, I submitted two wrong answers and had to take the long way around before remembering how to compute a circumcenter from middle-school geometry.

What the challenge is about

Prismantir was assigned to protect a VIP during DynaCon’s parade, and their team already had their hands full. They stopped the attacker before he even got out of bed, but his devices were already in place and active. The sky above the Glittercity was tuned to a dead channel. No one realized what was happening until Prismantir’s drones began falling from the sky like ducks. Your mission is to find where these deadly toys could have been hiding.

In plain terms: the Prismantir team was protecting a VIP at DynaCon’s parade and was already stretched thin on manpower. They caught the attacker before he even got out of bed, but his jamming devices were already running, and the radio channel above Glittercity had been tuned to dead silence, and nobody realized something was wrong until Prismantir’s drones started falling from the sky one after another like ducks.

The goal: find where these jamming devices were hiding.

The challenge gives just one thing: PRISM_S05_DNCN_20260831.pcap, a roughly 198 MB packet capture with over two million packets.

First, confirm what kind of packets these are

The result shows a Linux cooked-mode capture v2 (linktype 276) capture, totaling 2.079 million packets over 3159 seconds.

Looking with tshark:

Every packet is 127.0.0.1:14550 <-> 127.0.0.1:45177, the standard MAVLink UDP port on loopback. Same as the previous challenge, One to Rule Them All, it’s the MAVLink v2 protocol (the 0xFD magic at the start), just wrapped in a full pcap (Linux SLL2 cooked capture + IPv4 + UDP) this time, rather than a bare byte stream.

Another performance problem, so hand-roll a parser again

tshark/pymavlink are far too slow for two million packets. Same as my experience in Connect the Dots, I just hand-rolled a parser, manually peeling apart the pcap record format, SLL2 header, IP header, UDP header, and MAVLink v2 header:

Written this way, two million messages parse in about three seconds, more than an order of magnitude faster. The parsed result shows a full patrol fleet of 10 drones (sysid 1–10) plus one ground station (sysid 255), the same fleet setup as in Connect the Dots.

Find the incident: filter warning-level system messages

MAVLink has a STATUSTEXT (msgid 253) message type dedicated to text status messages, with a severity field.

Filtering for severity ≤ 4 (warning and above), the attack scene immediately appears:

Three drones (sysid 2, 5, 3) show an identical GPS-jamming signature: the EKF (Extended Kalman Filter, the algorithm a drone uses to fuse sensor data and figure out “where am I now”) variance spiking, the EKF downgrading into LAND protection mode, both IMUs (inertial measurement units) stopping GPS aiding, and SmartRTL (smart return-to-launch) aborting due to an unreliable position.

sysid 9’s failure is a separate unrelated issue (telemetry buffer full), so rule it out.

Pinpoint the exact moment GPS was lost

STATUSTEXT timestamps actually lag; a more accurate approach is to look directly at GPS_RAW_INT (msgid 24)’s fix_type field, the first-hand signal of GPS fix status.

An easily-overlooked detail here: MAVLink fields are stored sorted by type size from largest to smallest, not in declaration order. If you build the struct format in the documented field order, mixed field sizes will misalign everything after. The safe approach is to check the message type’s real wire order with pymavlink:

In fact fix_type only ever takes two values:

1 (no fix) and 6 (RTK precision fix), with no gradual signal degradation in between, just a clean binary switch. That’s a clue in itself: it means a sharply-bounded jamming area, not the gradient of a naturally weakening signal.

Here I grab the moment each affected drone first shows fix_type=1, the coordinate where it truly crossed the death-zone boundary (10 to 14 seconds before the EKF actually declared failsafe):

sysidlatlon
236.0924468-115.2422644
536.0997050-115.2479014
336.0778960-115.2440574

I also cross-validated with SIMSTATE (msgid 164, the true coordinates reported by ArduPilot’s SITL simulator, bypassing EKF/GPS entirely) to confirm each drone really did end up near these coordinates.

But I guessed wrong twice

First: just averaging the three points.

Reverse-geocoding (Nominatim) landed in a Spring Valley area community called Spanish Trail. I submitted starpwn{Spanish_Trail} and starpwn{Spanish_Trail_Country_Club}, both wrong.

Second: all three points’ addresses pointed to the same larger-area community name, Spring Valley.

I submitted starpwn{Spring_Valley}, still wrong.

Where was the problem? The three points roughly form a near-collinear line, and taking a simple average of such a distribution corresponds to no meaningful geometric property. It’s not triangulation, just forcing an answer.

The correct approach: circumcenter triangulation

If the jammer’s effective range is roughly circular, then each drone’s “first crossing into the death zone” coordinate is, in theory, a point on this circle’s boundary, and should be roughly equidistant from the center.

And the point equidistant from three known points is the circumcenter of the triangle they form, the very thing taught in middle-school geometry.

Here I first project lat/lon into meter-unit planar coordinates with a simple local planar projection (to_xy / from_xy), because the circumcenter formula is planar geometry and applying it directly to lat/lon would distort due to Earth’s curvature; after computing the circumcenter I convert back to lat/lon. The result is a clean circle with a radius of nearly 2 km:

Dropping this coordinate on a map:

The marker lands precisely on a clearly-named park, Echo Trail Park, right next to the Spanish Trail golf course and the Flamingo Wash detention basin, open but with tree cover, a very plausible place to actually hide a jammer.

Flag

Takeaways

  1. MAVLink fields are laid out by type size, not the declaration order in the docs. Before hand-rolling a parser for a new message type, check the real wire order with pymavlink‘s mavlink_map[id].orders or the official XML definition. Don’t build the struct format from the docs’ field list order.
  2. A clean binary signal is more notable than a gradual noisy one. fix_type switching only between 1 and 6 with no intermediate values hints that this is a deliberately designed, discoverable event worth investigating specifically, rather than assuming real-world GPS naturally fades like that.
  3. Averaging is not triangulation. Taking the centroid of three roughly-collinear “boundary entry points” corresponds to no real geometric meaning; when those points represent “the boundary of entering a circular effective range,” the correct estimate is their circumcenter, and here that solution was clearly more accurate, landing directly on a named park rather than the vague result of a centroid landing on some random residential street.
  4. Cross-validate when you have ground truth. ArduPilot SITL’s SIMSTATE message reports the simulator’s true coordinates, bypassing the whole EKF/GPS judgment chain. Using it to confirm the jamming-entry coordinates ruled out “the drone actually drifted elsewhere,” letting debugging focus on the localization method itself rather than suspecting the data.
  5. When stuck on wrong answers, look at the map itself, not just the geocoder’s text. Reverse-geocoding APIs usually return the nearest street name, not necessarily the most prominent named landmark nearby (a park or golf course may be marked on OSM but not surfaced by a reverse-address query). Actually opening the map to see what’s around that coordinate is what made the named POI Echo Trail Park emerge.

entry.title: A Stray Drone Writing in the Sky with Its Flight Path | Connect the Dots | STARPWN 2026
entry.content:
🌐 中文版：繁體中文

In the same Prismantir drone-swarm world, this is the challenge with the shortest story but the most memorable payoff.

150 million bytes of raw telemetry, and at the very end you open an image to find a drone writing letters in the sky with its own flight path.

What the challenge is about

While known for their big eye in the sky, Prismantir huge drone fleet is also a behemoth to keep in control. Every night, each drone patrols its assigned block, following its route with clockwork precision. But tonight, one unit broke the formation. Can you trace where did it go?

In plain terms: Prismantir’s huge drone fleet patrols its assigned city blocks every night, following routes with clockwork precision. But tonight one unit broke formation, and the task is to find where it went. You get a single file: PRISM_S03_B10-30_20260830.raw, about 149.7 MB.

First, confirm the file format

Looking at the header with xxd:

Two things jump out immediately: the plaintext string ArduCopter V4.6.1, which is the ArduPilot drone firmware’s version string.

And every record starts with 0xFD, the MAVLink v2 frame start marker.

Manually peeling the first packet by the MAVLink v2 header format matches perfectly: payload length, sysid=1, compid=1, msgid=253 (STATUSTEXT), content "ArduCopter V4.6.1 (57591cb8)".

So this file is a raw MAVLink v2 stream with no extra wrapping. Unlike a typical .tlog, there’s no per-packet timestamp outer layer here, just MAVLink packets written one right after another.

pymavlink is too slow, so hand-roll a parser again

First I tried pymavlink:

It technically works, but parsing a 150 MB file this way, with pure Python walking the full ardupilotmega dialect lookup table, is slow enough to make you question your life choices.

Since MAVLink v2’s wrapping is itself simple (each field is at a fixed position, and the payload length is in the second byte), I just wrote a minimal parser:

Because this capture is a clean, uninterrupted stream, walking it linearly needs no resync at all, and all 4,158,449 messages parse in about 3 seconds, more than an order of magnitude faster than the general library. The rule of thumb here: if the standard library becomes the bottleneck and the protocol format is simple, it’s worth hand-rolling a dedicated parser.

Find the fleet

Tallying sysid (MAVLink’s marker for which vehicle sent a message) reveals 10 different drones (sysid 1–10).

Each sends roughly the same proportion of message types (HEARTBEAT, GPS_RAW_INT, GLOBAL_POSITION_INT, ATTITUDE, STATUSTEXT), perfectly matching the “a huge fleet patrolling simultaneously” scenario.

The STATUSTEXT contents are all just standard ArduPilot auto-mission logs (disarm, takeoff, fly to waypoint…), and no drone’s text log hides anything unique, so the information must be in the coordinates.

Plot each drone’s coordinates

Parse GLOBAL_POSITION_INT (msgid 33) to get each drone’s coordinates:

(MAVLink stores lat/lon as int32 scaled by 1e7, so divide back.)

The coordinates fall around latitude 36.11–36.16, longitude -115.19 to -115.32, which is Las Vegas on the map, and makes sense since this CTF is tied to DEF CON.

Overlay all 10 drones’ tracks (longitude, latitude; one colour per drone) on a single plot and the answer jumps out:

Nine drones’ tracks are tight, boxy street-grid patterns, each confined to its assigned rectangular block, matching the challenge’s “patrol your block precisely every night.” Only the red one (sysid 4) completely ignores block boundaries, sweeping across others’ turf in big loops, its shape clearly different from the other 9. That’s the one that broke formation.

It should be obvious by now: sysid 4 spells out BVLOS:

But those four letters aren’t the flag themselves.

Flag

BVLOS is a very common acronym in drone regulation: Beyond Visual Line Of Sight, meaning flying a drone beyond the operator’s unaided visual range. It fits the scenario well:

a drone that flew off to where no one could see it. Assembling the flag per the given example format (each word capitalized, underscore-separated):

starpwn{Beyond_Visual_Line_Of_Sight}

Takeaways

  1. Judge a file’s format by more than its extension. An undocumented .raw file can be identified and worked on just from the leading 0xFD magic byte and the plaintext firmware version string.
  2. When a general library hits a wall on large data, hand-rolling the protocol parse is often well worth it. MAVLink v2’s header is fixed-length and self-describing (the payload length is in the second byte), so a linear walk with struct.unpack_from is more than an order of magnitude faster than the full dialect library.
  3. sysid is the most natural way to split multiple vehicles mixed into one stream. When a capture might contain more than one vehicle, tally sysid first.
  4. The challenge name “Connect the dots” is literal. Spelling text with a flight path is a real-world amateur stunt (like Strava art), and taking the name as a “how to solve” hint rather than just flavour points straight at the solution: plot the ordered coordinate points and read them with your eyes.

entry.title: From One Captured Flight Controller into a Whole Drone Swarm | One to Rule Them All | STARPWN 2026
entry.content:
🌐 中文版：繁體中文

This is the challenge with the most complete storyline in STARPWN 2026, I think. Technically it’s not especially brutal. It just stitches a hard-looking puzzle together with a few basic but easily-overlooked protocol features, and the final solution is almost comically simple. That said, I stepped in every pothole along the way.

What the challenge is about

The backstory reads:

Prismantir’s team got hands on an enemy drone last night - the rest of its swarm went dark before anyone else could be brought in. Its flight controller landed on your desk this morning, still warm. One unit is all we get but word is they all share the same secret, so make it count before someone finds out and changes it.

In plain terms: we captured an enemy drone last night, and its whole “swarm” (a group of cooperatively flying drones) went dark and vanished before we could act. The captured drone’s “flight controller” (the drone’s brain, a board with sensors, GPS, and a radio module) is now on your desk, still warm. We have just this one unit, but intel says the whole swarm shares the same secret, so use it to the fullest before they notice and change it.

Three things are given:

ItemDescription
eeprom.bin (16,384 bytes)A raw memory dump of the captured drone’s flight controller: static, offline, won’t change again
Web UIA ground-station web backend showing a group of still-alive, still-flying drones
MAVLink Telemetry (tcp:host:port)A live connection you can talk to the drones with directly

Before diving in, some background: MAVLink is the most common comms protocol in the drone world, basically the shared language drones and ground stations use to talk. A ground station can ask a drone “how high are you flying, what’s your battery?” and can also command “fly to this coordinate” or “disarm.”

Normally this protocol has no encryption and no authentication, so anyone who can connect can eavesdrop or even impersonate the ground station and issue commands. To prevent this, MAVLink 2 added an optional feature called message signing: the ground station and the drone each hold the same 32-byte key, and before each command is sent, a signature is computed from that key plus an incrementing timestamp and appended to the packet; the receiver recomputes the signature and only executes if it matches.

There’s actually a real-world CVE for this: CVE-2026-1579.
The vulnerability stems from not enabling MAVLink 2.0 message signing, which after all is not enabled by default.

In other words, whoever has that 32-byte key can pretend to be a legitimate ground station and command the entire swarm. And the core of this challenge is that the key is printed in the captured drone’s memory.

First, see what’s in these 16KB

eeprom.bin is exactly 16,384 bytes, which is the standard size the open-source drone firmware ArduPilot uses under simulation (SITL, Software-In-The-Loop) to store data it needs to remember after power loss: flight parameters, mission waypoints, geofence settings, and of course the signing key we’re after.

Checking the StorageManager.cpp definition in the ArduPilot source, this 16KB space is internally carved into several fixed-size, fixed-position regions, like a hard drive split into partitions:

The problem is, going byte by byte through 16 KB in a hex editor is tedious and error-prone. A more efficient approach is to first scan which regions actually contain data by counting the non-zero bytes in each partition. A region that’s all 0x00 is usually empty and can be skipped first; only ones with content need a closer look. I wrote a few lines of Python against the StorageManager layout to tally each region:

With this table, “how to judge what’s normal” becomes much more concrete:

  • StorageParam (flight parameters): plenty of non-zero data, but parsed with ArduPilot’s parameter format (name + value entries), it’s all calibration values and sensor settings, normal parameters in reasonable ranges, with no odd strings or structures smuggled in. Normal.
  • StorageMission (mission waypoints): also has data, but parsed into waypoints it’s a very ordinary circular patrol (take off → loop → repeat), nothing hidden.
  • StorageRally / StorageFence (rally points / geofence): almost all 0x00, with StorageFence leaving just two residual non-zero bytes, a common forensic artifact of embedded storage “not actually wiping the underlying data after deletion,” not deliberately hidden.
  • The big unused middle: all zeros, skip it.
  • StorageKeys: this is the one that stands out. Its first 4 bytes are d1 fc 52 38, not noise but a recognizable magic number (next section explains why), which immediately says there’s a fixed structure here.

Zooming into StorageKeys‘s 64 bytes:

The StorageKeys block at offset 0x1F80 (8064 decimal) is where the MAVLink signing key lives, and the real meat of the challenge.

Decoding the key hit a classic pothole

ArduPilot’s GCS_Signing.cpp defines the C struct used to store the key:

There’s an easy trap here: this struct is not PACKED. In C/C++, without explicit tight packing, the compiler inserts padding between fields for CPU efficiency, aligning each field to a multiple of its own size. Here: magic takes 4 bytes (offset 0–3), and the next field timestamp is an 8-byte type, so the compiler requires it to start at a multiple of 8. But we’re only at offset 4, so the compiler inserts 4 bytes of 0x00 padding to make timestamp actually start at offset 8.

If you miss this padding and decode directly with struct.unpack_from('<IQ', data, offset) (meaning a 4-byte int + an 8-byte long with no gap), every subsequent field reads 4 bytes of garbage too far. The nastiest part of this bug is that it doesn’t error out. It quietly hands you something that looks like a key but is completely wrong. So the only reliable check is to compare the magic number after parsing: if it matches, your offset is right.

The actual parsing code:

The actual output:

The key is the first line’s magic. Compared against the definition copied from GCS_Signing.cpp:

The decoded magic = 0x3852fcd1 matches the hardcoded SIGNING_KEY_MAGIC byte for byte. That confirms two things at once: offset 0x1F80 is right (it really points to the start of the SigningKey struct), and the 4 padding bytes were skipped correctly (otherwise every field after magic would be misaligned and magic itself wouldn’t match). Since this “checksum” passes, the 32-byte key read afterward can be trusted:

Here’s the actual hex dump, with each field boxed in colour:

  • The red 4 bytes are the magic (little-endian, so the file order is reversed: d1 fc 52 38)
  • Grey is the 4 bytes of padding
  • Blue is the 8-byte timestamp; the green 32 bytes are the actual key to use

Use the key to connect to the live drone swarm

With the key in hand, the next step is to verify that “they all share the same secret” is literal: can this key dug out of an offline EEPROM authenticate directly against the still-flying drones online?

Python’s most-used MAVLink library, pymavlink, has built-in message-signing support:

The actual run: successfully received 1,397 parameters, meaning this key is the same one the airborne swarm uses, and signature authentication fully passed. The same key tested against the other 4 drones in the swarm was valid for all of them.

At this point I had full ground-station-level access, able to read any drone’s full parameter table, mission list, and even issue flight commands.

Stuck for a long time: a pile of reasonable-looking guesses that were all dead ends

After getting full control, I spent a lot of time guessing. Potholes I stepped in:

  • Comparing the 5 drones’ parameter differences for hidden messages
  • Plotting the flight paths to see if they looked like text
  • Checking the map webpage’s CSS filters
  • Listening to WebSocket packets, grabbing dataflash logs…

All dead ends, clean with zero clues. I even seriously considered a Lord of the Rings angle (the challenge is called One to Rule Them All, after all), and tested “verbs” like changing flight mode, triggering Return-to-Launch, and force-disarming, all of which just produced standard ArduPilot system messages, nothing.

The real breakthrough was going back to a feature I’d been using but not to its full extent: MAVLink FTP.

Ref: https://mavlink.io/en/services/ftp.html

The key turn: list the whole filesystem

Besides reading sensor values and issuing flight commands, MAVLink also defines a whole file-transfer protocol (via the FILE_TRANSFER_PROTOCOL message type), letting the ground station browse, upload, and download files in the flight controller’s internal virtual filesystem, like operating a USB drive.

This protocol has an OP_ListDirectory op code whose function is a genuine directory listing, equivalent to running ls in a terminal.

My biggest early blind spot: because I’d read the ArduPilot docs and knew a few common filenames (like @SYS/storage.bin, crash_dump.bin), I kept looking by “guess a filename → open it directly” and never actually ran a full recursive listing of the root. That’s basically shooting in the dark, since you can’t find a file you don’t know exists.

pymavlink has a fully-featured FTP client class MAVFTP, usable directly on the already-signed connection:

The full filesystem that came back:

Apart from DCIM/flag.jpg, every file and folder is exactly what a fresh ArduPilot SITL install already has. The name DCIM (Digital Camera IMages) is itself perfectly plausible (it feels like photos, and it’s on my phone’s memory card too), and it echoes the camera-control commands I’d seen earlier in the mission list. So it’s hidden under a normal-looking, non-suspicious path, not a dead-giveaway name like flag.txt.

Download the file, see the flag

Grab it with the same MAVFTP object:

The first attempt gave BurstReadFile failed, generic error, and the second successfully pulled down the full 40,536 bytes, confirmed a valid JPEG.

Opening it:

An aerial night shot of a brightly-lit stadium in the rain, with a message projected in glowing text on the roof. Zooming in on the rooftop text:

“machines never pledged to be allegiant”

This is the real Allegiant Stadium in Las Vegas (home of the NFL’s Las Vegas Raiders). The line itself is a pun: “allegiant” is both the stadium’s name and the English word meaning “loyal, faithful.”

It perfectly echoes the challenge’s core scenario: a captured machine that was never truly loyal to anyone, and the shared-key mechanism made it trivial to turn. The assembled flag:

Postscript: an early clue I didn’t understand at the time

Before finding flag.jpg, a side clue had already hinted vaguely at Allegiant Stadium, but I just couldn’t connect it to the answer at the time. Reading each swarm drone’s takeoff/landing coordinates via MAVLink and plotting them on a real satellite map, several drones’ coordinates landed precisely in the centre of the same building:

The oval building circled in red is Allegiant Stadium, its position relative to the highway interchange matching exactly. I took it for coincidence at the time and didn’t dig in; in hindsight it was the puzzle’s planted foreshadowing. The answer was set at this stadium all along, it just needed the FTP find of flag.jpg to actually read out the riddle.

Takeaways

  1. MAVLink FTP’s ListDirectory is a genuine directory-listing feature, so don’t treat it as just a “grab known files” tool. A full recursive listing of root takes only seconds and leaves nothing non-standard hidden, with no guessing needed.
  2. A plausible-sounding path name gets a pass more easily than an obviously suspicious filename. When inspecting a system, don’t rely only on the “that name looks weird” instinct; do the carpet-bomb listing anyway.
  3. When parsing C binary structures, always check for the PACKED attribute first. Without it, the compiler inserts padding to align fields, and a seamless format string silently misreads every subsequent field. To check whether parsing is right, verify any known fixed constant in the structure. If it matches, the offset is right.
  4. When many reasonable-looking clues all turn up clean and empty, it’s usually a signal: go back and check whether there’s a basic protocol feature you never actually used to the fullest, rather than inventing ever more complex hypotheses from the data you already have. This challenge’s final solution was, from start to finish, just the two most basic MAVLink features, message signing and file listing, with no fancy tricks.

entry.title: Dissecting NASA's HDTN Architecture: How Does Space DTN Actually Work?
entry.content:
🌐 中文版：繁體中文

Preface: from the concept of DTN to a space network that actually works

In the previous post, Why Space Networking Needs DTN: From TCP/IP’s Limits to Deep-Space Networks, I laid out the most fundamental differences between space networks and the terrestrial Internet. On Earth, we usually expect a complete, immediately-usable path between source and destination. Even if a packet is occasionally lost along the way, TCP can handle it through a whole set of mechanisms like ACK, timeout, and retransmission.

But in space, a disconnection doesn’t necessarily mean a fault. For example, the situation might be: a satellite flying out of a ground station’s visible range, a lunar rover entering a crater, or a spacecraft temporarily shutting off its comms module to save energy. Connections between nodes can also be affected by orbital position, celestial occlusion, antenna direction, and communication schedules.

So a space network can’t only look at is there a path to the destination right now? It must further consider: when is the next opportunity to forward data?, until then, which node should hold the data?, and if the contact window suddenly vanishes, how is transmission resumed?

These are the problems Delay/Disruption-Tolerant Networking (DTN) tries to solve.

My previous post already introduced DTN’s most core operating model:

But that’s still a relatively abstract concept. Because if we really want to deploy DTN on the ISS, satellites, lunar relay stations, or even future deep-space networks, what software components are needed behind the scenes? And there are many questions:

After data enters a node, how does the system decide whether to send immediately or temporarily write to disk?
When a contact window appears, who’s responsible for telling the system to release the data again?
When a path suddenly drops, how does the system recompute the next hop?

High-rate Delay Tolerant Networking (HDTN), developed by NASA Glenn Research Center, is exactly an implementation that turns DTN from an old abstract concept into an engineering system. Let’s keep reading. [1][2]

What is HDTN?

HDTN stands for High-rate Delay Tolerant Networking. It isn’t a new protocol unrelated to DTN, but a DTN implementation designed for high-bandwidth needs. Recall that DTN solves the reliable-transport problem in space networks:

  • Nodes aren’t always connected
  • Communication delays can be very long
  • The network topology changes over time
  • Data may have to stay at a relay node for a while
  • The communication path may suddenly drop mid-transfer

But as laser comms, high-resolution imagery, scientific instrument data, and large file transfers increase, the system faces another problem:

Even if DTN can tolerate disconnection, can it transfer large amounts of data quickly when a contact window appears?

Early DTN implementations mostly ran in resource-constrained environments, prioritizing stability and mission needs over extremely high throughput. However, future space missions need not just the ability to transmit, but to transmit as much data as possible within a limited contact window. So NASA developed HDTN to improve DTN’s processing efficiency through modern hardware, parallel processing, and a modular architecture. [1][2]

Why does NASA need High-rate DTN?

In a Technical Memorandum released in 2022, NASA Glenn Research Center used the International Space Station (ISS) as the test and integration scenario for HDTN. The ISS does have computers, but not just computers; it’s a complex environment with many subsystems (an onboard computer usually has a great many subsystems), science payloads, radio equipment, and ground networks. [1]

When science data is sent from the ISS back to a research team, it may pass through multiple nodes:

The above is just one possible delivery path. Also, different data has different needs. Some may be software updates, some telemetry, some large science files, and some may include imagery and streaming content. Each kind of data differs in size, priority, and bandwidth need. And the ISS keeps moving in orbit, so the comms links won’t stay permanently stable. Some links may be temporarily available, and may suddenly drop.

This means the ISS network needs to simultaneously have:

  • High throughput
  • Local storage capability
  • Routing management
  • Disconnection recovery
  • Interoperability between different DTN implementations
  • Support for different underlying transports

HDTN’s goal is to build a high-speed DTN system that can automatically manage data flow in such environments. [1][2]

Understanding HDTN through a logistics system

Let’s return to the logistics analogy from the previous post, which compared DTN to an international logistics system (like DHL).

The traditional Internet is more like a real-time phone call:

DTN is more like logistics delivery:

When shipping a package, the sender and recipient don’t need to be online at the same time. The trucks, planes, ports, and distribution centers don’t need to form a complete transport line at the same second; the package can stay at a logistics center and wait for the next truck or plane. HDTN can be understood as the automated warehousing and dispatch platform behind this logistics system:

Logistics systemHDTN
PackageBundle
Consolidation center entranceIngress
WarehouseStorage
Flight and truck scheduleContact Plan
Dispatch and route planningScheduler / Router
Shipping dockEgress
Next logistics centerNext Hop
The actual truck, plane, or ship usedConvergence Layer

This analogy should resonate, and you can probably see that HDTN doesn’t just send data out. What it really does is decide, based on future usable communication opportunities, whether data should be forwarded immediately now, held temporarily, or rerouted another way.

HDTN’s core architecture

I personally feel that text descriptions alone aren’t as clear as looking directly at Fig. 1 in the original paper. The figure below is the HDTN modules interaction, an overview of how all the internal modules interact. [1]

Fig. 1. HDTN modules interaction. Source: [1]

From this figure you can intuitively see that HDTN’s core components roughly include Ingress, Storage, Scheduler, Router, and Egress, with BPGen, BPSink, a Web Interface, the Contact Plan, and a CGR Client coordinating externally. [1] This separation of responsibilities is quite similar to the mainstream microservices or event-driven architecture in modern cloud systems, where each component focuses on a specific task and exchanges state through events.

Bundle

In an ordinary IP network, we often use the packet as the basic data unit. But in DTN, the main data unit is the bundle. A bundle can be understood as a standard shipping container in the DTN world. It contains not just application data, but also the source, destination, creation time, lifetime, and other metadata.

In a traditional network, a packet is usually expected to be forwarded immediately, but a bundle is different. From the start, it’s designed to be held at a node, wait, re-forward, and even cross multiple non-continuous contact windows. It’s also specifically noted that a bundle’s size isn’t fixed. Besides measuring how many bits can be transferred per second, you must also consider how many bundles the system can process per second. [1] In other words, the challenge of achieving high-speed DTN isn’t just network-card speed, because even with sufficient bandwidth, if every bundle requires heavy parsing, memory allocation, and state management, the CPU can still become the bottleneck.

Ingress

Ingress is the first stop after a bundle enters an HDTN node. It receives the bundle, parses the header, confirms the data’s source and destination, and decides the next step based on the current link state. The simplest logic is:

If the link is currently usable, Ingress can use a cut-through forwarding style, handing the bundle directly to Egress, reducing unnecessary disk I/O and I/O wait. If the link is currently unusable, the bundle first enters Storage. This is the first key decision in Store-Carry-Forward:

Can I forward now, or must I store first?

Storage

In an ordinary network, a router usually doesn’t hold packets for long; ideally a packet is forwarded immediately after reaching the router. If the queue fills up, packets may simply be dropped and left for the upper-layer protocol to handle again.

But in DTN, waiting may be a normal state. Suppose a lunar probe needs to send data via a relay satellite, but the next contact window won’t appear for two hours. In that case, the system can’t simply drop the data, nor retry infinitely. Storage‘s job is to let the bundle safely stay on the node, waiting for the next transmission opportunity.

HDTN’s Storage uses a multi-threaded implementation and can spread data across multiple disks. [1] The reason is intuitive: when large amounts of data enter a node at once, disk I/O and data management itself can become a performance bottleneck, so the Storage module is quite important. Unlike a backup component on terrestrial networks that can always be scaled out, it’s a core part of the space DTN architecture.

Contact Plan

On an ordinary terrestrial network, a router usually chooses a path based on the current network state (SDN), but a space network adds a very special dimension: time. The position changes of satellites, space stations, lunar relay stations, and ground stations are often predictable. A given link may not exist now, but appear ten minutes later, and disappear again five minutes after that. So DTN needs to handle a special piece of data: the Contact Plan.

The Contact Plan can be understood as a timetable of future contact windows.

This means:

In a real mission, the Contact Plan may contain more nodes, more windows, and different link rates. The biggest difference from terrestrial networks is: space routing isn’t judged only by “spatial topology,” but must also consider temporal topology.

Scheduler and Router

With a Contact Plan, the system also needs components to manage data flow according to the schedule. In this HDTN architecture, the Scheduler reads the Contact Plan and emits events based on link state: [1]

When Ingress receives a linkUp event, it knows a destination is currently usable and can hand the bundle directly to Egress. When Storage receives a linkUp event, it can also start releasing previously-held bundles to Egress.

Conversely, if a link drops, the system stops transmitting and reevaluates subsequent paths. On the other hand, the Router‘s job is to compute the next hop. The Router decides which node a bundle should go to next based on the Contact Plan and destination, then notifies Egress to update the Outduct.

HDTN’s routing mindset isn’t quite the same as ordinary shortest-path algorithms. An ordinary BFS or Dijkstra might only ask:

Which path is shortest right now?

But space DTN must also ask:

Which path will appear at the right time?
How long can this window last?
Is the usable bandwidth enough for this batch of bundles?
If this window is missed, how long until the next opportunity?

This is also the core concept of Contact Graph Routing (CGR); see the previous post too.

Version differences: the division of responsibilities between Scheduler and Router

A version difference should be added here. The Technical Memorandum describes Scheduler and Router separately: [1]

  • The Scheduler reads the Contact Plan
  • The Scheduler emits linkUp and linkDown
  • The Router communicates with the CGR Client
  • The Router passes RouteUpdate to Egress

But in NASA’s currently-public HDTN GitHub README, the Router’s responsibilities have been adjusted. The README currently mentions: [3]

  • The Router manages link-availability state based on the Contact Plan
  • The Router uses Dijkstra’s algorithm to compute the next hop
  • The Router recomputes paths after a link suddenly drops or the Contact Plan updates
  • The Router passes RouteUpdate to Egress

So when reading the HDTN architecture, note the paper’s publication time and the code version. But regardless of how the module boundaries shift, the overall design spirit hasn’t changed:

Manage link state based on the Contact Plan, and recompute a bundle’s next hop when network events occur.

Egress

Egress is a bundle’s last stop before leaving an HDTN node. It receives bundles from Ingress or Storage, and sends them to the appropriate Outduct and next hop based on the Router’s computed result.

In HDTN, two terms describe the direction of data in and out:

NamePurpose
InductEntry point for receiving external data
OutductExit for sending data to the next hop

You can think of the Induct as a logistics center’s unloading dock and the Outduct as its shipping dock. The same node may have multiple Outducts, each leading to a different next hop. The Router’s job is to tell Egress which exit to use now.

Event-Driven Architecture: what to do when a link suddenly drops?

Space networks don’t always run according to the ideal schedule; there are too many influencing factors. Even if the Contact Plan predicts a link should be usable, the real environment can still have:

  • Sudden signal-quality degradation
  • Antenna-tracking failure
  • Temporary comms-equipment anomaly
  • A link dropping early
  • A Contact Plan update
  • A next-hop node not responding

So HDTN can’t rely only on static scheduling; it also needs an event-driven architecture to notify other modules when state changes. HDTN uses ZeroMQ pub-sub sockets to pass events. [1] What’s that? For example, when Egress finds a link has suddenly vanished, it can emit a LinkStatus change notification:

After the Router recomputes the next hop, it notifies Egress to update the Outduct.

Notice this flow is a lot like the event-driven architecture in modern distributed systems:

This design means HDTN doesn’t have to cram all logic into one large program, and lets different modules keep relatively clear responsibility boundaries.

Convergence Layer

As the previous post said, the Bundle Protocol isn’t meant to completely replace TCP, UDP, or other underlying protocols; it’s more like an overlay network, handling cross-node, cross-time data-forwarding logic.

But when a bundle actually has to move from one node to another, it still needs to ride on some actual transport. That’s the purpose of the Convergence Layer.

Using the logistics system again:

Network conceptLogistics analogy
BundleStandard shipping container
Bundle ProtocolInternational logistics rules
Convergence LayerThe actual truck, plane, or ship used
Physical LinkRoads, air routes, or shipping routes

HDTN supports several Convergence Layers, including: [1][3]

  • UDP Convergence Layer
  • Simplified TCP (STCP)
  • TCP Convergence Layer Version 3 (TCPCLv3)
  • TCP Convergence Layer Version 4 (TCPCLv4)
  • Licklider Transmission Protocol (LTP)

Each Convergence Layer suits different scenarios:

Convergence LayerCharacteristic
UDPSimple structure, but doesn’t guarantee reliable transport on its own
STCPRelatively lean, suited to efficient data sending
TCPCLSends bundles over TCP, supporting fuller DTN node connection management
LTPDesigned for high-delay and intermittent links, suited to space comms

LTP

Among the Convergence Layers HDTN supports, LTP is particularly worth noting. LTP stands for Licklider Transmission Protocol, a transport protocol designed for long-delay environments, especially suited to scenarios like deep-space comms where ordinary low-delay assumptions don’t hold. [6]

Suppose a link’s one-way delay is two seconds, so the round-trip time (RTT) can reach four seconds. In that case, if the system stops and waits for a response after every small chunk, overall throughput will be terrible. So HDTN’s LTP implementation needs to maintain many sessions simultaneously to keep the link continuously transmitting.

While an earlier session is still waiting for a response, later sessions can keep sending data. Test results indicate that once link delay exceeds one second, increasing the number of concurrent LTP sessions is an important factor in achieving gigabit-level data rates. [1]

This is a lot like the pipeline concept in ordinary high-bandwidth networks: don’t let the whole link sit idle waiting for a single response.

How is HDTN different from an ordinary message queue?

If you’ve used Amazon SQS, RabbitMQ, Kafka, or other message queues, HDTN’s architecture may feel somewhat familiar.

They do share some things in common:

Message QueueHDTN
MessageBundle
QueueStorage
ProducerBundle Source
ConsumerDestination Node
BrokerDTN Node
RetryRetransmission
Routing RuleContact Plan / Router
Durable StorageBundle Storage

But the problems HDTN faces are more special. An ordinary message queue usually assumes the underlying network is roughly available. Even with a brief disconnection, the service is expected to recover in a relatively short time.

HDTN, however, must accept:

  • The network may not exist for a long time
  • The next connection may be minutes or hours away
  • Nodes keep moving
  • Contact windows are predictable but very limited
  • Bandwidth, delay, and error rate are highly asymmetric
  • A relay node itself may also be temporarily offline

So HDTN isn’t just moving a message queue into space; it redesigns how data is stored, routed, scheduled, and transmitted in an extreme network environment.

HDTN’s complete data flow

Stringing the earlier components together, a bundle’s lifecycle in an HDTN node is roughly as follows.

Scenario 1: the link is currently usable

This reduces unnecessary Storage I/O and suits data that can be forwarded immediately.

Scenario 2: the link is currently unusable

This is the most typical Store-Carry-Forward flow in DTN.

Scenario 3: a sudden drop mid-transfer

For HDTN, a disconnection isn’t a system crash, but another event to handle.

Viewing it through a distributed-systems lens

From a software-engineering standpoint, the most interesting thing about HDTN isn’t just space comms, but that it’s essentially an event-driven distributed system. It needs to handle:

  • Asynchronous events
  • Durable storage
  • Pipelining
  • Route updates
  • Backpressure
  • Retry
  • State synchronization
  • Fault recovery
  • Multiple underlying transports
  • Interoperability between different DTN implementations

These problems aren’t rare in existing cloud architectures, but space networks push the conditions to a more extreme direction. A ground system might treat a few seconds of timeout as a service anomaly, while a space system may have to incorporate several minutes of waiting into its normal flow. Another difference is that a ground system may require a service to recover connectivity as fast as possible, but a space system must accept that no usable path exists at all right now. One last observation: time in terrestrial networks is usually just a performance metric, while in space DTN, time itself is part of the routing topology.

ISS testing: HDTN is more than a theoretical architecture

The Technical Memorandum also compiles interoperability and performance tests between HDTN and other DTN implementations, including: [1]

  • Interoperability tests between HDTN and DTN Marshall Enterprise (DTNME)
  • Bundle Protocol Version 6 (BPv6) and Version 7 (BPv7) tests
  • Transmission tests of different Convergence Layers
  • Simulated delay and packet loss
  • Using HDTN as a gateway node
  • Simulations with the ISS network topology
  • LTP long-delay link tests

One point worth mentioning is that, to find the cause of the low data rate in the SDIL tests, they later ran a series of “4-box” tests locally at GRC to simulate the data flow between ISS payload, ISS onboard gateway, ground gateway, and ground node. [1] These tests compared not only protocols but also different deployment environments: including a fully KVM-based virtual machine, an LXC container, native hardware (bare metal), and a ZBook + KVM image combination close to the actual ISS onboard gateway. [1]

The result is interesting: although iperf3 showed these environments all theoretically had decent baseline bandwidth, when actually running end-to-end DTN tests, the KVM VM environment showed significant performance loss; in contrast, LXC performed closer to native hardware, and native hardware could reach near line rate. [1] Also, once they included the ZBook + KVM gateway image the ISS actually uses, performance dropped noticeably again; even after trying to adjust the VM’s core and memory configuration, the improvement was slight. [1]

In other words, an important takeaway from this experiment isn’t just that HDTN can run, but that the virtualization layer itself can become a bottleneck. The authors explicitly note at the end that these local tests made them suspect the low data rate in the earlier SDIL tests might not have been solely a VPN or DTNME-version issue, and that KVM itself may also affect performance more significantly than originally expected. [1]

Another notable test simulated a link with about two seconds of one-way delay and four seconds of RTT. The results show that simply increasing bandwidth isn’t enough. The system also needs to tune LTP sessions, pipeline limit, buffer, and other parameters to maintain higher throughput under high-delay conditions. [1]

This illustrates one thing:

Space network performance isn’t a single-NIC or single-protocol problem, but a systems-engineering problem for the whole data-processing pipeline.

HDTN project status

NASA has made the HDTN source code public on GitHub: [3]

GitHub: nasa/HDTN

The currently-public project is written in C++ and built with CMake. It appears to support multiple operating systems and hardware platforms, including Linux, Windows, macOS, FreeBSD, OpenBSD, Raspbian, and ARM64. [3]

Main dependencies include:

The main modules currently in the code include:

A test method is also provided; you can observe HDTN’s data flow with tcpdump and Wireshark:

Next Hop: does HDTN have to run on a large server?

Having understood HDTN’s basic architecture, a natural question arises:

Since HDTN is already split into Ingress, Storage, Router, and Egress modules, does it have to run fully on a high-end x86 server?

This doubt is reasonable; deep-space exploration intuitively seems to pair with high-end servers. But future space missions can’t rely only on large servers. Future lunar bases, satellites, probes, ground stations, and edge nodes may have different:

  • CPU architectures
  • Memory capacities
  • Storage space
  • Energy constraints
  • Thermal conditions
  • Bandwidth needs
  • Mission roles

So the paper’s future work mentions some directions worth researching:

  • Can HDTN be ported to the ARM platform?
  • Can it run on a Raspberry Pi?
  • Can different modules be split across multiple devices?
  • Can an edge device become a space DTN node?
  • How much does performance drop under limited hardware resources?

NASA has since also researched the Raspberry Pi and ARM platforms. [3]

I’ll leave this for the next post to explore:

How to run NASA HDTN on a Raspberry Pi?
From ARM porting and CMake build modifications to distributed deployment

Closing

The previous post introduced why DTN suits the space environment.

This one further breaks down NASA HDTN’s software architecture, explaining that Store-Carry-Forward isn’t an abstract term but an engineering flow completed by multiple components together.

HDTN’s core components include:

ComponentFunction
BundleA data unit that can be passed across time and nodes
IngressReceives bundles and decides whether to forward immediately
StorageHolds bundles when a link is down
Contact PlanDescribes future usable contact windows
Scheduler / RouterManages link state and computes the next hop
EgressHands bundles to the correct Outduct
Convergence LayerLets bundles ride on actual transport protocols
ZeroMQ EventsSynchronizes state when a link fails or the schedule changes

To summarize HDTN’s design spirit in one sentence:

HDTN doesn’t assume the network always exists; it lets data wait safely when the network doesn’t exist, and keep moving forward when the next communication opportunity appears.

This architecture isn’t only applicable to the ISS; it may also become an important underlying capability for future lunar, Mars, and deep-space infrastructure.

entry.title: Why Space Networking Needs DTN: From TCP/IP's Limits to Deep-Space Networks
entry.content:
