Preface: can we still get online smoothly in space?

I recently watched the livestream of NASA’s Artemis II lunar flyby mission. Watching the rocket lift off, I felt I’d witnessed another milestone for humanity.
In recent years, progress from NASA, the Commercial Lunar Payload Services (CLPS), SpaceX’s Starship, and various countries’ investment in lunar and deep-space missions has made space infrastructure no longer just a sci-fi concept but increasingly a matter of engineering practice. But as an engineer, a very practical question came to mind: “If we want to develop technology in space, or even build bases, can we take our existing terrestrial network architecture and use it directly in space?” To answer this, I dug into some related papers and technical documents. This post is my study notes and summary.

Intuitively, we might think: “Just make the antennas bigger, push up the signal power, and launch a few more relay satellites, and we can extend the Earth’s Internet into space, right?” But in reality, the challenges space networks face are absolutely not simply insufficient bandwidth or weak signals.

The most fundamental problem is that the basic assumptions of the entire network environment completely change in space.

The Internet on Earth usually assumes that an end-to-end path is clear most of the time, and packets reach their destination in a very short time. A disconnection is usually treated as an “abnormal condition.” But in space networks, extremely long delays, intermittent connectivity, and communication interruptions are the norm. NASA’s introduction to DTN (Delay/Disruption-Tolerant Networking) also notes that DTN aims to provide a more reliable, standardized way of transferring data in long-delay, interruption-prone environments like space communications (NASA).

DTN’s core isn’t to find a way to make the speed of light faster, but to frankly accept that “delay and interruption are unavoidable,” and redesign network transport as a system that can store, wait, hand off, and recover.

Why isn’t the Earth’s Internet suitable for the space environment?

Every day we scroll our phones, call APIs, and log into remote servers, all of which silently rely on a set of TCP/IP assumptions we take for granted:

  • There’s definitely a connected path between source and destination at this moment
  • Round-trip latency (RTT) is extremely low, usually milliseconds to a few hundred milliseconds
  • If a packet is lost, it usually means congestion, equipment failure, or transient interference
  • A disconnection is an exception, not the norm
  • The routing topology changes, but never dramatically at the scale and speed of celestial motion

On Earth these assumptions are very reasonable. Even for intercontinental connections, latency usually stays within what TCP can tolerate; and even if some router in the middle fails, the underlying routing protocols quickly find an alternate route.

But the space environment is an entirely different story.

In space, the Earth, Moon, Mars, satellites, probes, and ground stations are all in relative motion. The contact window between communication nodes may only appear at specific times. On top of that, different antenna angles, individual equipment energy limits, different orbital positions, and even celestial occlusion all directly determine whether a given link is up at that moment.

NASA’s ION-DTN teaching materials also note: extreme distances, extremely high data loss rates, topology changes from orbital motion, and spacecraft operating discontinuously to save power all make space communication several dimensions more complex than terrestrial networks (ion-dtn.readthedocs.io).

We can use a table to quickly contrast the two:

DimensionTerrestrial network assumptionSpace network reality
Path connectivityAn end-to-end path usually existsAn end-to-end path may temporarily not exist
Network latency (RTT)Usually extremely short (milliseconds)Can be seconds, minutes, or even longer
View of disconnectionAn anomaly or errorA normal state
Topology stabilityRelatively stableConstantly changing with orbits and contact windows
Retransmission costRelatively cheapVery expensive, and can miss the contact window
Node stateEquipment mostly online 24/7Spacecraft often in low-power, offline, or occluded states

On terrestrial networks, a disconnection usually means something is broken, but in space networks, a disconnection is very likely just an everyday part of the network topology.

Three fatal flaws of TCP/IP in the space environment

1. The scale of delay: from milliseconds to “minutes”

If you took intro to computer science in college, you know TCP’s design relies heavily on ACKs, timeouts, retransmission, and congestion control. These mechanisms work great on Earth because RTT is short. But in space, distance amplifies delay mercilessly:

  • Between low-orbit satellites and ground stations, it might barely stay in the milliseconds-to-tens-of-milliseconds range
  • Earth-to-Moon one-way light travel is about 1.3 seconds, so RTT reaches 2.6 seconds
  • For Earth-to-Mars, delay varies with the two bodies’ orbital positions and can reach from several minutes to over twenty minutes

This means that if we insist on establishing a traditional TCP session between Earth and Mars, the connection might time out just during the handshake and waiting for a single ACK. Worse, TCP would misinterpret this physically long delay or occlusion-based disconnection as network congestion, triggering rate reduction and retransmission that utterly cripple throughput.

2. Intermittent connectivity: the other side isn’t always there

Space nodes aren’t always mutually visible. Imagine these scenarios:

  • A lunar rover drives into a crater and may not have line of sight to Earth
  • A probe on the far side of the Moon must wait for a relay satellite to fly over before it can send data to Earth
  • A satellite may temporarily shut off its comms module to save its energy budget
  • The rotation and revolution of the Sun, planets, and satellites themselves constantly cause signal occlusion

The space version of the networking problem may not be “is there a complete path to take right now?”
but rather: since there’s no path right now, when is the next available communication opportunity? Until then, who should hold onto this piece of data?

3. Treating interruption as the norm: disruption as topology

As mentioned, a disconnection on Earth means a fault or anomaly, but an interruption in space is often just because a satellite flew out of visible range or an antenna is slewing. So space networks need not a simple, aggressive retry mechanism, but a network architecture that incorporates “interruption” itself into its normal operating model. And that’s exactly the impetus for DTN’s birth.

DTN: Store-Carry-Forward

DTN stands for Delay/Disruption-Tolerant Networking.

It’s a network architecture designed specifically to handle long delays, intermittent connectivity, unstable links, and high error rates. IETF RFC 9171 explicitly states that DTN is an architecture suited to highly stressed environments (IETF Datatracker).

Traditional networking’s logic is straightforward:

DTN’s logic is:

The aerospace industry usually calls this pattern Store-Carry-Forward. When a DTN node receives data, it doesn’t need to forward it immediately. If the next hop isn’t currently in visible range, it can safely “store” the data on local disk or memory, and then “forward” it when the next contact window appears.

DTN’s mindset is no longer about finding a path that’s connected right now, but about planning how data should traverse a series of “future” communication opportunities to finally relay to its destination.

A real-world analogy for DTN

Here’s an analogy: if TCP/IP is like a real-time phone call, then DTN is more like an international logistics system. When you ship a package, the sender and recipient don’t need to be online at the same time, and the trucks, planes, and logistics centers don’t need to be connected into one line at the same second. Your package first reaches a consolidation center (Store), flies across the Pacific with a plane (Carry), and once it reaches the destination country’s sorting center, is handed to a local driver for delivery (Forward).

That’s also how DTN works:

PropertyTraditional InternetSpace DTN
AnalogyReal-time phone callPostal / logistics system
Data unitPacket (forwarded immediately)Bundle (can be held)
Path dependencyNeeds a continuous end-to-end pathRelies on a series of future communication opportunities (contacts)
Time toleranceExtremely sensitive to timeoutsCan tolerate long waits
Communication modelSession-orientedMessage/object-oriented
View of disconnectionA failureA normal state
Routing considerationBased on the current topology stateBased on a dynamic topology with a “time axis”

In other words: in space, waiting itself is part of what the network protocol must handle.

Bundle Protocol

In the DTN world, the most central protocol is the Bundle Protocol (BP).

If the basic data unit of a traditional IP network is the packet, then DTN’s basic data unit is the bundle.
You can think of a bundle as a standard shipping container in the DTN world: it doesn’t just carry data, but also includes the source, destination, creation time, lifetime, and the metadata needed for subsequent routing, security, and status tracking.

This is also the biggest difference between a bundle and an ordinary packet. A packet usually assumes it will be forwarded immediately by the network; a bundle is designed to be held by a node, sent later, handed off across nodes, and continue waiting for the next transmission opportunity after an interruption.

The most modern Bundle Protocol version is BPv7, defined in IETF RFC 9171. CCSDS (the Consultative Committee for Space Data Systems) also published a BPv7-based experimental space-communication specification in 2025. This means BPv7 is no longer just an academic concept, but is increasingly being incorporated into the standardization foundation for future space data systems and mission interoperability (ccsds.org).

The point of the Bundle Protocol isn’t to slice data smaller, but to turn data into mission-level message units that can be “stored, waited on, handed off, and tracked.”

What’s actually inside a bundle?

To aid understanding, we can simplify a bundle into this structure:

The most important are the Primary Block and the Payload Block.

The Primary Block provides the basic information needed for this bundle to be identified and processed in the DTN network, such as source, destination, and lifetime. The Payload Block carries the actual mission data to be sent. Extension Blocks provide extra capabilities such as security, routing-assist info, or other metadata.

In other words, a bundle isn’t just the data itself, but a data container with context. It knows where it came from, where it’s going, and how long it can live, and it can carry extra information so relay nodes can still make forwarding decisions without an end-to-end connection.

The internal structure of a Bundle Node

Having understood bundles, the next question is: who’s responsible for handling these bundles?

In the BPv7 architecture, the conceptual node responsible for sending, receiving, and processing bundles is called a Bundle Node, a DTN node composed of several functional components. The CCSDS BPv7 Experimental Specification describes a Bundle Node as any entity that can send and/or receive bundles. Architecturally, it mainly consists of three conceptual components:

  • Application Agent (AA)
  • Bundle Protocol Agent (BPA)
  • Convergence Layer Adapter (CLA)

Ref: Graphical Representation of a Bundle Node. Source: CCSDS 734.20-O-1, “Bundle Protocol Specification, Experimental Specification,” Figure 1-1 4

This figure can be understood as follows:

ComponentFunction
Application Agent (AA)Interacts with upper-layer applications, including handling application data and administrative records
Administrative Element (AE)Generates and processes administrative records, e.g. bundle status reports
Application-Specific Element (ASE)Handles the actual application data, e.g. science data, telemetry, or mission payload
Bundle Protocol Agent (BPA)Executes the Bundle Protocol’s own procedures: receiving, processing, storing, and forwarding bundles
Convergence Layer Adapter (CLA)Sends bundles over different underlying networks, e.g. TCP, UDP, LTP, or CCSDS link protocols

In short, the AA handles application-layer data, the BPA handles the Bundle Protocol’s core logic, and the CLA handles actually sending the bundle over some underlying network segment.

This layered design suits space networks well, because the same Bundle Node may face several different links at once. For example, it interacts with ground systems over TCP/UDP on one side, and communicates with spacecraft over LTP or a CCSDS space link on the other. The upper-layer application only needs to hand data to BP; whether a given segment goes over the terrestrial IP network, a lunar-surface local network, or a deep-space link is handled by different CLAs.

Convergence Layer

So BP isn’t meant to replace TCP, UDP, RF, optical comms, or the CCSDS link layer. More precisely, BP is an overlay layer responsible for DTN-level data-delivery semantics, not the actual transport details of each underlying link segment.

BP uses the so-called Convergence Layer (CLA) to decide how this container should be transported over the current segment. On Earth it might go over TCP/UDP; in space it switches to LTP (Licklider Transmission Protocol) or the CCSDS link layer.

What actually sends a bundle over a given link is the CLA, which you can think of as the different modes of transport in a logistics system:

DTN architectureLogistics analogy
BundleStandard shipping container
BPALogistics dispatch center
CLATruck, ship, plane, or rail
Underlying networkActual roads, routes, or rail network

In the ground segment, a bundle might be transported over a TCP/UDP convergence layer, while over long-distance or interruption-prone space links it might switch to LTP or CCSDS-related link protocols.

In short: BP coordinates the long-term strategy from departure to arrival, while the Convergence Layer only handles the short haul from this stop to the next.

Having understood bundles, Bundle Nodes, and the Convergence Layer, DTN’s basic operating logic becomes clear: data is first encapsulated into a bundle, stored and processed by Bundle Nodes, and handed off stop by stop across various underlying networks via different CLAs.

But the next question arises:

If nodes in space aren’t always connected to each other, how does a Bundle Node know when it can hand off data? And which next hop should it choose?

This brings us to a crucial concept in DTN routing: the Contact Plan.

Contact Plan

Having understood the Bundle Protocol, the next question is: how does a space network do routing?

On terrestrial networks, routers usually decide a packet’s next hop based on the current network topology. But in a space network, a link being down now doesn’t mean it’s down forever; it may just be waiting for the next orbital position, the next ground-station contact window, or the next time a satellite enters comms range. So in DTN, we first need an important concept: the contact, a communication opportunity.

In DTN, a contact means: “an opportunity for two nodes to send data to each other during a specific time window.” It’s not just a connection; it carries time and capacity attributes, for example:

Collect all known future contacts and you get a Contact Plan.

If a terrestrial network’s routing table is a flat map of the current network, then a space network’s Contact Plan is a three-dimensional timetable with a fourth dimension (time). It’s a bit sci-fi, and the following helps illustrate it:

So you can think of a Contact Plan as a space topology map with its own time axis.

Contact Graph Routing (CGR)

With a timetable, we need an algorithm to plan the route. Traditional network AS protocols like OSPF or BGP only care about where a path exists right now, but in space the decision logic must become:

  • When does this path become available?
  • How long is the contact window? Is it enough to transfer all the data?
  • Is the next relay node’s disk full yet?
  • Is there a route that departs later but arrives earlier?

To solve this, Contact Graph Routing (CGR) was born.

CGR doesn’t find a path on ordinary network nodes, but on a graph built from future communication opportunities (contacts), using a modified Dijkstra algorithm to find the optimal solution (NASA technical report).

So compared to a traditional graph problem, in the CGR world, spatial distance isn’t the only consideration; the timing opportunity is the key that decides whether data can arrive.

NASA LunaNet

DTN is absolutely not a concept that only lives in papers or simulators; it’s already core to NASA’s plans for the future lunar network architecture.

To support future lunar missions, NASA proposed LunaNet. It isn’t a single satellite, but a standardized network framework. The goal is to let different countries’ probes, different vendors’ relay satellites, and even lunar-surface bases all interconnect, forming a Lunar Network of Networks (NASA).

In this architecture, DTN is the cornerstone of LunaNet’s reliable data transport.

Even if a probe can never talk directly to Earth, as long as there’s a solid Contact Plan and the DTN protocol, scientific data can still be sent back to Earth steadily, relay by relay, like a relay race.

An extreme distributed system!?

If you’re like me, an engineer with more of a cloud-infra background, you can actually think of DTN as a distributed system operating in an extreme environment.

Because space networking isn’t just an underlying comms protocol; it actually covers a large and complex set of systems-engineering topics:

Distributed systems conceptSpace DTN’s corresponding implementation
QueueingBundle queue / priority scheduling
SchedulingContact-aware forwarding
ReplicationCustody transfer (handing off custody and backup)
Fault ToleranceDisruption-tolerant delivery
Resource AllocationAllocating node storage (buffer) and energy
ObservabilityBundle status reports / trajectory tracing
SecurityBPSec / node identity authentication

In ground systems, we mostly pursue speed, that millisecond-level real-time consistency, but in space networks we can only rely on eventual delivery, because in space, reliability isn’t defined as delivering immediately, but as the data never being lost no matter how many disconnections and waits it goes through. These data may be key metrics from exploration equipment or expensive spacecraft, or scientific observation data; either way, they’re worth waiting for.

Advanced topics and future challenges

Although DTN standards are gradually maturing, in practice there are many hardcore pits left to fill:

1. Capacity-aware Routing

CGR is great at finding paths, but what if a relay node’s buffer is about to overflow? What if multiple high-priority science missions are all competing for the same contact window? Perfectly integrating a node’s storage capacity and link bandwidth into routing decisions is a major hot area right now.

2. ML-assisted vs Deterministic Routing

Some propose bringing machine learning into DTN to predict the best route. But in expensive space missions, explainability and determinism are often preferred over black-box AI. That is, how to make a routing algorithm both adapt to dynamic changes and let the ground control center precisely track and override decisions is, I think, one of the directions for deeper research into future space networks.

3. Security-aware Routing

When a space network becomes a multi-national, multi-institution shared network, security becomes paramount. How do you prevent malicious nodes from attacking, jamming or tampering with the Contact Plan, or even paralyzing other nodes’ buffers by sending junk bundles? These all need tighter trust mechanisms to guard against, and security is an issue in every field.

A simple Space DTN lab

This sounds like tech only NASA is qualified to play with, but we can actually set up a minimal proof-of-concept (PoC) environment with an ordinary computer and Docker, because it’s essentially a distributed system with extreme properties.

We only need to carve out three nodes:

You can deliberately set the connection between A and B to only 60 seconds, and observe how Node B buffers the data, waits for the contact window with Node C to arrive, and finally forwards the data.

You can use tc netem to simulate tens of seconds of extreme delay, or use the open-source ION-DTN or HDTN to test a BPv7 implementation. Going a bit further, you can hook up Prometheus and Grafana to observe DTN’s core behavior under disconnection, delay, and contact-window constraints. Without actually launching a rocket, you can experience the design logic of deep-space communication architecture right on your laptop.

Closing

The Earth’s Internet is so great probably because it’s built on a stable, low-latency environment where everyone is almost always online. Fixed servers, data centers, networking equipment, and undersea cables weave all of this together. But in space, distance itself brings unavoidable delay, and orbital motion brings relentless disconnection. None of this can obviously be brute-forced away by adding bandwidth.

The fascinating thing about DTN is that it completely breaks our craving for real-time connectivity: data hitches rides through the universe, relaying step by step toward its destination.

entry.title: initrd vs initramfs | Linux Kernel
entry.content:
🌐 中文版：繁體中文

Introduction

Early in boot, a temporary filesystem is needed to perform initialization and configuration during the early boot stage. There are two mechanisms for using a temporary filesystem: initrd (Initial RAM Disk) and initramfs (Initial RAM Filesystem). initrd is the earlier approach, and most boot flows today use initramfs.

initrd

initrd (Initial RAM Disk) is a temporary root filesystem used in early Linux boot. It takes the form of a gzip-compressed block image, loaded at boot into a virtual RAM disk (e.g. /dev/ram0) and then mounted by the kernel as the initial root.

It usually contains:

  • The drivers needed to mount the real rootfs
  • A linuxrc (an init-like early user-space script)
  • Initialization scripts to mount /proc, /sys, and so on

Booting with initrd

To boot via initrd, it must be loaded into memory at the bootloader stage, and the bootloader must tell the kernel the initrd’s memory address. But how does it know the initrd address?

Very old bootloaders told the kernel the initrd’s start address and size as parameters via the kernel command line; but in newer bootloaders (GRUB), the initrd is passed to the kernel through the boot protocol structure rather than the command line.

The kernel command line above means: set the console to tty0 at baud rate 115200, mount the rootfs over NFS (fetching the NFS rootfs from a private IP), and finally load and mount a RAM disk from physical memory address 0x10800000 with size 0x14af47.

In the bootloader you can set the start memory addresses for the kernel image and initrd. Here’s an example with U-Boot:

U-Boot can also load the kernel image and initrd image over the network, saving the development time of flashing everything to flash ROM.

Overall flow:

  1. The bootloader loads the kernel image and initrd image into RAM
  2. The bootloader passes the initrd’s address and size via the boot protocol (or command line)
  3. After the kernel starts, it gets the initrd image from RAM
  4. It decompresses the initrd .gz into /dev/ram0
  5. It mounts /dev/ram0 as the temporary root filesystem
  6. The kernel spawns an early process to run linuxrc
  7. linuxrc mounts /proc and /sys, loads drivers, and mounts the real rootfs
  8. linuxrc calls pivot_root or switch_root to switch to the real rootfs
  9. The initrd RAM disk is unmounted and its memory freed

This linuxrc is a script containing the commands needed before mounting the real root filesystem, such as mount -t proc /proc /proc or busybox sh.

After linuxrc finishes, the initrd early stage ends, at which point pivot_root / switch_root switches to the real rootfs, and only then is the initrd RAM disk freed.

In the kernel source, the prepare_namespace() function in init/do_mounts.c decides where the rootfs is and where the mount point is. Within it:

  • initrd_load() checks whether an initrd exists, and if so decompresses and mounts it
  • mount_root() mounts the real rootfs
  • Finally init_chroot("/") completes the switch
initrd flow

Switch to light mode to view, button at bottom right

Let’s trace initrd_load, since it tries to load the initrd. Reading the code, we find: if the kernel enabled CONFIG_BLK_DEV_INITRD (initrd support, which you can check in the kernel config editor), it tries to load the early root filesystem from the initrd image passed in by the bootloader. On success it returns true, which tells the kernel: “I’ve already mounted the initrd, you don’t need to try mounting another rootfs.” On failure, or if not enabled, it returns false, and the kernel proceeds to mount_root() to mount the real rootfs.

initramfs

initramfs’s purpose is actually similar to initrd:
both provide a temporary root before the real root filesystem is mounted, letting us:

  • Load necessary drivers
  • Do some early-userspace initialization
  • Finally switch to the real rootfs

The difference is entirely in implementation:

  • initrd: a traditional filesystem image (e.g. ext2) that’s gzip-compressed. After the kernel decompresses it, it’s placed on a RAM disk like /dev/ram0 and mounted.
  • initramfs: a cpio archive (usually gzipped too). The kernel unpacks the cpio directly into rootfs (ramfs or tmpfs), with no block device and no intermediate /dev/ram0 layer.

For a built-in initramfs (compiled into the kernel), its unpacking roughly happens at:

  • After start_kernel() calls a sequence of initializations
  • Entering rest_init() → kernel_init() → kernel_init_freeable()
  • which calls populate_rootfs() to unpack the compile-time initramfs cpio into rootfs

Later, do_basic_setup() calls do_initcalls() to initialize various drivers and subsystems. So roughly speaking: initramfs is unpacked and mounted before do_basic_setup().

kernel_init_freeable

Switch to light mode to view, button at bottom right

do_initcalls flow

Switch to light mode to view, button at bottom right

overall flow

Switch to light mode to view, button at bottom right

In the kernel source tree’s usr/ directory, you can see the initramfs-related files:

The flow is roughly:

  • You set INITRAMFS_SOURCE in the kernel config, which can be a directory or a cpio file list
  • The build system calls gen_initramfs.sh to read your INITRAMFS_SOURCE
  • Then gen_init_cpio produces a cpio archive initramfs_data.cpio
  • This cpio is then converted to C/ASM data (initramfs_inc_data, initramfs_data.S)
  • and finally linked into the kernel image

In other words:

You can package a “mini rootfs” into the kernel at compile time, without separately preparing a standalone initrd image.

BusyBox example, a minimal initramfs

Suppose we want a super-minimal initramfs needing only: a busybox binary, an /init or /bin/sh to serve as init, and a /dev/console device node. Its file tree might look like:

Here’s why there’s a symbolic link from init to /bin/busybox: when the kernel uses initramfs, it first looks for the /init executable in rootfs. If found, it runs it as the init process (PID 1); if not found, and neither rdinit= nor init= is specified, it proceeds to the subsequent root-mount flow to mount the real rootfs.

You can see this default in init/main.c:

The ramdisk_execute_command char pointer points to this executable.

If you add rdinit=/bin/sh or rdinit=/bin/busybox to the kernel command line, you can override this behavior and directly specify the first program to run on the initramfs. This is a common usage: rdinit=/bin/sh with busybox drops you straight into a shell in early userspace to debug the boot flow.

entry.title: PVE VM Live Migration Based on CPU Power Consumption | PVE Series 2
entry.content:
🌐 中文版：繁體中文

Preface

In the previous post we covered how to do live migration of VMs in Proxmox VE. Now we’ll add a condition to trigger migration. Since my need here is power consumption, I need to know how to get CPU power consumption info.

Getting CPU power consumption info

There are several ways to get CPU or other hardware power consumption. The simplest is powerstat to view CPU power in a Linux/Unix environment. Also, if the host has a BMC and supports IPMI, you can use ipmitool to get the host’s power-consumption info.

Aside: Proxmox VE itself actually supports an IPMI watchdog. You can uncomment it in /etc/default/pve-ha-manager to use the IPMI watchdog, since the default is the OS-level softdog. But if the motherboard doesn’t support it, just use the default.

Here are a few commands to check whether your host supports IPMI:
sudo apt-get install ipmitool
Check whether the BMC (Board Management Controller) exists and is running properly; if it returns no info or shows an error, the server may not support IPMI:
sudo ipmitool mc info
Or check with dmidecode:
sudo dmidecode | grep -i ipmi
If the server returns no IPMI/BMC-related info, the hardware may not support it.

Let’s try getting the info with powerstat:

This command takes at least 60 samples, one CPU power reading per second, and finally outputs the average consumption. You can use this result in a script as a condition for migration.

Migration scenario

After getting CPU power simply, next let’s introduce the migration scenario. Continuing the two-node architecture from the previous post, when node A judges its power consumption exceeds a threshold, it migrates; and if the target node is powered off, it wakes it up to migrate. We can implement this with a bash script.

Before

After

This simple bash script first sets a low threshold of 6 watts, for experimental convenience, basically ensuring the node always migrates. Here I’m actually migrating the VM on node pve2 to node pve. The POWER_CONSUMPTION=$(powerstat -R 1 60 | grep -oP 'CPU:\s+\K[0-9.]+') gets the average CPU power over 60 samples via powerstat, taking one minute (a limitation of the command). Then wakeonlan wakes the remote host, and qm performs the PVE node migration.

QM

qm is the QEMU/KVM Virtual Machine Manager, a handy command-line tool PVE provides. Its migrate option migrates the VM with the given VM ID to another node, and if the VM is running you need to add --online for live migration. If you’re interested in the qm command, see its manual.

Wake On LAN (WOL)

Wake On LAN (WOL), also called “network wake-up,” lets a computer on the same LAN send a command to a powered-off or sleeping host to boot it back to operation. To use this, first confirm the motherboard supports WOL; if it does, you need to enable the PCI/PCIe wake-up feature in the UEFI/BIOS.

How it works

When I first looked up WOL, I was curious how a powered-off computer can still receive a packet to wake it. The secret is that when a computer is off or sleeping, there’s still a trickle of power to give the NIC or host minimal operating capability, so it can listen to other packets on the LAN, continuously receiving and checking broadcast info from the same LAN.

The host responsible for waking a node broadcasts a Magic Packet on the LAN. This Magic Packet usually starts with 6 consecutive FFs: FF FF FF FF FF FF, followed by the MAC address, and sometimes a 4-to-6-byte password.

This Magic Packet is broadcast on the LAN, and once the sleeping/powered-off host parses the content with its minimally-operating NIC and finds the info in the Magic Packet matches the local host, it starts the boot process. That’s also why the bash script above appends the MAC address after wakeonlan.

Enabling WOL in the BIOS

Enter the BIOS on each of the two nodes to enable it, then save changes and reboot.

Command test

Here I first power off node B and try to wake it from node A.

From the history you can also see node 2 successfully booted from a powered-off state.

The experiment

But the command test showed that the boot wait time also needs to be considered, so we can change the script to the following.

This adds a retry mechanism: after sending the Magic Packet, it tries to ping the host to check whether it’s alive. Of course I confirmed I’m not blocking ICMP packets, so after boot it should definitely be pingable. The max retry count is 12, with a 10-second wait between retries, so it waits at most 2 minutes.

These numbers are just for experimental convenience; whether to change it to backoff retry in real operation is up to you.

Here I wanted to reverse the experiment, first powering off node 1 PVE.

Then on node 2 PVE2 I run the script above. As expected, it first checks whether the average CPU power over one minute exceeds the threshold (6 watts), which it definitely will, so it then wakes the pve node, keeps pinging node 1, and after two retries, node pve is available and migration starts, completing successfully.

If you observe the Ubuntu VM’s memory metric, you’ll see a gap, which is the expected downtime during migration. When I handled MQ issues at AWS, I’d also see such gaps in some instances’ memory or CPU metrics during maintenance windows, which usually indicates an underlying instance replacement or restart, possibly for maintenance or a security patch.

Closing

This post did a simple little experiment: from one node in the PVE cluster, we woke another PVE node on the same LAN and did a live migration. If I later have another host available, I’ll cover using the HA (High Availability) cluster in PVE.

Reference

IPMI watchdog
https://blog.jason.tools/2019/02/pve-ipmi-watchdog.html

qm
https://pve.proxmox.com/pve-docs/qm.1.html

entry.title: Hands-On Proxmox VE VM Live Migration | PVE Series 1
entry.content:
🌐 中文版：繁體中文

Introducing Proxmox VE

Proxmox VE (PVE) is an open-source virtualization environment that can support both LXC (Linux Container) based containers and kernel-based VMs, i.e. KVM, the virtualization technology that uses the Linux kernel as a hypervisor.

Proxmox also handles the guest’s hardware requests through QEMU, which sits between host and guest, translating them to the real hardware. Running together with KVM brings a boost in instruction-processing performance, so virtualization can run at near-local speed.

Physical node setup

Flashing the Proxmox VE image

Prepare a USB and put the Proxmox VE ISO image on it. I chose the Proxmox VE 7.4 ISO Installer.

PVE image official download

Then prepare the nodes and adjust the boot order on each host; enter the BIOS and set USB as the first priority. While you’re there, check whether KVM is enabled in the BIOS; you must enable it first. In my environment, it’s under Intel Virtualization Technology in the BIOS’s Advanced settings; enable it.

After booting normally, the installation wizard appears; just follow it through. Once installed, log into the node you set up via the web, and you can start building the cluster.

Building the cluster

Confirm node info

There are two nodes now; before building the cluster, confirm /etc/hosts:

Starting

First go to node 1’s Datacenter, find Cluster, and choose Create Cluster.

Name the cluster (here it’s LabCluster), choose your cluster network, then click Create.

After creation, the screen looks like this; you can see node 1 pve added to the cluster.

Next we need to join the other nodes to this cluster. Find Join Information under Cluster and copy the info it shows.

Then go to the second node pve2 (a separate host in my case) to join the cluster. Find Join Information under Cluster and paste in the join info you just copied. Once joined, both nodes can see each other.

If you now hastily create a VM and think you can migrate it, you’d be wrong. Your backup node will error because it can’t find the VM’s config file, like this:

Right, migration still needs two conditions:

  • The VM config file must be shared between nodes, or more completely, the VM disk must be shared
  • Also, the ISO image used to create the VM must be shared

To achieve both, you need a shared-storage solution.

Migration flow

Let me add some context on our migration flow. In this post we’ll migrate manually through the PVE interface: two PVE nodes, a pre-built shared-storage architecture, a VM created on that architecture, then migrating that VM from one node to another.

So next we’ll build the storage architecture with Ceph.

Introducing Ceph

The Ceph Storage Cluster, also called RADOS (Reliable, Autonomic Distributed Object Store), provides a reliable, self-managing distributed object store. Developed in C++, this cluster is the software storage system at the bottom of the Ceph architecture, where all the environment’s data lives. It has self-healing and self-management capabilities, and is composed of automatically-operating OSD storage nodes and lightweight monitor programs.

Ceph components

  • Ceph OSDs
    • Ceph’s daemon (ceph-osd)
    • Stores data, handles data replication, recovery, etc.
    • Provides monitoring info to the Ceph Monitor by checking ceph-osd heartbeats
    • For high availability (HA) and redundancy: at least 3 Ceph OSDs are needed
  • Monitors
    • ceph-mon
    • Maintains maps showing cluster state, including the monitor map and OSD map
    • Responsible for managing authentication between daemons and clients
    • For high availability (HA) and redundancy: at least 3 Ceph Monitors are needed
  • Managers
    • ceph-mgr
    • Tracks runtime metrics and the Ceph cluster’s current state, e.g. storage utilization, current system load
    • For high availability (HA) and redundancy: at least 2 Ceph Managers are needed
  • MDSs:
    • The Ceph Metadata Server (Ceph MDS) stores metadata for the Ceph filesystem
      • That is, a Ceph block device or Ceph object storage doesn’t use MDS
    • If you want to create a Ceph Filesystem (CephFS), you also need to create an MDS beforehand
    • Ceph MDS lets POSIX filesystem users run commands like ls or find without burdening the Ceph storage cluster

Ceph is a distributed storage system, supported at the bottom by a cluster of multiple servers (the PVE cluster we just set up). If you need to expand storage or scale the system, just add more servers to the cluster, which makes scaling very simple. In this architecture, Ceph is highly reliable, with the system automatically healing and managing itself. When data is written, it’s automatically replicated to multiple nodes, so even if a node fails, the whole system keeps working and the data isn’t corrupted. This design lets Ceph provide a stable and secure storage solution.

Installing Ceph

First install Ceph on every node; there are two nodes here, so both need it.

Click Start quincy installation (I didn’t specify a version, just used the one offered).

During download, it asks whether to continue; type Y.

After it finishes, it asks you to specify a network interface.

After a successful install, it prompts the next steps, which we’ll follow:

  • Install Ceph on every node
  • Add additional Ceph Monitors
  • Create a Ceph OSD on each node
  • Create a Ceph Pool

Repeat the install flow above on the other nodes. Once every node is installed, checking Health should show a warning OSD count 0 < osd_pool_default_size 3, which is normal because no OSD has been created yet.

Creating a Ceph OSD

To create a Ceph OSD, you first need idle disk space. So first find a disk on each node to configure. Enter Disk on the pve node and format an idle disk; if you have no idle disk, you can use a USB external drive.

Then under PVE > Ceph > OSD, click Create: OSD, choose the disk you just formatted, and click Create.

Do the same steps on the other nodes to install OSDs.

Once installed, you can see the OSD type and status in the OSD view on both nodes.

Also, for redundancy and high availability, you can create two additional Ceph Managers (active-standby).

Per the suggestions in this article:

  • The ceph-osd process consumes CPU during operation, so each ceph-osd process is usually bound to a CPU core.
  • The ceph-mon process isn’t very CPU-intensive, so you don’t need to reserve too much CPU for it.
  • ceph-mds is also very CPU-intensive, so it needs more CPU resources.
  • ceph-mon and ceph-mds need 2G of memory, and each ceph-osd process needs 1G (2G is better).

Creating a Ceph Pool

A Ceph Pool combines OSDs across nodes, and it’s where our VM disks will later be stored. On the pve node, go to Ceph > Pools and choose Create: Ceph Pool. Give the pool a name, here syncbricks-ceph. You also need to specify the pool size; normally Min.Size is at least 2 and Size defaults to 3, but since I only have two hosts, I set size to 2 for now, letting both OSDs join the Ceph Pool.

After creation it should show a warning, because PVE defaults to wanting 3 OSDs but there are only two.


There are two OSDs currently online, so this is normal for now. Also, after the Ceph Pool is created, you’ll find syncbricks-ceph appear under both nodes. Now the two nodes can share the VM disk, enabling the later VM migration.

Creating a Ceph File System

Ceph File System (CephFS) is a POSIX-compliant filesystem built on top of the Ceph distributed object store RADOS. CephFS aims to provide a highly-available, high-performance file-storage solution for various applications, usable as scratch space for high-performance computing (HPC) and shared storage for distributed workflows.

In CephFS’s architecture, file metadata is stored in a RADOS pool separate from file data, and served through an elastically-scalable MDS cluster, which supports higher-throughput workloads. Clients can directly access RADOS to read and write file data blocks, so workloads can scale linearly with the underlying RADOS object store, without any gateway or agent mediating data I/O.

Data access is coordinated by the MDS cluster, which manages a distributed metadata cache, with clients and MDSs jointly maintaining metadata state. The MDS consolidates metadata changes and efficiently writes them to the RADOS journal, storing no metadata locally. This design lets clients collaborate quickly and consistently under a POSIX filesystem.

With the intro done, let’s continue. So far we’ve handled sharing the VM disk; next we’ll share the VM ISO image. If it isn’t shared, a later migration will throw the error Can't migrate VM with local CD/DVD, meaning it must be done the shared way.

Per this thread, sharing an ISO image requires at least these steps:

  1. Create Ceph File System:
    • Ensure CephFS is created with at least two MDS on standby
  2. Add Ceph FS:
    • Mount CephFS on the nodes so all nodes can share the same ISO image

Creating MDS

So we create an MDS on each of the two nodes.

Then on node 1 do Create: Ceph FS, naming it cephfs.

After creation, cephfs appears on both nodes, and you can upload an ISO image to the shared filesystem. Here I uploaded the Ubuntu 22.04 Desktop image.

Creating a VM to test

This time I create the Ubuntu VM on the pve node. During creation, when setting the OS, choose Use CD/DVD disc image file(iso), set Storage to the Ceph filesystem cephfs just created, then choose the image you want from the filesystem.

When the creation flow reaches the Disks part, remember to set Storage to the syncbricks-ceph just created.

Then create the VM.

After it’s created, you need to enter the VM to install Ubuntu, which I won’t detail here.

Manually testing migration

Once the VM is created, select it under pve, right-click, and a Migration option should appear, letting us migrate manually.

We migrate VM 100 from node pve1 to node pve2. Afterward you can see the VM’s position on the left has appeared under pve2, meaning the migration succeeded.

So far so good. For the next step, I want to use a script to auto-migrate based on conditions like CPU usage or CPU power consumption. This process will also need node 1 to power on a shut-down node 2, which uses the interesting Wake On Lan (WOL) feature; I’ll leave that for the next post.

Proxmox VE

https://kawsing.gitbook.io/opensystem/andoid-shou-ji/pomoxve/jian-li-cong-ji
https://www.linuxyes.com/blog/linuxyes-3/post/proxmox-ve-replication-ha-9
https://blog.tenyi.com/2020/01/proxmox-ve-two-nodes-ha-cluster.html
https://medium.com/彼得潘的-swift-ios-app-開發教室/工控機安裝proxmox-ve-pve-94a09647d95f

Ceph
https://www.linuxtek.ca/2023/01/27/ceph-clustering-with-proxmox/
https://kawsing.gitbook.io/opensystem/andoid-shou-ji/pomoxve/ceph-object-storage
https://kawsing.gitbook.io/opensystem/andoid-shou-ji/pomoxve/ceph-object-storage/ceph-xu-yao-da-liang-ji-yi-ti

entry.title: Passing Functions in C/C++: A Deep Look at Function Pointer Address Changes
entry.content:
🌐 中文版：繁體中文

Function Pointers

When you declare a function in C/C++, it gets allocated a starting memory address, and a function pointer can be used to point to and store that function address. So we can use a function pointer to (1) call a function or (2) pass it to another function.

Usage

Declaration:

Remember to assign the function’s address to the function pointer, which you can do with the address-of operator &. See the example below:

The output of this code is 3. If we integrate it with the binary tree class built earlier, the code looks like this:

The upper part, class TreeNode and class BT, defines the binary tree structure; ignore that for now. Notice that under the BT class we declared a function returnRoot whose only job is to return the node passed in, which isn’t very useful. Then in main, we define a single node with the integer value 1, set it as the tree’s root, and then come to where the function pointer is used:

This declares a pointer to a BT class member function, whose parameter and return value are both TreeNode*.
The parameter and return value match returnRoot above.

We take the address of BT’s member function and give it to the func_ptr pointer variable:

Then we print the result. Since returnRoot returns a node, we print its node value:

Note here that because func_ptr is declared as a pointer to any BT class member function, accessing it requires an initialized BT class object, which here is T.

Output: 1

Member function pointers

Just now the function pointer was declared and accessed in main. But what happens if we want the function pointer to be a member inside a class?

From my own experiments, the difference you feel is in how the caller (main) accesses it:

Inside a class, the function pointer declaration is the same; you still need to specify which class’s member function this pointer accesses.

But access in main needs care. Since this function pointer still belongs to the BT class, assigning the function address also requires accessing it through the class object T:

And the call needs even more attention, since the function is accessed through a member function pointer:

  • *T.funt_ptr points to the target member function, so another object is needed to call the pointer
  • T.*T.funt_ptr uses the leading T to access the pointer that points to the target function

Practical uses of function pointers

  • Callback Function: Function pointers are often used to implement callbacks, as in event-driven architectures or interrupt handling.
  • Dynamic Dispatch: When there are multiple functions with similar interfaces but different implementations (polymorphism), function pointers can switch between them.
  • Function Table: Function pointers can be stored in an array or other data structure to build a function table, selecting which function to call by index.

I think the function table is a very powerful construct. The system call table maintained in the Linux kernel, for instance, is itself a function pointer table, mapping syscall numbers to the corresponding kernel handler functions. Each system call uses a unique syscall number to index into this table’s corresponding function pointer.
For the detailed mechanism, see this article.

The low-level flow

Let’s switch to another example to actually see the memory changes when using a function pointer:

example.cpp

This defines two functions, and we can use a function pointer to call add and subtract separately. We compile the program in a Linux environment and then launch gdb:

I have gdb-peda installed, which makes the display much nicer; for installation see this article.

When the program reaches func_ptr = &add;, GDB pauses execution. From the assembly above you can see:

The lea instruction computes a memory address. Here RAX will be set to an address based on an offset from RIP. This offset is used to load the address of the add function into RAX, which can later be used to call add.

So at this point we can check what’s in the RAX register at the top. RAX is given the address of the add function, which means the function pointer is being initialized.

Let’s see what the next line executes:

This line stores the value in rax into the address at base pointer minus 0x8, which should be the location of the function pointer.

Then we move to the next instruction, which we can trace with the s command (line 17):

Now we can check func_ptr‘s value to see whether it points to the add function’s address, and the result clearly does point to the add function’s memory address:

Then we can run r to continue to the next breakpoint, where the function pointer is assigned to the subtract function.

Single-stepping all the way to the func_ptr = &subtract; line, then print func_ptr:

Again you can see this instruction:

This also loads the subtract function’s address into RAX. We can type n to see the next instruction:

This line does the same as before, storing the value in rax into the function pointer’s location.

Then we move to the next instruction, tracing line 22 with n, where the function finishes and prints the result.

At this point we can also check whether the function pointer points to the subtract function’s memory address.

The answer is yes again. If we run to int result1 = func_ptr(10, 5);, we can also observe how the registers change. If the display is too cluttered, you can view register state with the command below. RIP is the next CPU instruction to execute, and RSP is the stack pointer representing the top of the current stack frame, so these two registers reveal the flow during a function call:

These are rip and rsp before entering add:

And these are rip and rsp after entering add:

You can see the stack differs by about 2 bytes, which can also be seen in the stack view:

Before entering add:

After entering add:

Those 2 bytes include the return address back to main, 0x55555555521e. We then continue with s until we jump back into main, and from the code section you can see we’re at the instruction address right after the previous function’s return address, 0x555555555221.

Finally, print result1 to check the result:

which is 15.

This experiment gave me a better understanding of function pointers and the memory changes during a function call.

Clarifying the concepts

In C/C++, where a pointer variable’s memory address lives depends on how it’s declared:

  • If the pointer is a local variable declared inside a function, like int *ptr;, the pointer itself is stored on the stack.
  • If the pointer refers to a dynamically-allocated block, like int *ptr = new int, the pointer itself is still on the stack or global area, but the object it points to is on the heap.
  • If the declared pointer is global, it’s stored in the global/static area; a static variable like static int* ptr works the same way.
  • The pointer itself is never stored in the code area, but a function pointer points to a function’s entry point in the code area.
    • For void (*func_ptr)() = &myFunction;, the value stored in this pointer (the function address) is in the code section, while the pointer itself is still on the stack or in the global/static area.

Closing

I now understand the memory behavior corresponding to function pointers better. Given the chance, I’ll later actually implement a function table using function pointers.

entry.title: FreeRTOS_Note
entry.content:
AWS FreeRTOS

FreeRTOS includes libraries for connectivity, security, and over-the-air (OTA) updates. FreeRTOS also includes demo applications that show FreeRTOS features on qualified boards.

FreeRTOS is an open-source project. You can download the source code, contribute changes or enhancements, or report issues on the GitHub site at https://github.com/FreeRTOS/FreeRTOS.

FreeRTOS - Architecture

FreeRTOS contains two types of repositories

  • single library repositories
    • Each single library repository contains the source code for one library without any build projects or examples.
  • package repositories
    • Package repositories contain multiple libraries, and can contain preconfigured projects that demonstrate the library’s use.

FreeRTOS Kernel concepts

The FreeRTOS kernel is a real-time operating system that supports numerous architectures.

Basic components including:

  • A multitasking scheduler.
  • Multiple memory allocation options (including the ability to create completely statically-allocated systems).
  • Intertask coordination primitives, including task notifications, message queues, multiple types of semaphore, and stream and message buffers.
  • upport for symmetric multiprocessing (SMP) on multi-core microcontrollers.

No malloc() but pvPortMalloc

When RTOS objects are created dynamically, using the standard C library malloc() and free() functions is not always appropriate for a number of reasons:

  • They might not be available on embedded systems.
  • They take up valuable code space.
  • They are not typically thread-safe.
  • They are not deterministic.
  • For these reasons, FreeRTOS keeps the memory allocation API in its portable layer.

entry.content:
Intro - What is AWS IoT Device Shadow?

In real world, sometime it is difficult to get the actual device state in real time in such IoT scenarios.

A device shadow can overcome this challenge, Device Shadow can consider a virtual virtual representation of a device which managed by the IoT Things resource created in AWS IoT Core.

The Shadow document is a JSON or a JavaScript notation doc that is used to store and retrieve the current state information for a device. You can use the shadow to get and set the state of a device over MQTT topics or HTTP REST APIs, regardless of whether the device is connected to the internet.

Shadow Document

Refer to the json above, you can check there 3 state properties in shadow document.

  • desired
    • Apps specify the desired states of device properties by updating the desired object
  • reported
    • Devices report their current state in the reported object.
  • delta
    • AWS IoT reports differences between the desired and the reported state in the delta object.

You can consider the flow of Shadow a finite state machine, for AWS IoT Core, it will also check if there are delta event, that means there difference between Desired and Reported states

So how can we update the state of a shadow? The answer is clear,

By subscribing/publishing messages to the certain MQTT topics

Shadow Topic

ShadowTopicPrefix valueShadow type
$aws/things/thingName/shadowUnnamed (classic) shadow
$aws/things/thingName/shadow/name/shadowNameNamed shadow
TopicClient operations allowed
ShadowTopicPrefix/deletePublish/Subscribe
ShadowTopicPrefix/delete/acceptedSubscribe
ShadowTopicPrefix/delete/rejectedSubscribe
ShadowTopicPrefix/getPublish/Subscribe
ShadowTopicPrefix/get/acceptedPublish/Subscribe
ShadowTopicPrefix/get/rejectedSubscribe
ShadowTopicPrefix/updatePublish/Subscribe
ShadowTopicPrefix/update/acceptedSubscribe
ShadowTopicPrefix/update/rejectedSubscribe
ShadowTopicPrefix/update/deltaSubscribe
ShadowTopicPrefix/update/documentsSubscribe

For detail explanation about these shadow topics, see the documentation - https://docs.aws.amazon.com/zh_tw/iot/latest/developerguide/device-shadow-mqtt.html

The state changes of Device Shadow

Take this picture for example, the update flow is:

  1. The MQTT client publishes a $aws/things/myLightBulb/shadow/update message to the server. The message carries the desired state {"state": {"desired":{"color":"green"}}}
  2. IoT Server responds with $aws/things/myLightBulb/shadow/accepted, indicating that the update message has been received. At the same time, it publishes $aws/things/myLightBulb/shadow/delta to notify the device to update, and then publishes $aws/things/myLightBulb/shadow/update/document as update record
  3. After receiving the message, the Device performs the corresponding update operation and publishes a message $aws/things/myLightBulb/shadow/update {"state"{"report":{"color":"green"}}} to the IoT Server after completion. Notification updated
  4. After receiving the post-update message, IoT Server responds with $aws/things/myLightBulb/shadow/accepted to indicate that the update message has been received. Publish another $aws/things/myLightBulb/shadow/update/document as an update record

What is Amazon SQS?

By official definition

Amazon SQS is a message queue service used by distributed applications to exchange messages through a polling model, and can be used to decouple sending and receiving components—without requiring each component to be concurrently available.

Scenario

The Fanout scenario is when a message published to an SNS topic is replicated and pushed to multiple endpoints, such as Kinesis Data Firehose delivery streams, Amazon SQS queues, HTTP(S) endpoints, and Lambda functions. This allows for parallel asynchronous processing.
For example, you can develop an application that publishes a message to an SNS topic whenever an order is placed for a product. Then, SQS queues that are subscribed to the SNS topic receive identical notifications for the new order. An Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2) server instance attached to one of the SQS queues can handle the processing or fulfillment of the order. entry.title: AWS Lambda Notes: Provisioned Concurrency and Reserved Concurrency
entry.content:
🌐 中文版：繁體中文

Recap

Earlier I covered a basic intro to Lambda, Lambda runtimes, permission configuration, and observing initialization time and function execution time from the logs.

At the end I left one question:

What happens if we use the AWS CLI to invoke the function, opening three terminal tabs to invoke our Lambda at the same time?

Experiment 1: setting Reserved Concurrency

We run this command:

They all actually succeed, producing three log streams in CloudWatch.

But if we tweak something, setting Reserved Concurrency to 1 and clicking save, then rerun the CLI invocation, let’s see what happens.

Now only one request returns 200; the rest are throttled, returning a TooManyRequestsException error message:

This brings us to Lambda’s mechanism for handling large volumes of simultaneous requests.

First, what is Reserved Concurrency? And what is Unreserved Concurrency?

Reserved Concurrency

Concurrency means multiple requests at the same time. To handle these simultaneous requests, a Lambda function scales automatically. The nice thing about serverless is that you don’t have to think about how to configure scaling for Lambda, like setting up auto-scaling.

In Lambda, for a single function, the user only needs to consider “how many instances do you need to reserve for this Lambda function at any time?“

That’s when you can consider setting Reserved Concurrency for your function.

Reserved Concurrency is the maximum number of concurrent instances allocated to a function. When a function has Reserved Concurrency, no other function can use that concurrency.

If you set Reserved Concurrency to 1 in the Lambda console, 1 is deducted from Unreserved Concurrency.

This setting is a regional limit. If you set Reserved Concurrency to 100 for a function, the remaining 900 is shared by other functions in the region.

How much concurrency can you reserve for a function?

The answer is UnreservedConcurrency - 100 concurrency.

That is, a function can’t monopolize all concurrency for itself; at least 100 concurrency is left for other functions to share.

How do you decide how much concurrency to reserve for your function?

You can decide by observing the CloudWatch metric ConcurrentExecutions [1]. This metric shows the number of concurrent requests to your function across different time periods in a day. If this function receives at most 30 requests at once per day and the function is important to you, you can consider reserving 30 Lambda instances to handle requests.

Also worth mentioning: setting Reserved Concurrency for a function is free.

Provisioned Concurrency

Some might wonder: if the function scales with requests, then starting a new execution environment introduces latency for time-sensitive requests, right?

Image source: AWS official docs

That thinking is correct; see number 4 in the figure above, which is exactly this situation.

It means 3 execution environments are handling 3 requests, but when the 4th request comes in, a new Lambda execution environment must be initialized. That inevitably introduces latency, waiting for the runtime to start, the Lambda code and dependencies to download, and the code outside the handler to run (if any).

The point of Provisioned Concurrency is “pre-initializing multiple environment instances for a function to help reduce cold-start latency”.

Cold start latency is the uncontrollable delay while the Lambda execution environment is starting and loading (not including Function Init, the initialization time for code outside the handler). I’ll cover this part later.

Back to Provisioned Concurrency: if it’s set, the figure looks more like the one below.

Suppose Provisioned Concurrency is set to 4. Then four Lambda execution environments are initialized from the start, and subsequent requests reuse those four. This guarantees four initialized Lambda environments always exist, which suits time-sensitive requests so they don’t take the initialization delay hit.

So how do you set Provisioned Concurrency? [2]

Note: setting Provisioned Concurrency for a function costs money.

Experiment 2: setting Provisioned Concurrency

There’s a prerequisite before setting Provisioned Concurrency: publishing a version of your function.

Every function defaults to $LATEST before a version is published, but Provisioned Concurrency can’t be set on the $LATEST version; that’s a limitation.

First find Publish new version under Version on the main page.

Then fill in this version’s description and click Publish.

It redirects to the Version 1 Lambda console (slightly different from the $LATEST console). Now you should see the Provisioned Concurrency configuration screen; click it to set concurrency for Version 1.

Below, enter the number of Lambda concurrency instances you want to keep in a warm-start state.
Notice “10 available”. Where does this number come from?

That number is actually your function’s Reserved Concurrency count.

Go back to the $LATEST version console.

Below you can see our setting is 10.

So the amount of Provisioned Concurrency we can set depends on the Reserved Concurrency set for that function.

Here we set Provisioned Concurrency to 5.

It takes some time to build the concurrency.

Then let’s test the configured Provisioned Concurrency.

First, here’s the test code (in the Version 1 function):

We trigger the Lambda function via the AWS CLI:

The --qualifier parameter takes a version name or alias name.

Before actually triggering it, pause and observe the invocation logs in CloudWatch.

You’ll find multiple execution environments have already warmed up.

Why the count exceeds the Provisioned Concurrency number isn’t confirmed.
Maybe for availability?

After opening multiple terminals to send requests, you’ll find the same thing: because the execution environments are already warm, there’s no need to re-init, and requests run on existing environments via container reuse.

Reserved Concurrency vs. Provisioned Concurrency

Image source: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/zh_tw/lambda/latest/dg/lambda-concurrency.html#reserved-and-provisioned

Here’s an official comparison figure explaining the difference between these two kinds of concurrency.

Below is my summary of the difference:

RC (Reserved Concurrency)PC (Provisioned Concurrency)
Cost:FreeCosts money
Characteristic:Ensures a certain number of Lambda execution environments existEnsures a certain number of Lambda execution environments exist, with a certain number already initialized
Reaction at limitThrottled TooManyRequestIf RC quota remains, scales up the environment count, but still with cold starts; if no quota, throttled

Also see the official comparison table [3].

Burst Concurrency

Burst Concurrency also aims to handle sudden spikes in requests.

But facing a sudden surge of many requests, Lambda may not be able to scale up immediately, in order to prevent the function from over-scaling and consuming too many resources.

So to match the function’s surge rate, you can set Burst Concurrency to increase the maximum rate at which Lambda execution environments are created. This is an account-level setting.

The Burst Concurrency limit differs by region:

  • us-west-2, us-east-1, and eu-west-1 are generally capped at 3000
  • ap-northeast-1, eu-central-1, and us-east-2 are capped at 1000
  • Other regions are 500

Taking us-east-1 as an example, Burst Concurrency scales 500 units per minute (additional Lambda execution environments) until demand is met or the 3000 cap is reached.

Requests exceeding the limit are throttled (status code 429).

If interested, see the official docs on Burst Concurrency [5].

Cold Start

What does Lambda do during the Init phase?

  • When the Lambda service receives a request to start a Lambda function via the Lambda API, the service itself downloads the function code.
  • This code is stored in Lambda’s internal S3 bucket.
  • If the function is built as a container, the function code is stored in Amazon ECR.
  • It then builds an environment with the specified memory size and runtime.
  • It then runs the initialization code outside the function handler.

Per [4], all the steps above except running the function’s init code fall within the cold-start range. Running the code outside the handler counts as warm start, which is the part we can control.

How can a function stay “warm”?

The official docs explain it via a pinging mechanism. The main approach is setting an EventBridge rule to invoke the function once a minute to keep the execution environment active.

The currently-recommended way to mitigate cold starts is still Provisioned Concurrency.
There’s also SnapStart, which I’ll cover later.

References

[1] https://docs.aws.amazon.com/zh_tw/lambda/latest/dg/configuration-concurrency.html#estimating-reserved-concurrency
[2] https://docs.aws.amazon.com/zh_tw/lambda/latest/dg/provisioned-concurrency.html
[3] https://docs.aws.amazon.com/zh_tw/lambda/latest/dg/lambda-concurrency.html#comparing-reserved-provisioned
[4] https://docs.aws.amazon.com/zh_tw/lambda/latest/operatorguide/execution-environments.html#cold-start-latency
[5]https://docs.aws.amazon.com/zh_tw/lambda/latest/dg/burst-concurrency.html

entry.title: Getting to Know Lambda, feat. a Small Container-Reuse Experiment
entry.content:
🌐 中文版：繁體中文

Preface

First off, why does serverless always come up alongside Lambda?

Let me introduce this service.

FaaS (Function as a Service)

Once you talk about serverless computing, its core concept comes up: Function as a Service (FaaS). Here’s Wikipedia’s explanation of FaaS:

FaaS is a cloud computing model. Built on Platform as a Service (PaaS), serverless computing provides a micro-architecture where the end customer doesn’t need to deploy, configure, or manage server services; the server services needed to run the code are all provided by the cloud platform.

Right, the core of this concept is letting users focus on designing products or business logic without worrying about deploying, configuring, or setting up servers.

The first to put this concept into practice and launch a service was AWS’s Lambda, released in 2014. (Microsoft’s Azure Functions followed, of course.)

Lambda functions

Lambda runs your code on high-availability compute infrastructure and performs all administration of the compute resources, including server and operating system maintenance, capacity provisioning and automatic scaling, and logging. With Lambda, all you need to do is supply your code in one of the language runtimes that Lambda supports [1]. [name=AWS Documents]

Behaviorally it’s basically the figure below. There’s some upstream trigger, usually a service that invokes the Lambda function, or a manual invocation via the AWS CLI. After Lambda finishes running the function, it returns the result to the original service and can forward to a downstream destination, which is usually another service.

Now suppose you’re a beginner just getting into Lambda. You might be eager to open the Console, use the sample code (or, for some people, delete the sample without reading it and just paste in your local code), test the Lambda function with the default event, and then find it doesn’t work.

Don’t rush. Before diving in, it’s best to have a concept of the Lambda runtime and Lambda program model.

Basic specs

  • RAM
  • Storage

Configuration, RAM

RAM is proportional to CPU processing power, so raising RAM also raises CPU processing speed.
128MB to 3008MB

Reference:
https://koding.work/aws-lambda-performance-is-related-to-memory-size/

Lambda Runtimes

Lambda supports development in multiple programming languages via runtimes. Each major programming language version has its own runtime. These runtimes provide the basic language libraries and execution environment.

Mainstream languages have officially-supported runtimes, like NodeJS, Python, Java, Go, Ruby, and so on, and you can also define a custom runtime. For example a C++ runtime; the official docs provide a GitHub repo and a post on how to use such custom runtimes [3].

I’ve defined a Perl runtime myself, but you’ll need to write your own images. :(

Also, Lambda runtimes are all developed on Amazon Linux. So if you need a custom runtime, it’s generally recommended to spin up a t2.micro EC2 (choosing an Amazon Linux AMI) and build the runtime there.

Lambda programming model

The programming model Lambda provides is common across all runtimes. It defines a handler to process incoming events. This approach essentially tells Lambda the function’s entry point. The runtime passes an object containing the invocation event and context into the handler, such as the function name and request ID.

If you create functions with different runtimes, you should see handlers in different languages in the console’s code block.

Handler (Python) [4]

Handler (Java17)

Handler (Go)

And so on.

Also, although a freshly-created Lambda only has the single Lambda-Handler file, you can actually access the /tmp directory in the Lambda execution environment. Each execution environment provides 512 MB to 10,240 MB of disk space in /tmp, in 1 MB increments [5]. I’ll get into the specifics when I cover the Lambda execution environment lifecycle.

Permissions

In Lambda, operations are performed on behalf of the source service mainly through an execution role.

So what is a Lambda execution role?

A Lambda function’s execution role is an AWS IAM role that grants the function permission to access AWS services and resources. For example, you can create an execution role that has permission to send logs to Amazon CloudWatch and upload trace data to AWS X-Ray. This page provides information on how to create, view, and manage a Lambda function’s execution role [6].

The biggest difference between an execution role and a regular role is that when the function is invoked, Lambda automatically provides your function with temporary credentials by assuming this role. The developer doesn’t have to call sts:AssumeRole in the function code.

The necessary setup for this is the role’s trust policy, which must specify the Lambda service as a trusted principal:

Once you have the execution role, you can attach policies to it, either AWS-managed policies or your own.

Of course, if you choose “Create a new role with basic Lambda permissions” when creating the Lambda, it creates a role with the LambdaBasicExecutionRole policy.

This policy basically grants the Lambda function the ability to create a log group, create log streams within it, and write logs.

When the Lambda is invoked, a log group containing the Lambda name is created in CloudWatch. If my Lambda is named TestInvocations, the log group name is /aws/lambda/TestInvocations.

And underneath will be the corresponding log stream.

There’s something interesting here: each time you change the function or make a configuration adjustment (e.g. changing the timeout), the next invocation produces a new log stream.

That’s because each new configuration needs to be applied to a new sandbox, which reinitializes a new Lambda execution environment.

If you open a log stream, you’ll find every invocation comes with different messages:

  • START
  • (Print Output, if there are any)
  • END
  • REPORT

The span from Start to End is when Lambda is executing, and the timestamp difference for this span is bounded by your Lambda timeout setting. Let’s do a small experiment on this.

Experiment 1: Lambda timeout

Create a Lambda function named TestInvocation, choosing Python3.11 for the runtime and keeping default permissions. Then edit the code under the Code section of the Lambda console.

After creation, you get an empty Lambda handler. Here we import time and add a 3-second delay inside the handler. Then click Test; there’s a test JSON event you can use directly.

After testing, go to the Monitor page and click “View CloudWatch logs”.

This jumps to the corresponding log group in CloudWatch. Click the newest log stream by timestamp to observe the result.

You can see there’s a 3-second gap between Start and End, with “sleep for 3 seconds” printed.

Sharp eyes will notice one log entry shows “Task timed out after 3 seconds”. That’s because a freshly-created Lambda function has a default timeout of 3 seconds. You can change this under “Configuration” in the Lambda console.

The maximum timeout is 15 minutes. So let’s set 15 minutes and change the handler’s delay to about 14 minutes to test.

This is a hard limit, meaning you can’t open a support case to raise the quota [8].

After waiting 14 minutes, the logs confirm it did run for 14 minutes.

One thing not mentioned in the earlier log screenshots is INIT_START, the initialization phase that occurs every time an execution environment is initialized. The initialization phase includes Extension Init, Runtime Init, and Function Init [7].


image from AWS official docs

The first two init phases are more about building the execution environment, starting the runtime, downloading the deployment package into the environment, and so on. But at the Function Init phase, one more thing happens: it runs code outside the Lambda handler.

Here, outside the handler:

That’s a bit vague. Suppose you declare a global variable outside the handler, or initialize a DB connection outside the handler. These are well-suited to doing outside the handler, run during the span from Init-Start to Start, and as long as the same execution environment keeps being used, whatever Function Init does runs only once. This brings us to a Lambda characteristic called container reuse.

Experiment 2: a Lambda characteristic, container reuse

First, container reuse requires noting that a Lambda execution environment is a container. An ordinary Docker-like container environment tears the container down once execution finishes, but in Lambda’s use case it isn’t suitable to shut the environment down after every execution. Instead it keeps waiting for the next invocation request.

You can observe this characteristic in the logs. If you invoke the Lambda three times in a row on the Lambda page, you’ll see the subsequent invocation requests all appear in the same log stream, following after the previous invocation’s logs.

In other words, for the same Lambda execution environment, Lambda finishes one execution and goes straight on to the next request, meaning the same Lambda sandbox can be reused.

If you’re interested in Lambda container reuse, check out this official blog:

Understanding Container Reuse in AWS Lambda
https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/compute/container-reuse-in-lambda/

Here’s another interesting point: if you invoke using the Lambda console’s Test button, it waits for execution to finish before letting you click Test again.

What happens if we use the AWS CLI to invoke the function, opening three terminal tabs to invoke our Lambda at the same time?

Other key concepts

  • Lambda execution environment
  • Cold start
  • Lambda deployment package
  • Lambda synchronous / asynchronous invocation
  • Lambda networking

References

[1] https://docs.aws.amazon.com/zh_tw/lambda/latest/dg/welcome.html
[2] https://docs.aws.amazon.com/zh_tw/lambda/latest/dg/lambda-runtimes.html
[3] https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/compute/introducing-the-c-lambda-runtime/
[4] https://docs.aws.amazon.com/zh_tw/lambda/latest/dg/python-handler.html
[5] https://docs.aws.amazon.com/zh_tw/lambda/latest/dg/lambda-runtime-environment.html
[6] https://docs.aws.amazon.com/zh_tw/lambda/latest/dg/lambda-intro-execution-role.html
[7] https://docs.aws.amazon.com/zh_tw/lambda/latest/dg/lambda-runtime-environment.html#runtimes-lifecycle
[8] https://docs.aws.amazon.com/zh_tw/lambda/latest/dg/gettingstarted-limits.html#function-configuration-deployment-and-execution
