Preface

In today’s business environment, providing high-quality, efficient customer service is one of the keys to success. Amazon Connect is a powerful cloud contact center that helps businesses easily build highly reliable contact centers and interact seamlessly with customers. This post will walk you step by step through integrating a Lambda function into Amazon Connect to achieve more custom functionality.

We’ll follow these steps to do the integration:

Step 1: Create a Connect instance

First, we’ll create a Connect instance in the Amazon Connect console.

In the Amazon Connect console, choose Add Instance. This step requires setting your instance-alias, which creates a unique access URL for your Connect instance.

This step adds an admin; you’ll need to set a username and password.

For the remaining steps just click Next, and finally create the instance.

Creation takes a while, so you can create the Lambda function in the meantime.

Step 2: Create a Lambda function

Go to the Lambda console and choose to create a Lambda function. Our Lambda’s region is the same as the Connect instance’s region, both us-east-1.

Choose Author from Scratch, name the function TestConnect, and choose Python 3.11 for the runtime. Keep everything else default, then create the function.

After creation, modify the Lambda code, adding a line in your handler.

Then click deploy.

Step 3: Add Flows to Amazon Connect

In this step, we’ll add Flows to the Connect instance. We’ll use the Lambda function just created, letting Amazon Connect invoke it in certain situations.

Go to the Connect instance you just created and click Flows in the left navigation.

Scroll down to AWS Lambda, choose the Lambda name you just created, then click Add Lambda Function.

Step 4: Configure contact flows

In this step, we’ll configure contact flows so Amazon Connect triggers the Lambda function and performs custom actions in certain situations. We’ll set a voice prompt and the action taken when the Lambda function is triggered.

Open the access URL of the Connect instance you just created.

A screen like this appears.

In the left panel, find Routing and choose Flows.

Open it and choose Create Flow.

The first step is to enter a name for your flow; here I called it TestConnect-LambdaFlow. At first only an Entry appears on the canvas. Search for Lambda Invoke in the left search bar, and an Invoke AWS Lambda function block appears; drag it onto the center canvas. Click the dots in the top-right of Invoke AWS Lambda function and choose edit setting; an edit window appears on the right, where you enter the ARN of the Lambda function you created, then click Save.

Then search for Play Prompt in the left search bar and drag it onto the center canvas, again clicking the top-right dots and choosing edit setting.

Choose the Text-to-speech or chat text option, and below enter the message shown when the customer first joins the chat. Here I entered:

Hi there, this flow section will try to invoke Lambda function.

Click Save when done.

Then search for Disconnect under Terminate in the left search bar and drag it onto the center canvas.

Finally connect all the block arrows; the overall flow looks like the figure below.

The Lambda function is invoked whether it succeeds or not, but the prompt is only triggered on success; on failure it disconnects directly, and a failed Lambda invocation also disconnects directly.

Finally click Save, then Publish.

Be sure to click Publish; if you don’t, your configured flow won’t appear on the dashboard.

Step 5: Test the chat

Once everything is configured, we’ll test. Through a simulated chat interface, we’ll check whether the Lambda function is triggered successfully and verify the integration works as expected.

Click the icon that looks a bit like the Windows logo at the top of the left panel, choose Dashboard, and return to the main screen.

Click Test Chat, and the Test Chat page appears; click Test Settings in the top left.

A settings menu appears; under Contact Flow choose the flow you just created, then click Apply.

After clicking Apply, a simulated chat interface appears showing the customer joining the chat. Since our setting always disconnects regardless, we can go back to the Lambda page to check whether the function was triggered.

Step 6: Check the logs

Finally, we’ll check the Lambda function’s logs to confirm it was invoked correctly and ensure the integration’s reliability.

Back in the Lambda console, click View CloudWatch logs.

Open the newest log stream and you’ll find the string Invoke Success!, confirming our Lambda was invoked successfully.

Conclusion

Through this post, you’ve learned how to integrate the customer-service flow using Amazon Connect and a Lambda function, and achieve custom customer interactions. Let’s take this integration journey together!

entry.title: ⚙️Configuring Error Retries on Lambda
entry.content:
🌐 中文版：繁體中文

Preface

This is another problem I ran into while solving a case, but I’d never actually configured retries on Lambda, so in the spirit of experimentation I tried it out in my own environment.

Error retries in Lambda are usually for re-sending an invocation request after an asynchronous invocation fails. For asynchronous invocations, Lambda places the event in a queue and returns a success response containing no other information. A separate process reads events from the queue and delivers them to your function.

The diagram was made with ZenUML
https://app.zenuml.com/
https://mermaid.js.org/syntax/zenuml.html

Creating the Lambda

Creating the Lambda is simple: create a function named TestInvocations using the NodeJS.14.x runtime.

Modifying the Lambda handler code

Edit the code under the Code section of the Lambda console main page, changing index.js:

Once edited, click deploy to upload the modified code.

Configuring retries

In the Lambda console main page, go to the Configuration tab, select Asynchronous Invocation, then Edit.

Retry attempts can be set to at most 2. When your Lambda function errors after receiving an asynchronous invocation, it retries twice and then the event is discarded. You can additionally configure a Dead Letter Queue (DLQ) to store the discarded events for later processing.

For details, see the official docs: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/zh_tw/lambda/latest/dg/invocation-async.html#invocation-dlq

Triggering the Lambda

We can invoke the Lambda function via the AWS CLI.

If you haven’t set up the AWS CLI, see this doc to configure it >> https://aws.amazon.com/cli/

Here --invocation-type is set to Event, meaning you’re invoking the Lambda asynchronously.

It then returns status code 202, meaning your request has been accepted by Lambda but won’t be processed immediately (since it’s asynchronous).

Reference:
https://docs.aws.amazon.com/zh_tw/lambda/latest/dg/API_Invoke.html

For Lambda synchronous and asynchronous invocation, see the corresponding official docs:
https://docs.aws.amazon.com/zh_tw/lambda/latest/dg/invocation-async.html
https://docs.aws.amazon.com/zh_tw/lambda/latest/dg/invocation-sync.html
As for their architectural differences, I can write a separate post to organize that later!

Observing the results

Go to the Monitor tab in the Lambda console and click View CloudWatch logs, which opens the CloudWatch Logs main page.


Each time you create a Lambda, its execution role is given a policy named AWSBasicExecutionRole by default, which includes permission to create CloudWatch log groups and CloudWatch logs, and creates a log group named /aws/lambda/<your Lambda name>. Under this log group are many log streams, and a new log stream is created each time you change your Lambda function and re-trigger it.

Select the newest log stream and you’ll find three invocations: the first is the one we triggered, and the second and third are the retries we configured.

Trigger request 1

Retry 1

Retry 2

Here you can observe that the logs after invocation show the error message, with the first retry one minute after the first failed request, and the second retry two minutes after the first retry fails, after which it doesn’t retry again. You can also see that the request ID on retry is the same as the original, which you could probably use to judge whether an invocation is a retry and whether the event has already been processed.

Conclusion

When developing Lambda code and doing related configuration, always pay attention to the invocation type and its corresponding settings, so you don’t mix them up unknowingly.

References

https://azole.medium.com/aws-lambda-reuse-and-retry-behavior-ffaac616d869
https://docs.aws.amazon.com/zh_tw/lambda/latest/dg/invocation-retries.html

entry.title: 🗃️Deep Dive: How the malloc Function Allocates Memory
entry.content:
🌐 中文版：繁體中文

Deep Dive: How does the malloc function allocate memory?

Preface

Dynamic memory allocation is an important concept. It lets a program allocate and free memory dynamically as needed during execution, rather than relying on statically-allocated blocks set up in advance. This flexibility lets a program use memory resources more efficiently and handle problems of various sizes and complexities.

C’s malloc function is a widely-used dynamic memory allocator. It lets programmers dynamically allocate memory blocks of a specified size at runtime. An important property of malloc is that it ensures the allocated block is valid and accessible while in use, while freeing it appropriately to avoid memory leaks.

But you might be curious how malloc implements allocation at a low level, and how it accurately allocates the freed-up memory to the caller. That’s the topic we’ll dig into here. We’ll focus on malloc’s low-level implementation, especially how the system decides on and allocates a suitable memory address for us when we call malloc.

Before exploring this, let’s review the basics of dynamic memory allocation. In C, we can use malloc to allocate memory dynamically. Its prototype is:

malloc takes a positive integer size, representing the size (in bytes) of the block we want to allocate. It tries to find a contiguous block large enough and marks it as allocated. If it finds a suitable block, malloc returns a pointer to the start of that block; otherwise it returns NULL to indicate failure.

Although malloc looks relatively simple, its low-level implementation is a complex task. Different operating systems and compilers may use different algorithms and strategies to perform memory allocation. So we’ll dig into these internal mechanisms to understand how malloc allocates memory, and discuss the trade-offs and performance implications.

Next, we’ll enter the low-level world of malloc and lift the veil behind it. We’ll look at several common memory allocation algorithms, including fixed partitioning, dynamic partitioning, and paging. These algorithms will help us understand how malloc works and how to optimize memory usage performance.

With this question, we can dig into the principles.

How memory is allocated

Memory allocation in an operating system is mainly implemented by a memory allocator. In the early days, glibc’s default allocator was dlmalloc.

But dlmalloc has a problem: once multiple threads call malloc, only one thread can enter the critical section. The improvement to this is ptmalloc2, forked from dlmalloc: once multiple threads call malloc, memory is allocated to each thread immediately.

Since memory allocation fundamentally happens across multiple threads, dlmalloc easily causes poor performance. In ptmalloc2, when multiple threads call malloc at the same time, memory is allocated immediately, because each thread maintains its own separate heap segment, and the freelist data structure maintaining each heap segment is also independent.

This behavior of maintaining per-thread freelist structures and heap segments is called a per-thread arena.

Compile and run:

We can check the process’s memory allocation by PID.
Per the program output above, its PID is 74:

You can see the heap segment is:

After calling malloc, check the memory allocation again:

We find that after freeing, the allocated memory isn’t released immediately. It’s first returned to the glibc malloc library, and the freed block (chunk) is added to the main arena’s bin (in glibc malloc, the freelist is called a bin). Then if the user requests a new block, malloc won’t ask the kernel for new memory but instead looks for a free chunk in the bin; only if the bin has no available chunk does it ask the kernel again.

entry.title: 📑GitHub Actions Study Notes
entry.content:
🌐 中文版：繁體中文

I didn’t actually have CI/CD experience before, so I wasn’t too familiar with the common CI/CD platforms out there. But recently, due to a project need, I had to use GitHub Actions to build a CI/CD pipeline for a BreakSentence API in Azure Cognitive Services. With the delivered requirements still vague 😭, I figured I’d first understand this feature and make a record.

Basic introduction

GitHub Actions is a CI/CD platform that can automate building, testing, and deployment. Users can create workflows to build and test every pull request to a repository, or deploy merged pull requests to a production environment.

Components

The component terms that make up GitHub Actions are:

  • Workflow
  • Event
  • Jobs
  • Runner
  • Steps
  • Action

First, how these components work together: when some event occurs in a repository, the GitHub Actions workflows you configured are triggered. An event here could be, for example, a pull request or an issue being created, and so on.

The workflow you define contains one or more jobs, which can be processed in parallel or sequentially. Each job runs on its own virtual-machine runner or inside a container. Each job contains one or more steps that run a script you define or some action. An action is the smallest unit in GitHub Actions, a reusable extension, usually some common command (?😥).

🔀Workflows

  • A workflow is one or more jobs configured to automate a process. You define a workflow by writing a YAML file, and it’s triggered when an event occurs, or can be triggered manually.
  • Workflows are defined under the .github/workflows path in the repo.
  • A repo can have multiple workflows responsible for various tasks.
    • For example, one workflow for building and testing
    • And another for deploying the app to production after a release

✴️Events

An event represents a specific activity in a repository, such as:

  • pull request
  • open issues
  • pushes a commit to repo, etc.

For the events that can trigger workflows, see this doc:
https://docs.github.com/en/actions/using-workflows/events-that-trigger-workflows

🗂️Jobs

A set of steps is called a job, and it runs on a runner. Each step may be a shell script or an action that runs. Steps run in order, and since each step runs on the same runner, data can be shared between steps. For example: one step builds the app, then another tests it.

You can also set job dependencies; once one job depends on another, it waits for the other to finish before starting its own task.
https://docs.github.com/en/actions/using-jobs

📑Actions

An action is a program designed specifically for the GitHub Actions platform to perform complex, frequent, and repetitive tasks.
Using actions reduces the amount of repetitive code in workflow files.
An action can do things like pull a repository from GitHub, set up the correct toolset for the build environment, and configure authentication with your cloud provider.

Creating actions: https://docs.github.com/en/actions/creating-actions

📦Runners

A runner is a server that runs a workflow, and each runner runs one job at a time.
GitHub provides Ubuntu, Windows, and macOS runners to run workflows.
There are also solutions for those needing large runners: https://docs.github.com/en/actions/using-github-hosted-runners/using-larger-runners
If the needed environment requires a different OS or special hardware configuration, you can host your own runner: https://docs.github.com/en/actions/hosting-your-own-runners

Creating a workflow

GitHub Actions uses YAML to create workflows. Each workflow is stored in its own YAML file placed under the .github/workflows path.

Creating an example workflow

  • Create the path: .github/workflows
  • Create learn-github-action.yml inside .github/workflows
  • Commit the change and push it to the repository

Workflow file explained line by line

Reference: Workflow Syntax

  • name: specifies the workflow name, which appears in the repository’s Actions tab
  • run-name: the text message shown each time the workflow runs; here it’s the repo username + “is learning GitHub Actions”

  • on: specifies the activity that triggers the workflow; here it uses the push event, so the workflow runs whenever someone pushes a change to the repository
  • jobs: groups the jobs in the workflow together
  • check-bats-version: a custom job name
  • runs-on: sets the job to run on a runner with the latest Ubuntu Linux OS; this specification triggers creation of a hosted virtual machine
  • steps: groups all the steps under the check-bats-version job
  • uses: specifies a step’s command or action
    • actions/checkout@v3: runs the v3 version of the actions/checkout action. This step checks out your repo onto the runner and lets you operate on your code. Whenever your workflow runs against the repository’s code, you should use the checkout action.
    • actions/setup-node@v3: installs the specified version of Node.js (version 14 in this example)
  • run: the run command tells the job to execute a specific command on the runner. In this example it tells the job to run npm install bats on the runner, and the next step checks the bats version

Finding and customizing actions

An action can be defined in:

  • The same repository as your workflow file
  • Any public repository
  • A published container image on DockerHub

GitHub Actions Marketplace

Marketplace link

The Marketplace has many actions provided by other contributors that you can download.

Each action provides the corresponding YAML syntax you can copy and paste into your own workflow file. If an action requires input, you need to configure the workflow additionally; see this doc:
https://docs.github.com/en/actions/learn-github-actions/finding-and-customizing-actions#using-inputs-and-outputs-with-an-action

Adding an action in the same repository

Example file structure

Example workflow file

syntax: ./path/to/dir

And action.yml is for providing metadata for the action.

Adding an action from a different repository

In this case, under uses in your workflow file you specify {owner}/{repo}@{ref} to indicate the referenced action’s repo, e.g. actions/setup-node@v3.

Referencing a container on DockerHub

Here the syntax changes to: docker://{image}:{tag}

entry.title: Buffer Overflow Vulnerability Experiment
entry.content:
Introduction

Buffer Overflow Vulnerability is one of the most common and severe security vulnerabilities in the field of software and system security. In the complex software systems of today’s digital age, the threat from hackers or malicious users is ever-present. Buffer Overflow Vulnerability is one of the most concerning threats among them due to the significant threat it poses to computer systems.

In simple terms, a buffer overflow vulnerability occurs when code attempts to store data in a predefined size of memory block known as a buffer. If the amount of data input exceeds the maximum capacity of the buffer, the excess data will overflow into adjacent memory areas, potentially overwriting instructions or data that control program execution, leading to unexpected behavior.

The fundamental cause of buffer overflow vulnerabilities is negligence and errors in program design. When developers fail to handle user input correctly, especially when they do not perform sufficient validation and restrictions on the input, it may lead to such vulnerabilities. Attackers often exploit these unchecked inputs by sending specially crafted malicious data, triggering buffer overflow attacks. This attack method has been around for many years and has caused numerous serious security incidents throughout history.

In the past, several well-known buffer overflow vulnerabilities have been widely reported, some of which have had profound impacts on global information security. For example, the infamous Code Red and Nimda worms utilized buffer overflow vulnerabilities to rapidly infect tens of thousands of hosts. Similarly, the Slammer worm exploited a buffer overflow vulnerability in Microsoft SQL Server, causing a sudden surge in global internet traffic. These events emphasize the need for the entire tech industry to take buffer overflow vulnerabilities seriously.

SQL Slammer - https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SQL_Slammer

So, this article aims to conduct a simple experiment on buffer overflow vulnerabilities to provide at least a conceptual understanding.

Environment Setup

In terms of environment setup, we use the Windows Subsystem for Linux (WSL) platform to configure the development environment and use Ubuntu 20.04 LTS as the development environment. We will install the necessary tools in this environment, including Python3, Pwntool, and the PEDA plugin for GDB debugging.

WSL provides a feature to run Linux distributions on Windows systems, enabling us to perform Linux-related development work in a Windows environment. Ubuntu 20.04 LTS is a stable and common Linux distribution widely used in development and testing environments.

Before configuring the environment, we need to ensure that WSL is installed and running. Installation instructions for WSL can be found in the Microsoft official documentation or relevant online tutorials.

https://learn.microsoft.com/zh-tw/windows/wsl/install

Next, we need to install Python3 and Pwntool in WSL. Pwntool is a common Python library used in CTFs, specifically designed for exploit development.

Before installing Pwntool, we need to make sure that git is installed in WSL. If not installed, it can be done using the following commands:

Next, we can install Pwntool as follows:

Now we have completed the installation of Python3 and Pwntool in WSL.

Finally, we will configure the GDB DEBUG environment, using the PEDA plugin to assist us in practicing buffer overflow vulnerabilities.

Lastly, here is a simple C program buffer_test.c used as the target for demonstrating the buffer overflow vulnerability. The program includes a uname() function that uses the gets() function to receive user input, but it does not perform sufficient validation on the input, potentially leading to a buffer overflow vulnerability.

buffer_test.c

The program contains the risky input function gets, used for practicing Buffer Overflow.

Experimental Steps

Compile the Program

First, we need to compile the code named buffer_test.c for further experimentation. During compilation, we need to disable the Stack Canary protection mechanism using the following command:

-fno-stack-protector : Disable the Stack Canary protection mechanism.

Check Protective Measures

Before starting the experiment, it is necessary to confirm the security protective measures of the target program. The checksec command can quickly check the relevant security measures of the target executable:

Confirm the Target

Before launching an attack, we need to identify the target. In this experiment, our goal is to execute the target function, so we need to find the memory address of that function and overwrite the function’s return address.

Confirm Function Memory Address

Use GDB to query the memory address of the target function:

From the above image, the starting address of this function is 0x0000000000401196 . Knowing the address of the function, the next step is to understand how to overwrite the ret address from input.

Testing

Before launching an actual attack, let’s run the program in GDB and observe its behavior:

The program will prompt the user to input a name, and after entering the name, it responds with "Hello, {name}". Since the array in the original program that holds user input is only 16 bytes (RBP ~ RBP-16), we can observe its behavior by inputting data exceeding 16 bytes.

As shown in the image, when input exceeds 24 bytes, a buffer overflow occurs, and a crash occurs after the v character. This indicates that we need at least 24 bytes of input to successfully overwrite the function’s return address.

So, it can be covered with 8 Bytes to overwrite the ret address.

RBP shows only up to ‘qrstuvwx’, meaning it crashed when input reached 24 bytes.

Actual Overwriting with Python

為了進行實際的攻擊，將使用 Python 撰寫攻擊腳本。這個腳本將使用 Pwntools 函式庫來進行攻擊，蓋過程式中的函式返回位址，使之執行 target 函式。

To carry out the actual attack, a Python script will be used to overwrite the program’s function return address. This script will use the Pwntools library to perform the attack and execute the target function.

The attack script attack.py is as follows:

In the attack script, the process() function is used to execute the buffer_test program. Then, the recvuntil() function is used to wait for the program to display the prompt “input your name:”, after which the pre-calculated address of the target function is added to the input data. Finally, the interactive() function is used to enter interactive mode to observe the results of the attack.

  • recvuntil(): receive until, can receive a specific string, and execute the xx command when the target string is reached.

  • p8()、p32()、p64()

    • p32: pack data (32-bit integer) for data // u32: unpack
    • p64: pack data (64-bit integer) for data // u64: unpack

Convert to address

  • sendline(payload): send payload and newline
  • interactive()： enter interactive mode, used to execute local or remote executables

Execute the Attack Script

Finally, we run the attack script to perform the attack:

After a successful attack, the program will execute the target function and display the message “Oh No! Your Hacker.” This proves that we have successfully exploited the buffer overflow vulnerability.

Successfully executed the target function!

Remember to ensure compliance with relevant laws and regulations when applying the knowledge gained in real-world environments, and only conduct security testing and exploitation in legally authorized situations.

🌐 中文版：繁體中文

When running an ordinary user account on a Linux system, you sometimes need to run commands that require superuser privileges, such as updating packages or downloading files. But if the ordinary user hasn’t been granted sudo privileges, those commands won’t run. To let an ordinary user use sudo, we need to configure the sudoers file.

This post covers how to configure sudo permissions along with some other interesting account-access settings.

The sudoers config file

On a Linux system, the sudoers config file specifies the sudo privileges for users, groups, or aliases. It’s usually located at /etc/sudoers.

To avoid making a bad change to the sudoers file, we should edit it with the visudo command.

visudo checks for configuration errors when saving, such as bad permissions or syntax problems. Note that the sudoers file should only be edited with visudo; editing it directly with something like vim may hit read-only or write-failure issues, and you’ll see read-only, cannot override.

Open the sudoers file for editing with:

Once it’s open, add new configuration lines below the root line, specifying what privileges to grant which user or group.

Other interesting account-access settings

passwd with the -l flag

The passwd command’s -l flag locks an account’s password. When we lock an account’s password, the system changes the password hash (stored in /etc/shadow) to a value not yet used in the system. A locked password shows a leading exclamation mark (!) in front of the password hash in /etc/passwd. So after locking an account’s password with:

other users won’t be able to switch to the root user via sudo su and similar commands.

We can also change an account’s shell with the chsh command.

The screenshot above shows the output of the passwd command, where the root user’s default shell is /bin/bash. Notice that many others are /usr/sbin/nologin, which means that account cannot log in locally or remotely. So if you change root’s shell to /usr/sbin/nologin, nobody can access the root account.

Those are a few tricks for configuring sudo permissions and changing an account’s shell. With these settings, we can better manage user privileges and security on a Linux system.
